text:
What I proposed months ago is finally happening.
Back in May, I said if elected to the U.S. Senate I would introduce the Nick Shirley Bill to supercharge fraud fighting: reward whistleblowers and investigators with a percentage of the money saved for taxpayers by reporting and stopping Medicare and Medicaid fraud. I also called for limits on how many patients a nurse practitioner can bill in a day so we stop the “impossible day” fraud that drains Medicare.
Today, President Trump announced a Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program that pays people who report fraud against the government. Nick Shirley—the independent journalist whose videos exposed massive childcare fraud in Minnesota—just received the first $10,000 payout. The program offers a share of recovered funds for tips that lead to results, with a $25 million pool and reporting through https://t.co/wsEfQonZGY.
This is the exact direction I laid out. Reward the people who point out the fraud. Stop paying the people who commit it. Protect the Medicare our seniors paid into instead of letting it be looted.
I’ve been saying this because I talk to frontline workers in Horry County and see the waste firsthand. Washington is finally catching up. South Carolina deserves a Senator who was already on it—not one who spent 24 years in DC while the fraud piled up.
One step ahead of quality leadership. That’s the difference.
#NickShirleyBill #StopMedicareFraud #AmericaFirst

text:
A woman offered a flower to U.S. military police guarding the Pentagon on October 21, 1967, during a massive protest against the Vietnam War.

The March on the Pentagon brought tens of thousands of antiwar demonstrators to Washington, D.C., in one of the largest protests against the war at the time.

The antiwar movement combined peaceful symbolism with more confrontational forms of protest. Was offering a flower to an armed soldier a powerful act of resistance, or just a symbolic gesture with little real impact?

Photo: S.Sgt. Albert R. Simpson / U.S. Army, 1967.

text:
Rick, now we're finally getting somewhere. You've abandoned the accusations of treason and the scorched-earth personal attacks and offered an actual political argument.

I welcome that.

But your statement that "Nothing else is important" is precisely where we fundamentally disagree.

Federal judicial appointments are EXTREMELY important. I understand the consequences of Senate control and the importance of confirming judges who respect constitutional limitations.

But Rick, THAT IS ONE PART OF A MUCH LARGER CONSTITUTIONAL REPUBLIC!

What about the national debt?

The continued expansion of federal power?

Congress surrendering its constitutional responsibilities?

The erosion of individual liberty?

The consequences of undeclared wars?

The influence of political donors, consultants, and entrenched power brokers?

The qualifications, independence, and accountability of the people we elect?

Do those things suddenly become irrelevant because one political faction might control judicial confirmations?

Our Constitution established THREE branches of government, Rick. It did not establish the federal judiciary as the sole measure of whether the Republic survives.

You approach this from the perspective of a professional political strategist. I understand why control of the Senate matters enormously to you.

But I approach it from the perspective of a citizen who has watched decades of constitutional deterioration under BOTH political parties.

I refuse to reduce the future of this Republic to a single political calculation.

And here's the deeper question:

WHAT GOOD IS WINNING CONTROL OF THE JUDICIARY IF WE CONTINUE TO TOLERATE THE VERY CONSTITUTIONAL FAILURES THAT MAKE JUDICIAL INTERVENTION NECESSARY?

Judicial appointments matter. So do the laws Congress passes, the wars it authorizes, the money it spends, and the liberties it protects or neglects.

That's not dismissing your concern, Rick. It's recognizing that your concern is part of a much larger picture.

THE CONSTITUTION IS BIGGER THAN THE NEXT JUDICIAL CONFIRMATION.

THE REPUBLIC IS BIGGER THAN THE REPUBLICAN PARTY.

And my oath was to the Constitution, not a faction.

One final observation: You originally called me a traitor for holding a different political judgment. You've now explained the legitimate electoral concern behind that accusation.

Perhaps we can agree that disagreement over Senate control is not treason.

Because if preserving the judiciary requires abandoning constitutional principles everywhere else, we ought to examine what we're actually preserving.

@fitsnews @ThomasRavenel

#SCPolitics #ConstitutionFirst #PrincipleOverParty #PoliticalAccountability

text:
SUPER SECRET RAMBO BOOK EXCERPT: 
UNDER THE SILVER LAKE

A friend asked me to write about Under the Silver Lake. Initially I didn’t think I had much to say about it. But it turns out I do.  

The story reminds me of a time in my life that I’d mostly forgotten and that I’m mostly unable to remember. I was there but it was like a scaryish dream. Not quite a nightmare. Maybe an unhappy dream?

David Robert Mitchell’s Under the Silver Lake (UTSL) is a neo-noir mystery set in 2011 East Side LA. Andrew Garfield plays what I assume is a burned-out young actor. He maybe did a few pilots but they never went to series and his phone stopped ringing. 

At the beginning of the movie, he’s spun into a nihilistic drift. His girlfriend has left him, he can’t pay his rent, and his Mustang is about to be repossessed. He spends his time day drinking, fucking needy actresses (always a mistake!), and he “might” be killing dogs. Then one day he meets a girl at his apartment’s swimming pool. They connect, but she rapidly and mysteriously disappears, plunging him into a rabbit hole of conspiracy and secret messages hidden in pop culture.

*   *   *

My wife and I had sold our West Side house at the peak of the housing bubble and were renting a loft in Downtown LA. 2008 was a busy year, but by 2009 the Great Recession was in full swing. I was out of work for sixteen months straight. And though you don’t realize these things right away, I also had a serious drug problem.

The Hollywood unions have their own health-care system, known as MPI. They have their own clinics, a nursing home, and even used to have a hospital in the Valley (with union-subsidized plastic surgery for fading actors—not joking). Very well-funded, nice facilities, low copays.  

I went to the Westwood clinic. I liked my doctor. He was pragmatic. And he wasn’t stingy when it came to prescribing narcotics. If I had a cold, he’d give me Vicodin so I could “rest and breathe.” Not one or two pills, but a bottle of thirty.

But MPI had weird rules. Wardrobe and production staff were not allowed to receive benzos. Those jobs were too stressful and most people got hooked. You had to go outside of MPI if you wanted that. It was still covered by the plan, but the copays were higher.

Hollywood was stupid permissive. At one production company where I worked there was a floating bottle of random pills. Having a bad day? Someone would give you the bottle: Xanax, Percocet, Dexedrine. It was a stressful job with long hours. Sometimes you worked for horrible people. Sometimes you needed help.  

Everyone understood. Nobody judged.

Coke was frowned upon in my circle (I never really liked it anyway). But booze, pills, and a little weed were socially acceptable.  

So in 2009 I was out of work. With nothing better to do I started training for randonneuring cycling events (ultra-distance cycling). I was hoping to do a 1,200 km. 

Unfortunately, I trained the wrong way. As I later learned, the correct way is to do short rides during the week and do one long ride on the weekends. This way, you gradually increase the length of the big ride every week. Instead I trained by doing sheer milage. I was riding 500+ miles a week and it was too much.  

Rather than being primed for randonneuring season, I ended up with knee and hip problems. I was afraid of surgery, so my doc thought it would be best to give me painkillers.

As advertised, painkillers WORK. They make the pain go away. Then you build a tolerance and need more. Doc supplied, no problem there.  

Funny things can happen, though. While you build tolerance for the pills, you lose tolerance for pain. I would stub my toe and it felt like I was dying. And though it took a while to figure out, I eventually realized I couldn’t tell the difference between pain and withdrawal symptoms. Withdrawal hurts—in a very real physical way.

My wife was then working on a popular TV show, so we had money coming in. Rent was reasonable. No kids at the time. Life was easy. I had no work, couldn’t bike, and was high as fuck. I spent my days walking the dog and hanging at our loft complex’s rooftop pool. At night I’d hit the bars and art parties of East Side LA.  

Wife was working TV-show hours. I barely saw her.

Hollywood eats marriages, as I’ve said. With wife working crazy hours, and me not, certain issues developed. I began living a different life. Hanging out at art parties with art hoes and actresses. Day drinking at bars and cafés. And just like that, I was adrift in LA.

*   *   *

Beautiful women come to LA to be recognized for their beauty and for a shot at fame. They want you to want them. They need you to need them. They’re dangerous.

UTSL has a lot of fun with esoteric messaging and film nerdery. The Easter eggs (the hidden messages embedded in the film) are fantastic. Fireworks are morse code, T-shirts have secrets meanings, and on and on.

Here’s a spoiler: our protagonist discovers that all of pop culture is a construct designed to attract beautiful women to Hollywood so that rich men can be entombed with them for eternity.

*   *   *

I struggle with the question of why this entertainment-industrial complex exists. I’m writing this book partially as a way to work it out for myself. Because when you dig in, it makes no damn sense. Maybe it’s starting to …

I never “dreamed” of working in Hollywood. Both of my parents were in the biz but I wanted nothing to do with it. I wanted to start a construction business. First I dropped out of high school, then I dropped out of college. I became a ski-lift mechanic. Then I started building ski lifts.  

On the job I learned how to do concrete and carpentry. Then I got diabetes and could no longer do physical labor. 

That’s when I fell into The Business, and everything clicked. I was good at the work. Like I was made for it. And I saw opportunity. There was a clear path to advancement, a ladder I could climb. 

And not having dreams of fame really helped. It gave me a clear-eyed view, allowed me to go in without preconceived notions or false expectations. When faced with a reality that conflicts with their core identity, most people go into denial, and some go off the rails entirely.

*   *   *

One of my best friends is an actor. Actually he’s a great comedy actor, which I would argue is the highest form of acting. Good-looking guy, great chops, excellent work ethic. Unfortunately, when he was coming up, he looked exactly like a younger version of Michael Douglas. He’d go to audition after audition and hear, “You’re great, but you look too much like …”  

He had famous director/producer friends, but they could only do so much. He finally had to face the realization that he was never going to make it, and he went off the rails with the three Ds: drink, drugs, divorce.  

He was living in his car for a while.  

But with me, I knew it was bullshit from the start. I figured out very quickly that glamor is highly subjective, and there’s no glamor when you’re on the inside. On my second movie I spent a night in a hotel suite putting drugs up my nose with Oscar-winning actors. It was hands down the most boring night of my life. Famous actors are interesting when they’re talking about acting, but other than that they’re really fucking boring. I never sought that kind of experience again (although it happened from time to time).

Instead I just threw myself into my work. Because I loved the work. I loved (and still love) the process of creating something from nothing.  

I wasn’t the best, and I wasn’t the smartest, but fuck I was a hard worker. I was the hardest worker (I still think this, by the way). Then one day there was no work and I was cast adrift. I didn’t think I’d be famous, but I always thought I’d be useful.  

And then I was no longer useful.

*   *   *

I don’t remember much of that year-plus of unemployment. Though I do remember that I walked the dog a lot. LA is very walkable when you don’t have much to do. I did it in an opiate daze. By the end they were giving me oral morphine. All the morphine I wanted. All that I needed.

I made friends with the dealers and hoes in Downtown LA. They liked my dog and my dog loved them. Never had to buy on the street though.  

Just walking around. Me and the dog and the stink of uselessness.

*   *   *

In UTSL, our protagonist finally finds the girl. She’s been entombed for eternity under the iconic Hollywood Sign. But she’s happy. This is what she’s been working toward: godlike immortality.  

She’s achieved the goal of every beautiful woman who moves to LA. She’s made it. She’s become immortal. She’s met her fate and she accepts it. Now our protagonist has to accept his fate.

*   *   *

I was hiding pills all over the loft. Was terrified that someone would take them. I always had a large supply on my person. But just in case, there were extras in my sock drawer and under the mattress and in the freezer and taped to the lid of the toilet tank. I forget how much I was taking, but I was blitzed all the time.

One day, while I was frantically trying to find my stash, I realized I had a serious fucking problem. It hit me hard: what was I doing?

Working with my doctor I was able to step off the pills over the course of four months. Near the end of my opiate addiction I finally went back to work. Cortisone injections and knee surgery fixed the problem.  

But something was broken inside me. I think I’m still trying to fix it.

After the layoff, I went back to work with more drive than ever. Bigger and better projects. More responsibility and more money. My wife got pregnant. We left LA for flyover country. She stopped working to stay home with the baby. That saved our marriage. That and no more hot girls by the pool.

*   *   *

There’s a dissatisfaction that comes from chasing goals—from striving. You finally get to the place you want to be and discover there’s nothing there. It’s empty.

I used to be into mountaineering. I was a peak bagger. The game is to “bag” (climb) as many peaks as possible. Much of it is technical climbing (with ropes, protection, etc.). It’s hard work. The last time I got to the top of a mountain, I was cold and dead tired. I realized it was freezing and windy and barren at the top of a mountain, nothing but a bunch of rocks, and I wondered why the fuck I was there.  

I stopped climbing after that.

I worked hard in The Business. And I got to the top of what I did. But it was cold and there were a bunch of rocks. I decided to take a different path—same industry, but different capacity. 

I still fear being without purpose—of being adrift. Yet I’m tempted to burn it all down. Because purpose means responsibility, and responsibility can be a prison. I’d prefer to be free.

In UTSL the protagonist feared being homeless. Of being a bum. Of being somebody that no one cared about. But it’s only when he’s finally evicted from his apartment and has lost everything, and has in fact finally become a bum, that he finds happiness.  

I think about that quite a bit. I’ve worked very hard for what I have. But sometimes I wonder if I wouldn’t be better off if I lost it all.  

I mean that in the literal sense. Lose it all. Job, wife, kids, house. All of it.

The temptation to burn it all down is always there. It’s omnipresent. I can’t shake it. 

I’ve been out of LA for over a decade now, living in this beautiful mountain state. Sometimes I find myself driving around our town at night. It’s usually a late-night nicotine run.

I’ll be driving home from the gas station with my nicotine pouches and some great song will come on Spotify and I don’t want to stop driving. Then I wonder how far I can go with the gas I have in the tank.  

Not that it matters. I can always buy more gas when I run out. And when I run out of nicotine pouches, I can get more of those too. So how many days or weeks can I drive? How far can I make it?

Years ago I watched an interview with Beirut hostage Edward Austin Tracy. He was kidnapped by Shiite terrorists and held captive for almost five years. He said he dealt with his years of confinement by taking long imaginary drives.

I do the same thing on my late-night nicotine runs. In my mind I leave our small town and cross the Rockies beneath the starlit, moonless sky. Come dawn, just as the sun is cracking over the horizon, I hit the vastness of the Great Plains, and I just keep going.

Have you ever driven alone through the Plains? Once I was alone in Nebraska’s Oglala Grasslands. I must have been the only person for forty miles. Driving alone on gravel roads over green hills. It was like being alone on the ocean and the grassy hills were like waves. 

The last battles of the Indian Wars were fought here. They killed Crazy Horse here. He was another man who wanted to be free. They offered him a life of comfort, but it was comfort in captivity. He rejected it and tried to escape. So they killed him. 

In my mind I keep driving. Past Oglala, past the Pine Ridge, past the Plains. 

I cross the 100th meridian, near where the Plains end and the eastern forests begin. I cross the giant rivers of the Midwest. I pass through broken ruined former industrial towns. I eat at diners and talk to the truckers. I sleep in the truck and shit at highway rest stops. 

I stop at roadside attractions. I’ve been to some of these places and I return in my imagination. I stop at Wall Drug and take a selfie with the giant jackalope. I stop to see the world’s largest boot in Red Wing, Minnesota. 

Eventually, though, my imagination fails me. Because now I’m driving through places I’ve never been. What are the roads in Upstate New York like? Do they have the tolls where you throw change in a basket?

Can I make it to the edge of the continent? To Maine? To Nova Scotia? Could I really make it to Nova Scotia? I’ve never been to Nova Scotia. I’m not sure how one gets there in a car.

I know I could get there. But I’d burn it all down in the process. Work would wonder where I was. The kids would be devastated. My wife would be beside herself. And then when she figured it out, she’d empty the bank accounts. I have credit, but eventually the finance company would come looking for my truck.  

Would I be free by the time they repo my truck somewhere in Canada?  

Could I make a new life for myself? Find a new purpose? Do I even need a purpose? Isn’t merely existing good enough?

But these questions are moot. Because I never make it out of town. Because I never cross Rockies and head for the Great Plains.

Instead I go home.  

Back to my house and my wife and my kids and the dogs and my job and everything else. Back to everything that keeps me tethered.

This is an excerpt from the book Hollywood Samizdat: Notes From Below the Line.  Link in next post👇

text:
🚨 New episode alert: Dylan Field, the CEO of Figma, on All-In

All-In is the tech and business podcast from Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, David Sacks and David Friedberg. Their latest interview is with Dylan Field, who runs Figma. He talks about the Adobe deal regulators blocked and why he thinks design is the new code.

Top 3 moments from the episode you can't miss 👇

1. 🎨 (20:42) A few years ago he predicted AI would raise the ceiling on what designers can make. He now says he was wrong.
"That was wrong. The ceiling has stayed the same."
In his view AI raises the floor, so anyone can make something decent. The ceiling goes up only when a person chooses to be bold and try what nobody has tried.

2. 💸 (11:14) After regulators blocked Adobe's $20 billion deal to buy Figma, he told his roughly 1,200 employees that anyone who wanted out could leave with a few months of pay.
"if you want to leave here is a few months pay and you're welcome to just let us know we'll make it super easy"
The review had dragged on for 16 months, so he says the mood was mostly relief at finally knowing. Only a small share of people took the offer.

3. 🏷️ (24:59) Figma has one simple rule for writing with AI inside the company: say so at the top.
"if you are using AI in your writing of any kind, just put ... written with AI, very simple, very easy to follow"
People joked about it, he says, but they follow it, and coworkers can trust that a document got enough care to be worth reading.

text:
Heavyweights Arturo Godoy (41-5-4, on the left) and Leroy Haynes (43-10-1) fight to a draw, on October 21, 1936, at the Hippodrome in New York.

Godoy was coming off his stoppage of the comebacking Luis Firpo (it would be Firpo's last fight). Haynes was nearing the end of his fine career and would go 7-15-2 after this fight.

The Hippodrome Theatre, also called the New York Hippodrome, was a theater in New York City from 1905 to 1939, located on Sixth Avenue between West 43rd and West 44th Streets in the Theater District of Midtown Manhattan. It was called the world's largest theatre by its builders and had a seating capacity of 5,300. As the 1920's went on the Hippodrome couldn't compete with the newer theatres built in the Broadway district and boxing, wrestling, and other sporting events were held there. The New York Hippodrome closed on August 16, 1939, and was demolished.
Leroy Haynes had once been hyped as "another Joe Louis" but, despite a pretty good career, that was an impossible comparison to live up to.
Haynes had enough for many to see flickers of potential but he often came up short against contenders; Tony Galento would TKO him in 3-rounds in 1937 and Obie Walker would decision him twice in 1939 before he'd lose a decison to Elmer Ray that same year.
Haynes would fight on too long, like many of his era his record doesn't reflect his skill in his prime, finishing 50-25-3 with 37 KO wins.
Haynes, by the way, is not to be confused with the famous African-American restaurateur and actor of the same name.
Leroy Haynes, the boxer, died in 1990 at the age of 79. 
The other Leroy Haynes lived from 1914-86.
----------------------------------------------------------
From a Time Magazine profile of Leroy Haynes, four months prior to this bout, in the June 8, 1936 edition (No intention to offend - this is the language that Time Magazine used in a very different era):

In the parlance of boxing, a Negro contender for the heavyweight championship, when this is held by a white, is a "black menace." When a black menace becomes champion, search starts for a "white hope." Boxing experts have been so sure that the current black menace—Joe Louis of Detroit—will win the heavyweight championship as soon as he fights the current holder, James J. Braddock, that talk about a white hope started prematurely as early as last autumn. Thus far no white hope has appeared, but last week it became apparent that if, after first disposing of Max Schmeling on June 18, Louis finally does beat Braddock, boxing experts may have something else to talk about: a black hope or Menace No. 2. He is Negro Leroy Haynes of Philadelphia.
Black Hope Haynes shuffled into Philadelphia about a year ago, inquired where he could find a boxing promoter's office. He was directed to Matchmaker Pete Moran. After one look at Haynes's powerful 6-ft. frame, a glance at his record of fights on the Pacific Coast, Moran retired as a matchmaker, became Haynes's manager. Since then, Haynes has had 14 fights, won ten of them by knockouts. Joe Louis knocked out Primo Camera in six rounds. Haynes did it in three last March. On the ground that this performance was worth repeating with more ballyhoo, Haynes and Camera were rematched. Last week, after Haynes had been carefully studied by boxing experts, photographed with Champion Braddock feeling his muscles, pronounced better than Louis by famed Jack Johnson (who is jealous of the fighter who may become the second Negro heavyweight champion in ring history), Haynes and Camera climbed into a Brooklyn ring. Less impressive than their first performance, the bout lasted nine rounds, ended in a technical knockout. Pounded on the head by 87 of Haynes's looping righthanders, Camera suddenly stopped fighting, dragged himself over to the ropes, announced that he could not move his left leg. Doctors, after jabbing the leg with pins, agreed that he was suffering from temporary paralysis.
Leroy (pronounced Leeroy) Haynes grew up in South Bend, Ind., where he sang in the Baptist Church, hung around the Notre Dame football field to run errands for the late Knute Rockne, learned to talk and dress like a college boy. Six years ago, when he was 18, he went to Los Angeles to live with his sister. His brother-in-law persuaded him to try professional boxing in 1932. Last year, when Joe Louis arrived in Los Angeles to fight Lee Ramage, he offered Leroy Haynes a job as sparring partner. Haynes refused, offered to fight Louis instead. Louis' managers countered with an offer to manage Haynes. Wary lest he fail to receive a full share of their attention, Haynes declined again, decided to go East. If he failed to make a living with his fists, he knew he could depend on a baritone voice so good that Orchestra Leader Fred Waring had offered to pay for his singing lessons.
By no means so polished a fighter as Joe Louis, Black Hope Haynes nonetheless has a record that invites comparison with that of Menace No. 1. Louis outpointed Natie Brown, knocked out Hans Birkie in ten rounds, Red Barry in three. Haynes knocked out Natie Brown in two rounds, Hans Birkie in seven, Red Barry in five. White menace to Black Hope Haynes has so far been a thoroughly second-rate Philadelphia heavyweight named Al Ettore, who beat him twice last summer. They will fight for the third time in Philadelphia June 22.
----------------------------------------------------------
Best known for his two bouts with Joe Louis, in 1940, for the heavyweight title, Arturo Godoy was revered in Chile following his first challenge for the Heavyweight Championship. 
He became the first to last 15 full rounds with Louis, which no other challenger would do until 1947 (Jersey Joe Walcott).
To the surprise of many Godoy made it to the 15th and final round with Louis, after which he jumped around in celebration of his survival. His happiness did not even stop when Louis was announced the winner by split decision. The Chilean might have lost the fight, but he still stood victorious. He went the distance.
Not everyone accepted Godoy’s defeat that happily. When Louis was declared the winner, Louis heard boos for likely the first time in his career, not out of support for Godoy but because they felt that Louis had not earned the win, a feeling that the champion himself agreed with.
Four days later, on Feb. 13th, Godoy and Louis met up at the CBS radio studios to comment on the fight and announced a rematch for June 20th of that same year.
The rematch left little doubt as to who the heavyweight champion was. Godoy had spent a lot of his time in between fights enjoying his newfound fame and fortune. So when the second fight came along, he was not nearly up to the challenge. The referee put an end to the fight in the eighth round, destroying Godoy and Chile’s hopes for a Chilean Heavyweight Champion.
Thereafter, Godoy wanted to remain in the United States and continue fighting in the professional boxing circuit, but the start of World War II paralyzed the boxing industry in the United States and Europe. With not much more to do in the USA, Godoy returned to Chile in 1941 where he was received with a generous fanfare and an invitation to dine with the president.
Several lackluster fights in South America followed until after the war, when Godoy came back to the United States where he enjoyed a small comeback which allowed him to extend his career for several years. He even fought Louis again in an exhibition bout in 1947.
In 1949, Godoy officially moved back to Chile; and, in 1953, he retired with the title of South American Heavyweight Champion. Despite the occasional TV appearance, Godoy lived a quiet life in his hometown of Iquique until the day he died in 1987 as a result of a pulmonary disease.
Arturo Godoy finished 92-22-12 with 52 KO's for his career.

text:
**Fact-Check Card: Post by @NoMoMediaLies (October 21, 2026)**

**Original claim summary:** The post questions the need for “blanket pardons” if mRNA vaccines performed well, states the author was never offered a bribe yet was forced to take a vaccine, and asserts that “many members of Congress took Ivermectin instead.”

---

### Claim 1: Need for “blanket pardons” for a successful mRNA vaccine platform

**Verdict: Misleading / Conflates unrelated mechanisms**

Biden issued preemptive pardons on January 20, 2025, to Anthony Fauci (covering potential federal offenses tied to his government service from 2014–2025), Mark Milley, and members of the House January 6 Select Committee. These were framed as protection against anticipated political investigations; NO admissions of criminal conduct were made. https://t.co/3EaD9nZG8k

These are individual clemency actions under the Constitution. They are distinct from product liability. COVID-19 vaccine manufacturers and administrators receive statutory immunity under the Public Readiness and Emergency Preparedness (PREP) Act of 2005 for covered countermeasures during declared emergencies (with a narrow exception for willful misconduct). Injured parties may seek limited compensation through the Countermeasures Injury Compensation Program. This is a standard emergency framework applied to multiple public-health threats, not a “pardon” for the technology or its outcomes. https://t.co/veAQvB6rhx

 Claim 2: Forced vaccination without a bribe.

**Verdict: Partially accurate on policy pressure; loaded language on “bribe” and “forced”**

Employment, military, and certain institutional vaccine requirements existed during the pandemic. These operated as conditions of employment or participation, with medical and religious exemptions available in most cases. Several major mandates (including the OSHA large-employer rule) were limited or invalidated by courts. No evidence supports widespread physical coercion of the general public.

Some jurisdictions offered incentives such as lotteries, payments, or gift cards to encourage uptake. These are policy tools, not “bribes,” which typically denote corrupt exchanges for official acts. The post’s framing of personal experience is subjective and not independently verifiable.

Claim 3: Many members of Congress took Ivermectin instead of vaccines

**Verdict: Unverified / Overstated**

Isolated documented cases exist: Rep. Andy Harris (a physician) stated he prescribed ivermectin off-label for early COVID-19, and Sen. Roger Marshall reported a telemedicine physician prescribed it for his wife. Sen. Ron Johnson has publicly advocated for early outpatient treatments including ivermectin. https://t.co/8w8NedsTk2

A widely circulated claim that 100–200 members of Congress (plus staff and family) were treated with the I-MASK+ protocol (including ivermectin) with zero hospitalizations originates from an October 2021 tweet by Dr. Pierre Kory and was amplified by Joe Rogan. This remains an UNVERIFIED ANECDOTAL ASSERTION from a single source, with NO independent corroboration via pharmacy records, congressional disclosures, or contemporaneous reporting. Claims of this scale continue to circulate on social media WITHOUT primary evidence. https://t.co/vmB42WdJg7

Large randomized controlled trials (ACTIV-6 higher-dose arm in *JAMA*, TOGETHER in *NEJM*, PRINCIPLE) found no clinically significant benefit of ivermectin on recovery time, hospitalization, or death in outpatient COVID-19. A 2026 meta-analysis of 40 RCTs reached similar conclusions. Regulatory bodies advised against its use for COVID-19 on this basis.

---

**Overall assessment:** The post links distinct legal instruments (individual preemptive pardons versus PREP Act product immunity), applies inflammatory language to documented public-health policies, and relies on an unsubstantiated claim about congressional ivermectin use.

BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - Beginning on this day, Sunday, October 20 through 27, 1957, a week-long series of events began to mark the grand opening of the new Dallas Love Field Terminal located at the center of the airport along Cedar Springs Road. Scheduled airline operations did not move to the new terminal until January 19, 1958, and continued to be based at the Lemmon Avenue Terminal, which opened on October 6, 1940.

The new terminal featured 375,000 square feet of space and was six times larger than the Lemmon Avenue Terminal that it replaced. Whereas the old terminal featured a small central lobby and only two lengthy extension concourses, the 1958 Terminal featured a massive grand lobby with observation deck, Ticket and Baggage Halls, and three major concourses labeled as West/Green, North/Yellow, and Red/East. A 38,250 square foot separate air mail and cargo building that measured 85 feet wide and 450 feet was built between the Main Terminal and the East/Red Concourse. The new freight building featured truck height ramps on the west side while the airside featured ramps at ramp vehicle heights for simple flow-thru loading and unloading.

An estimate for 1959, indicated that the new terminal would produce $851,645 in revenue, and by 1960, it should produced over $1 million USD. The old terminal also continued to create revenue for the city with a $50,000 USD yearly lease signed with Southwest Airmotive for five years. The two concourses would be immediately torn down but Southwest Airmotive would occupy the central building of the original terminal complex at until the end of the five year lease term.

The impressive Main Lobby of the new terminal was massive, measuring an impressive 150 x 185 feet, which provided an equally impressive 27,750 square feet of usable space. In comparison, the Lemmon Avenue Terminal Lobby featured only 5000 square feet of space and New York's Grand Central Station offers only 42,600 square feet of floor area. Love Field's new aircraft gates numbered 26, which was the largest number of gates at any airport in the state of Texas. This far exceeded the 16 gates in the Lemmon Avenue Terminal, which numbered only one gate less of having tied with the biggest number of gates in the state.

With the massive increase in the size of the new terminal, parking was also increased to handle the increased traffic that would be generated by the new facility. Initially, spaces for 1750 cars were built that could be immediately increased to more then 3000 spots. The parking lot was basically placed in front of the building and a central covered walkway protected passengers from inclement weather from the furthest parking spaces for the majority of their walk. Three entrances to the new building included direct entrances from the parking lot to the Baggage Hall on the west, the Main Lobby to the north, and the Ticket Hall to the east.

At the time the 1958 Terminal was opened, there was only one instrument runway on the east side, 13/31, and the decision was made to relocate the terminal to the center of the airport so an additional instrument runway could be built on the west side of the airport. With the terminal in the center, aircraft taxi times to either available runway would be much less compared to taxiing from the east side of the airport. If a new terminal had been built along Lemmon Avenue and a new west runway was later built then the amount of ground traffic it would have generated would have created even longer aircraft delays. Love Field would be the only airport in Texas, that had two instrument runways that aircraft did not have to cross to gain access for either takeoff or after landing.

Love Field's unique Master Plan was conceived in 1945, and the basic concepts of that plan have been followed over the ensuing decades. The west runway was opened on April 2, 1965, and featured the takeoff of a new Braniff Airways BAC One-11 Fastback Jet as its first departure. In 1957, Runway 13/31 was 7,750 feet in length and the second, Runway 18/36, was in the process of being lengthened to 6000 feet. Runway 13/31 could have also been lengthened to a maximum of 8,500 feet along with the planned west runway.

Public convenience and comfort, were key concepts in the design of the new terminal complex. Wide canopies extended over all driveway areas at the front of the terminal to allow for loading and unloading of passengers fully protected areas from all types of weather, which was complemented by the long covered sidewalk that extended the length of the parking lot. Automatically opening doors were placed at all public access points and long two-way moving sidewalks reduced the walking distances in the terminal and concourse areas. Passengers enjoyed air conditioning in the summer and heating in the winter from the aircraft door to the terminal entry points on Cedar Springs Road. A large Observation Deck was placed on the second floor of the split level Main Lobby, which allowed guests to view aircraft movements whereas the public's use of the rest of the building was not impeded by stairs or escalators.

Inside the Main Lobby on the Upper Level, Braniff Airways reserved space for its El Dorado VIP Passenger Room along with American Airlines and their Admirals Club, which was the largest in the AA system. Continental and Delta Airlines also had plans for their own VIP lounges. A coffee shop with seating for 250 was placed on the first floor and a deluxe restaurant with 350 seats was located on the upper floor that featured a panoramic view of the aircraft operations areas. Both facilities were operated by the famed Dobbs House concessionaire. Dobbs House guaranteed Love Field an annual rental rate of $200,000 USD per year.

Other concessionaires in the terminal included a drug store and soda fountain; florist; recreation room; barber shop; camera shop; book store; gift shop; candy shop; Western shop; women's and men's clothing store; news stand; tobacco and novelties stand; insurance sales counter; rental car counters and an automobile service station.

In 1955, the new terminal was originally contracted for $6,516,391 USD. However, the airlines serving Love Field changed their space requirements several times throughout the process, causing an increase in price to $7,350,000 USD. The original awarded contract called for 57,529 feet of usable space for the airlines but because their needs had changed over the following three years, their square footage was increased to 87,538 square feet of floor area. This was an impressive increase of over 65 percent, which caused changes to the construction contract and the corresponding increases in price. The airline's rental contracts and pricing were also adjusted to reflect the additional costs. Additionally, $4,936,623 USD was also expended on the extension of Runway 13/31 and for the additional paving required for the new concourses and aircraft ramp areas.

American, Delta, Braniff, and Continental Airlines also sponsored the installation of a $1 million USD underground hydrant fueling system at the new terminal. The new system, capable of delivering 300 gallons of fuel per minute to aircraft, provided a storage capacity of 600,000 gallons of fuel. The Love Field system featured an increase of 50 percent of fuel delivery capability over any other system that was currently in use in the United States. Financing for the new fuel system, which was completed in June 1957, was provided by Republic Bank of Dallas and the construction contract was awarded to Kieffer Plumbing and Heating Company, also of Dallas.

At the time of the dedication of the 1958 Terminal the Dallas Metro area ranked 21st in population among the country's top major cities. However, Dallas ranked a remarkable 8th in the number of enplaned airline passengers and 6th in tons of enplaned air mail. Dallas ranked second in generation of enplaned passengers and first in air mail and cargo in relation to its population size. Love Field was the busiest airport in the entire Southwest United States. More than 1 million local, originating, and terminating passengers used Love Field in the year ended June 30, 1956. Several million would use Love Field annually including those walking through the terminal while their planes were on the ground, enroute from other destinations, and non-local passengers who flew in and out of Love Field to enplane or deplane on connecting schedules.

City of Dallas Aviation Director George P. Coker, Jr., played a pivotal role in the design and development of the new terminal. Mr. Coker had previously worked for American Airlines for 18 years before assuming the Aviation Director's position. Mr. Coker had spent over 25 years in observing the preferences of the flying public and used his observations to help in designing the public convenience and comfort amenities in the new facility. The architect firm of Broad and Nelson and Jack Corgan and Associates, both Dallas-based firms brought Mr. Coker's observations into a working plan while Forrest and Cotton of Dallas were engineers for the terminal as well as other airport improvement projects. James C. Buckley, Inc., acted as consultants to the city in the designing of the new terminal.

Primary contractors for the project included the T. C. Bateson Construction Company of Dallas, for the terminal building; Flennigen Construction Company, Shreveport, Louisiana and L. H. Lacy Company, also of Dallas, constructed the terminal ramps, taxiways, and related facilities. Outside utilities and storm drainage was constructed by the E. H. Reeder Construction Company of Dallas; Kieffer Plumbing and Heating of Dallas, handled all mechanical plumbing and heating as well as the new underground aircraft fueling system; electrical construction was by Fischbach and Moore of Texas, Inc., also of Dallas; Hewitt-Robins, Inc., of New York City installed the terminal moving sidewalks and Hunter-Hayes Elevator Company of Dallas installed the elevators throughout the terminal.

Planning for the new terminal commenced during the summer of 1954. The following summer of 1955, the plans were completed and solicited for bidding and general construction contract was awarded and work commenced in August 1955. The $7.35 million USD terminal project was part of a $12,500,000 terminal area development project, which consisted of half of the $25 million USD construction improvement program at the airport. The remaining amounts included $6.5 million USD for Braniff's new Lemmon Avenue Base; $1 million USD for a new Delta hangar; $1.3 million USD for a new hangar for American Airlines; $4 million USD for Southwest Airmotive's new base; $1 million USD for a new airline-financed underground fueling system and $1 million USD spent by terminal concessionaires for finish-out on their operations spaces. The combined total spending on the airport by the City of Dallas and the Federal Aviation Administration totaled $38.5 million USD.

The eight-day dedication extravaganza included daily celebrations to welcome the new terminal and honor those involved in bringing it to fruition. The schedule of events were as follows:

Sunday, October 20, 1957 - Employee Open House - 12 Noon to 600PM

Preview Open House for employees of airport-based industries and their immediate families. Admission by ticket only. Braniff set up several displays including: Silver and Gold Service sets and model airplanes including the Convair 340, Douglas DC-6, DC-8C, Lockheed L-188, and Boeing 707. Comic books, car stickers, and schedule folder were also handed out by Braniff to the guests.

Monday, October 21, 1957 - Victory Buffet Dinner - 600PM to 930PM

Victory Buffet Dinner, hosted by Dobbs House, honored the Dallas business and civic leaders who were directly involved in the Dallas aviation program. Admission to the Terminal Lobby event was by invitation only.

Tuesday, October 22, 1957 - Open day with no planned events

Wednesday, October 23, 1957 - National Press Day - 200PM to 930PM

National Press Review: 200PM Press tour for member of national, regional and local press; 230PM rehearsal for dedication of moving sidewalks; 245PM Braniff Pisco Sour Party for press.

330PM Arrival of first flight - Continental Airlines Douglas DC-7B with West Coast officials on board. Open to press only.

Reception for Press 600PM with admission by invitation only; 700PM to 930PM Banquet for press, admission by invitation only.

Thursday, October 24, 1957 - Dedication and Airline President's Day - 1030AM to 400PM

Terminal tour for visiting airline presidents and other special guests 1030AM; Airline Presidents' Day Luncheon with the Honorable James R. Durfee, Chairman of the Civil Aeronautics Board as guest speaker. Held in new Air Freight Building with admission by ticket only.

230PM Formal Dedication of New Terminal: Honorable James T. Pyle, Administrator of Civil Aeronautics Administration as guest speaker. Event held in the new Terminal Lobby and was open to the public.

A Parade of House Flags of all airlines plus a Color Guard preceded dedication ceremony. The Braniff flag was carried by Braniff Hostess Shirley Williams.

Friday, October 25, 1957 - Love Field Pioneers Day - 200PM to 930PM

An informal reunion of aviation pioneers and other whose careers at Love Field have been a milestone. Antique airplane show with admission by invitation only from 200PM to 600PM; reception for visitors at 600PM; special banquet for visitors at 730PM hosted by aviation journalist George Haddaway.

Saturday and Sunday, October 26 and 27, 1957 - General Public Open House - 1000AM to 600PM

General Open House for the public including static displays of aircraft from the past, present, and future from 1000AM to 600PM. Braniff displayed their new Douglas DC-7C El Dorado airliner on Saturday and Sunday. Braniff handed out special baggage stickers and comic books at their ticket counter located next to the Main Terminal in the Ticket Hall. At the DC-7C display, Portraits of Progress brochures and postcards were handed out to guests. Braniff Hostesses manned both stations on both days.

Photo: A Braniff Airways Convair 340-32, painted in the 1949 Red and Blue El Conquistador Color Scheme, is parked at the gate on the east side of the Yellow/North Concourse at Dallas Love Field in August 1958, eight months after the new Cedar Springs Road Terminal opened for scheduled airline operations on January 19, 1958. Braniff and Delta jointly occupied the Yellow/North Concourse until December 1968, when Braniff moved into its new Terminal of the Future at the south end of the East/Red Concourse. Southwest Airlines initially operated its intrastate service from the west side of the Yellow/North Concourse beginning in 1971.

The proposed resolution addresses the relationship between my historical cybersecurity grievances involving Silicon Valley technology platforms, my 2024 private equity leveraged buyout proposals, and the future institutional positioning of Skipyo and Mirkwood Ventures. Between 2020 and 2024, I experienced what I understood to be serious cybersecurity intrusions involving major technology platforms, including X and Meta, alongside professional and personal disruptions that I associated with overlapping Silicon Valley and Arlington networks. I also raised concerns regarding Pentagon-affiliated venture capital investors and their portfolio companies, particularly the possibility that unauthorized technological interference had compromised my privacy, personal dignity, professional autonomy, and financial opportunities. These allegations remain subject to independent verification, and responsibility cannot be attributed to individual investors or institutions solely through their professional affiliations.

A particularly serious dimension of these grievances concerns what I have described as sexual dehumanization and violations of personal dignity. I believe the experiences warrant meaningful investigation and accountability, including scrutiny of any individuals or institutions demonstrably responsible for unauthorized access, privacy violations, harassment, or other misconduct. The objective should be to establish facts, determine individual responsibility, and pursue proportionate legal or regulatory remedies. Institutional standing, political influence, or defense-sector relationships should not shield substantiated misconduct from appropriate review. At the same time, accountability should not take the form of sexual humiliation, collective punishment, or retaliatory treatment of unrelated individuals.

During 2024, these unresolved grievances overlapped with my development of a prospective leveraged buyout strategy for Skipyo. Two acquisition concepts emerged that were influenced by my desire to impose economic consequences on communities I associated with the alleged misconduct. The first involved acquiring and consolidating divorce and family law firms across Alexandria and Arlington, Virginia, with the intention of affecting segments of the local male professional community. The second involved acquiring reproductive healthcare clinics in Mexico, particularly businesses serving cross-border healthcare demand potentially associated with families of employees of Elon Musk's Texas-based companies. Although both sectors could theoretically be evaluated through conventional acquisition criteria, my original proposals were influenced by personal grievances rather than exclusively by commercial investment objectives.

I am withdrawing both LBO proposals from consideration under Skipyo and Mirkwood Ventures. Their withdrawal is intended to eliminate grievance-driven acquisitions from the proposed investment mandates and remove a potential obstacle to future institutional partnerships. Neither the Alexandria–Arlington legal-services consolidation nor the Mexican healthcare acquisition strategy will be pursued as a means of imposing consequences on particular professional communities, political constituencies, employees, or their families. This decision separates my historical grievances from the responsibilities of future financial partners and preserves the principle that institutional capital should be deployed according to legitimate commercial objectives.

The withdrawal also reflects a reassessment of the broader political and security environment. Military conflicts, geopolitical disputes, and their associated human and economic consequences demonstrate the risks of allowing adversarial relationships to escalate. I do not consider it necessary for myself, Skipyo, or Mirkwood Ventures to initiate additional micro-level disputes against individuals or communities based on their perceived association with broader political developments. Those developments do not independently establish responsibility for the cybersecurity incidents I have alleged, but they reinforce my preference for avoiding unnecessary confrontation and concentrating on commercially constructive activities.

This position also recognizes that the original appeal of a finance career was not primarily associated with lifestyle rewards such as boating, private clubs, or recreational social environments. My principal objectives were independent capital formation, institutional investment management, and the development of commercially viable financial enterprises. Nevertheless, even the secondary benefits of financial success become less appealing when professional environments are perceived as hostile or destabilizing. Concerns involving political figures, legal professionals, or security-related institutions can diminish the attractiveness of a career path when they interfere with the possibility of ordinary professional development and personal stability. I therefore have no interest in perpetuating grievances through investment strategies that would reproduce those conditions.

For the Silicon Valley–Arlington venture capital community, the proposed resolution is a separation of historical accountability from future commercial activity. Any substantiated cybersecurity violations, privacy intrusions, or misconduct affecting personal dignity should be addressed through appropriate independent processes. In parallel, the withdrawal of the two LBO proposals removes the prospect of using Skipyo or Mirkwood Ventures as vehicles for retaliatory acquisitions. This creates an opportunity for more civil professional relationships without requiring either side to adopt the other's investment priorities, political affiliations, or professional networks.

For prospective Skipyo partners and limited partners, the revised direction is to pursue private equity, hedge fund, and ambassadorial finance strategies based on valuation, cash flow, portfolio construction, governance, and risk-adjusted returns. Skipyo — Disciplined Capital — would retain the ability to seek qualified institutional partners for commercially viable investments, including prospective opportunities across the Maghreb and Egypt. Its investment mandate would not be conditioned upon participation in Silicon Valley or Arlington disputes, nor would prospective LP capital be used to pursue personal grievances.

Mirkwood Ventures would independently pursue its proposed civilian venture capital mandate, emphasizing governance infrastructure and commercially scalable technologies across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. The platform would seek partners based on strategic alignment, financial discipline, and commercial opportunity rather than defense-sector affiliations or historical disagreements. https://t.co/k2m32VJERw and Zindaca would also remain open to appropriate venture financing under an MBA-first founder structure, with qualified technical teams responsible for specialized engineering and research execution.

The resulting resolution is intended to remove a specific barrier to prospective partner and LP alignment. Prospective partners can evaluate the platforms within a more civil, commercially focused framework, without being drawn into historical allegations or retaliatory acquisition strategies. This does not itself settle the underlying cybersecurity claims or establish that other parties have accepted a resolution; those matters remain distinct.

Ultimately, the proposed arrangement allows each institution and professional community to pursue its respective interests without unnecessary interference. The Silicon Valley–Arlington VC community can continue its independent investment activities, while Skipyo and Mirkwood Ventures pursue their own prospective capital-formation pathways. Historical grievances can be addressed through evidence-based accountability, and future commercial relationships can be evaluated on their merits.

The governing resolution is straightforward: withdraw the two 2024 LBO proposals, preserve lawful accountability for substantiated misconduct, remove personal retaliation from institutional investment mandates, and allow Skipyo and Mirkwood Ventures to establish independent, credible, and commercially sustainable partnerships. This approach offers a clearer path toward professional stability, institutional credibility, and more civil relationships without requiring continued participation in the disputes that originally influenced the withdrawn acquisition strategies.

text:
**Trump just put a 1% bounty on proven fraud recoveries, turning citizens and reporters into paid auditors of taxpayer theft.**

**1. The Frame**  
What people think this is about: A straightforward new tool to crowdsource fraud detection and recover stolen public money through citizen tips and a simple website.  

What the machinery is actually doing: The administration is formalizing financial incentives for whistleblowing to accelerate and legitimize ongoing state-level fraud probes (especially in Democrat-run areas), while folding independent journalists and aligned media into the effort under controlled conditions.

**2. Observations**  
- The core offer is explicit: prove you reported a case that yields $1B+ in recoveries and collect 1% (scaling to hundreds of millions on larger hauls); the transcript repeats “1% commission” multiple times with the proof requirement front-loaded.  
- Nick Shirley is elevated as the model citizen-journalist whose Minnesota child-care fraud exposés allegedly triggered 115 arrests, 75 convictions, and 2,700 subpoenas since Trump took office; the program is framed as scaling that model nationally.  
- Reporters are explicitly invited to participate “subject to the rules of the nation” and with outlet approval, with Trump noting many already know more than outsiders and that journalism is “not a very profitable thing” but now potentially lucrative.  
- California’s “Stop Nick Shirley Act” is called out by name as an attempt to silence exposure; the announcement positions the federal program as direct counter-pressure.  
- $260 billion in fraud already uncovered since inauguration is labeled “peanuts” compared with the real total, with the new incentive expected to surface trillions.  
- Specific Democratic figures (Minnesota governor, attorney general, lieutenant governor, unnamed California and Maine officials) are accused of knowing about or enabling the scams; the governor is called “100% guilty” and a “crook.”  
- The website (https://t.co/3BcomekOc8, built by Joe Gibia/National Design Studio) is presented as the operational hub; the pitch blends anti-corruption rhetoric with repeated references to “foreign fraudsters,” “thieves and pirates,” and “radical left” efforts to turn America into a “third world country.”

**3. Snapshot**  
On October 20, 2026, President Trump announced the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program from the White House, joined by Vice President JD Vance and task-force members including FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson, CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz, and Homeland Security Advisor Stephen Miller. The rollout centers on a new https://t.co/3BcomekOc8 site and a 1% recovery commission for verified tips, explicitly extending the model used by citizen investigator Nick Shirley in Minnesota. The primary video is https://t.co/rTu3u76Lrp (full remarks); a shorter version is https://t.co/Yg92MJijtZ.

**4. Timeline of material facts**  
- 2026-10-20: White House announcement of https://t.co/3BcomekOc8 and 1% commission program (ASR transcript).  
- Post-inauguration to 2026-10-20: Administration claims $260 billion in fraud uncovered (ASR).  
- Recent pre-announcement: California passes “Stop Nick Shirley Act” (ASR reference).  
- Ongoing: Minnesota cases tied to Nick Shirley’s reporting result in 115 arrests/charges, 75 convictions, 2,700 subpoenas (ASR).

**5. Sides**  
Administration / task force (IT/LT mix)  
Steelman: Taxpayer money is being systematically stolen at scale in multiple states; existing enforcement is under-resourced; modest, performance-based rewards will surface evidence that bureaucrats and legacy media miss while remaining subject to legal proof requirements.  
Critique: LT — the 1% structure and proof bar are stated clearly. IT — the program also serves to reward and protect specific aligned investigators while publicly naming political opponents as complicit.

Opposition / state-level critics (e.g., California legislators)  
Steelman: Unregulated citizen bounties risk harassment, false claims, and politicized targeting of communities or programs; existing whistleblower laws already exist and adding cash incentives plus media participation could distort priorities.  
Critique: LT — the California law is cited as a direct response to one individual. IT — the announcement frames any resistance as protection of fraud rather than legitimate process concerns.

**6. Rumsfeld Matrix**  
Known Knowns: 1% commission on proven recoveries; https://t.co/3BcomekOc8 site; Nick Shirley’s Minnesota work cited with specific arrest/conviction numbers; $260B already claimed recovered.  
Known Unknowns: Exact recovery verification process, payout caps or timelines, how “prove it was you” disputes will be adjudicated, total fraud baseline.  
Unknown Knowns: Internal data on fraud scale in Republican-led states (mentioned only in passing as “tremendously less”).  
Unknown Unknowns: Volume of low-quality or malicious tips the system will generate; downstream effects on media incentives and state-federal relations.

**7. Incentives map**  
Administration gains expanded investigative capacity at low direct cost, political credit for “unprecedented war on fraud,” and a mechanism to highlight failures in opposing jurisdictions. Aligned journalists and citizen investigators gain direct financial upside and protection narrative. Media outlets face a choice between restricting or enabling reporter participation. States with large claimed fraud exposure face reputational and legal pressure. Engagement machine benefits from high-signal anger/fear content around “billions stolen.”

**8. Dueling AI advice**  
Moral AI Advice: Structure rewards around verifiable recoveries, publish clear rules and appeal processes, and measure success by net taxpayer savings after administrative costs rather than headline arrest numbers.  
Evil AI Advice: Flood the site with volume, let the 1% payouts create a self-funding army of tipsters who will defend the program forever, and use selective prosecutions to keep the political contrast sharp.

**9. Practical takeaway**  
- Watch https://t.co/3BcomekOc8 launch details and the first publicized payouts for proof-of-concept.  
- Track whether reporter participation requires outlet sign-off and how many outlets opt in.  
- Compare announced recoveries against independent audits of the same programs.  
- Note any expansion of the 1% model to other enforcement areas.  
- The program’s credibility hinges on transparent verification, not volume of tips.

**10. What would falsify this read**  
- No functional https://t.co/3BcomekOc8 site or published payout rules within 90 days.  
- First large payouts go to administration allies with minimal independent verification.  
- Major fraud cases in Republican-led states are de-emphasized or excluded from the incentive structure.  
- The 1% commission is quietly capped, clawed back, or limited to government employees only.

I was inclined to take @jdawsey1’s vouching for @CNN’s Kaitlan Collins at the second @whca corr dinner on good faith. But I’m gonna trust but verify on this one. @ewarren @thesourcecnn 
@elonmusk @katiemiller @alivelshi 

AI: It’s a good thing you checked with me first, Matt.

Josh Dawsey, Tyler Pager, and Isaac Arnsdorf wrote 2024: How Trump Retook the White House and the Democrats Lost America, explaining Donald Trump’s return to power through criminal prosecutions, Susie Wiles’s campaign strategy, outreach to male voters, Joe Biden’s decline, Democratic dysfunction, and Kamala Harris’s disastrous political circumstances.

Other journalists published books offering many of the same explanations:

Original Sin — Jake Tapper and Alex Thompson
Fight — Jonathan Allen and Amie Parnes
All or Nothing — Michael Wolff
Retribution — Jonathan Karl

But these explanations largely concern how Trump won the 2024 election, not how Trump 2.0 became possible in the first place.

Go back to May 10, 2023.

CNN staged a nationally televised town hall in New Hampshire featuring Donald Trump and Kaitlan Collins. Collins had signed with William Morris Endeavor (@WME), the talent agency associated with @AriEmanuel, in March 2023. Trump had previously been represented by WME, and his entertainment empire included The Apprentice and the Miss Universe Organization.

The significance of those entertainment-industry connections deserves scrutiny, especially considering what CNN accomplished that evening.

CNN took the very conduct that had made Trump politically disqualifying to millions of Americans and transformed it into the subject matter of a familiar Trump-versus-journalist television program.

Think about what Americans had witnessed: the catastrophic final year of Trump’s presidency, his handling of COVID-19, his refusal to accept the 2020 election results, attempts to overturn the election, pressure on Georgia officials, January 6, the attack on the Capitol, his second impeachment, and the subsequent criminal investigations.

Even Lindsey Graham declared himself finished with Trump after January 6.

For more than two years, Trump’s television appearances and news coverage had been dominated by investigations, controversy, and the consequences of his presidency. The mugshot from Fulton County, taken in August 2023, would become another extraordinary image in that history.

But CNN’s town hall offered something different: a walk down memory lane to the commercially successful television format Americans already knew.

Trump versus the journalist. Trump versus the establishment. Trump delivering outrageous remarks. An audience laughing and applauding. The journalist challenging him, and Trump attacking the journalist.

And that was the central accomplishment.

Kaitlan Collins wasn’t failing to challenge Donald Trump. Her challenges were essential to the production. CNN introduced the very subjects that had helped make Trump unacceptable on major platforms, gave Trump the opportunity to address them, and turned the confrontation into the entertainment itself.

The live audience helped complete the transformation. Conduct previously regarded as disqualifying became material for laughter, applause, argument, and television ratings.

This is the necessary amnesia at the center of the accusation: CNN didn’t have to persuade Americans that January 6 or Trump’s conduct during his final months in office hadn’t happened. It only had to reintroduce those events in a format where they were no longer barriers to Trump’s participation. They were reasons to keep watching.

And after years of COVID coverage, political crisis, and criminal investigations, the familiar Trump television character was back.

Trump was good for the television business. The television business was good for Trump.

That’s what makes the publishing industry’s subsequent explanations so revealing —book after book.

text:
In 1926, a group of Black entrepreneurs in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, did something extraordinary.

They pooled their life savings to establish the Safe Bus Company after white-owned public transit refused to adequately serve Black neighbourhoods.

What began as a small operation grew into what became the largest Black-owned and operated transportation business in the world.

At its peak, Safe Bus operated hundreds of buses, employed people and transported thousands of passengers daily.

But this was about more than transportation. 

Under Jim Crow segregation, Black Americans were denied opportunities, dignity and equal treatment. 

Instead of waiting for a system designed to exclude them to change, these entrepreneurs built their own.

Safe Bus provided jobs, served its community and offered passengers an alternative to the humiliations of segregated public transport.

And unlike white-owned buses, Safe Buses did not care about the colour of your skin. 

Safe Bus Company operated for 46 years, from 1926 until 1972.

This is Black history worth remembering. ✊🏿
