Muslims rose to preeminence by relinquishing the traditions of the predecessors and turning to revelation. They turned and followed the Book of Allah. 
The umma fell from preeminence by turning from revelation to the traditions of its predecessors, recorded in books of traditions.
The reorientation from revelation to tradition was triggered by politics. Rulers with territorial aspirations felt restricted by revelation. 
They endeavored to enlarge the realm in “traditional” ways, through wars of aggression. But revelation forbids aggression. It permits fighting in self-defence or against persecution. 
Thus, rulers required a justification of wars of aggression. They engaged jurists for the purpose.  The justification of aggression required bypassing the prohibitions of aggression in revelation. 
The ulama furnished the justification by turning from revelation to tradition and the abrogation of all verses that restrict warfare to self-defense. This reinterpretation required reinventing Islam as a teaching of war. 
The ulama reinvented Islam as a religion of war, and Islam as Islamism. They cast the world in the context of the “clash” between the abode of peace against the abode of war. 
The reinterpretation of revelation required the politicization of exegesis and jurisprudence, too. Furnishing a justification for the territorial enlargement of the realm required the weaponization of exegesis and jurisprudence. 
The politicization of exegesis and jurisprudence required recourse to perceptions that contradict the teaching of revelation. 
Problematic perceptions encompass the perception that revelation is in parts unclear, incomplete and contradictory. 
They also encompass the perception that the use of reason to understand revelation is kufr, and the perception that tradition is revelation.
Unwarranted perceptions also encompass the perceptions that tradition is a “judge” of revelation, that revelation is subject to abrogation, and that jihad al-talab is a sixth pillar of Islam. 
A few of perceptions entail kufr and a few entail shirk. The assertion that the Book of Allah is in parts “unclear,” “insufficiently detailed,” and “contradictory” reflects kufr of all verses that teach the reverse. 
The perceptions that revelation is partly “unclear,” “insufficiently detailed” and “incoherent” also require rejecting the verse that teaches that the Book of Allah is the “truth from your Lord.” This is a further expression of kufr.
The treatment of tradition as revelation treats tradition as an “equal” to, and a “part of” revelation. This is shirk. The treatment of tradition as a judge of revelation is an expression of shirk, too, as it reverses the relationship between revelation and tradition. 
The abrogation all verses of reconciliation in revelation is an expression of kufr. For it requires rejecting all “abrogated” verses.
Recourse to the teaching abrogation also requires rejecting all verses which teach that we will “never find a change in the words of Allah.” 
The abrogation of revealed rulings on adultery and apostasy, and their replacement by rulings from traditions enable persons to act as “lawgivers.” 
The replacement of revealed rulings by rulings from traditions are also expressions of shirk, as Allah is the only Lawgiver.
The expressions of shirk and kufr indicate that exegesis and jurisprudence require rehabilitation to reconcile them with the teaching of revelation. 
But efforts to further territorial aspirations embroiled the umma in endless wars. For the means of establishing the sharia in the world required waging jihad al-talab. 
This set the umma on a warpath against the rest of the world. Eventually these wars brought the umma to its knees. 
Acts of extremism perpetrated under the banner of Islam expose the entire umma to the risk of retaliation by aggrieved parties. 
Recent events provide evidence of the tragic effects of misrepresentation and politicization of religion. Political Islam is the greatest threat to security since Nazism. 
The perception that reason and revelation are adversaries rather than allies is a misconception. It rests upon the assumption that faith is fundamentally irrational. Faith rests upon evidence. Reason and revelation reinforce rather than undermine each other. 
Why do believers turn from “religion” to reason? Do not all persons practice a particular way of life? 
A few persons turn to reason as they do not trust religion. And who could fault them in view of the harm perpetrated by extremists? 
But we turn to revelation, too. For unassisted reason does not explain “everything.” Parents teach their offspring about Allah. 
Adversity prompts people to turn to Allah. Who is a better teacher than the Almighty? The military say “there are no atheists in foxholes.” Why would that be? This is a “no-brainer.” 
A “near-death experience brings those who experience it nearer to God. A few remain committed, while others may drift away, again. 
Religion provides regularity in life. It offers solace and meaning. What is wrong with that? Unfortunately, faith is also subject to distortion. 
Thus, research is required to recover the true teaching of revelation, undistorted by personal aspirations of different parties. 
Integration – national as well as international – remains a challenge. Immigrants from Muslim nations are experiencing difficulties in “fitting into” their communities. Why is that? Is there a “disconnect”? Is anything is missing? 
Differences in values raise tensions. There is cultural trauma. Practices prohibited in Islam (same sex marriages) could be permitted elsewhere. 
The traditional perspective differs from present-day thinking. In a few ways traditionists drifted from the Book of Allah. They drifted to the ways of the forefathers, reflected in the traditions.
What is missing is knowledge of revelation. For the prevailing understanding is tainted by problematic and unwarranted presuppositions. At a point in the past, reason acquired a poor reputation. From that time, things went from bad to worse. 
The umma drifted from revelation to tradition as a result of the underappreciation of reason. With the turn from revelation to tradition, the knowledge of the umma became second-hand, if not second-rate. Following manmade traditions rather than revelation became the “new normal.” 
To reassure Muslims regarding the re-orientation from revelation to tradition, traditionists treated tradition as “supplementary” revelation, “revealed” to “clarify” what Allah allegedly did not make sufficiently transparent in the Mushaf. Hearsay became an “equal” to revelation. 
Was this a rational step in the right direction? Following tradition in preference to revelation was tantamount to a fallback to the traditions of the forefathers. 
Islam is an Abrahamic faith. Yet like the followers of the Old and New Testaments before it, the followers of the Book of Allah experience trials and tribulations. 
That Islam is associated with harshness is not surprising. The horror/honor killings, underage marriages, mistreatment of women, genital mutilation and the harshness of the sharia, where adultery, blasphemy, and abandoning Islam are treated as crimes meriting the death penalty, in a defiance of revelation, provide abundant confirmation of problems in tradition. 
Sectarian Muslims embrace a parochial perspective. This perspective presents a tribal perception that divests Islam of its universalism. The perspective attributes to Islam a tribal character.
The ”religion of peace” is presented as a “religion of war” by advocates of militant jihad and the propagation of religion by the sword. It is hardly a surprise that, against the background of these realities, Islam is perceived as a cruel religion.  
The woes of the umma are blamed on a host of “external” factors, such as occupations by foreign nations and crusades. However, there were “internal factors” too: 
"internal factors were in almost all cases due to the intellectual, moral, and spiritual bankruptcy of the Muslims themselves. Thus, primarily the Muslims them¬selves were responsible for their decadence. The machinations of the imperial¬istic nations were helped, or shall we say abetted, by the inefficiency of Muslim rulers and the colossal ignorance of the masses.  
The marginalization of reason that relegated the umma to the dustbin of history.
So long as the Muslims were in the vanguard of knowledge, they led the civilized world in culture, science, and philosophy. But as soon as they lost interest in free and independent inquiry, they ceased to exist as a dynamic force.  
From the eighteenth century in particular there has been a dearth of academic productivity within the Muslim community.  
But it is surprising as well as regrettable to note that not a single scientist of any repute existed in the entire Muslim world from the beginning of the twelfth/eighteenth century to the middle of the thirteenth/nineteenth century. On the other hand, what one finds in this period is a condemnation of the modern scientific knowledge because of its supposedly anti-religious tendencies.  
Muslims were satisfied to bask in the glories of the past. 
While the Muslims gloried in the achieve-ments of the past, they neglected the new weapons of inquiry which the West had discovered with the progress of science and technology. The result was a terrible catastrophe. Whereas the other nations progressed, imbued as they were with modern spirit of inquiry, the Muslims frittered away their energies in fruitless controversies of a theological and trans-empirical nature. Instead of imbibing the results of modern science and conducting inductive inquiries, what they did was to question the compatibility of modern know¬ledge with their mistaken views of religion and to pooh-pooh it because of its materialistic import."
The umma became trapped in the past. 
"The Muslims miserably lacked the courage to think for themselves and consequently flew to the past for shelter. But the inevitable result of mental procrastination was the creation of a society extremely rigid and immobile in outlook and intellectual framework."
At the root of the trauma of the umma lie methodological problems. 
The rejection of reason accelerated the turn from revelation to tradition. The result is confusion and alienation from revelation. 
The turn from revelation to tradition was triggered by the rejection of reason. For the turn from the Book of Allah to follow books of manmade traditions rested upon flawed reasoning. 
It rests on a poor rendering of three verses in the Book of Allah.  These verses encompass the verse saying that we have “a good example in the prophet,” that “whatever the messenger gives you, take it,” and that Allah exhorts us to “obey Allah and the messenger.” 
But the Book of Allah also refers to Abraham as a good example. Besides, does it follow from the prophet being referred to as a “good example” that we should follow books of traditions? This is a non-sequitur.  
The verse that is rendered to suggest that we should take “whatever the messenger gives us” refers to the distribution of war booty, not his traditions. This is a further non-sequitur.
The verse that renders heeding the messenger as meaning “following traditions” conflates “obeying the messenger” with “following traditions.” This is another non-sequitur.  
All three reveal flawed knowledge of revelation based upon fallacies. This should not be a surprise as these “arguments” were proffered by persons that rejected reason. 
It is not surprising that their “arguments” are less than reasonable. Further errors followed. These errors enabled the transmutation of Islam into its traditional and Islamist forms. 
The errors encompass the teaching of predestination in traditional Islam and the teaching of jihad al-talab in militant Islam, as a sixth pillar of Islam. The first rendered Muslims passive at home, while the second encouraged a militant posture abroad.
As a result, traditionists “equate” the revelations of Allah with texts reported in paraphrase by persons that were not prophets. 
This is tantamount to treating the books of traditions as “partners” of the Book of Allah. It is tantamount to “scriptural shirk.” 
Is it possible to ascribe “partners” to the Book of Allah without ascribing a “partner” to Allah? Are these reports the words of God? Are they even the verbatim words of the prophet? 
The reason the umma is experiencing difficulties it turned from Allah to the prophet, from the Book of Allah to the books of traditions, to rituals. In brief, the umma became traditional. 
But Islam is not traditional, except in so far as it re-iterates the messages of the previous revelations, the Tawrat and the Injeel. 
The Book of Allah is revolutionary. It warns us not to follow traditions of the forefathers tainted by shirk.
Not everyone listened. Accordingly, the umma is paying a price for its heedlessness. As a result of the turn from revelation to tradition, the umma is drifting. 
The repression of reason enabled a mis-rendition of key terms. It is common to change the meaning of words. Words are replaced by euphemisms, to reduce the opprobrium attached to words signifying vices. 
In this way, honoring checks replaced honoring parents. Gaming replaced gambling, and “interest” replaced usury. Even adultery is referred to as an “affair.” Are we unwilling to call a spade a spade? 
The transformation or re-invention of Islam as political Islam or Islamism was enabled by the conflation of terms that require being kept separate. There are no synonyms on Quranic Arabic. 
Words that were fused and confused encompass revelation and tradition, jihad in self-defense and aggressive jihad, sunna and hadith, wahy (inspiration) and tanzil (revelation), udwan (hostility) and qital (fighting) as well as nahy (discouragement) and tahrim (prohibition). 
The corruption of the knowledge of key words, enabled by the repression of reason, corrupted the knowledge of Islam. 
The intention was to make traditional” practices palatable and acceptable. The words whose meanings changed encompass: wahy, hikma, ibadat, salat, hawa, jihad, qalb, and mutashabihat. 
Revelation: The meaning of wahy (inspiration) changed from signifying the Book of Allah, to signifying traditions, too. This was justified by the assertion that tradition, too, is “revelation” (wahy).
Hikma. The meaning of hikma changed from signifying wisdom to signifying to tradition of the prophet.
Ibadat: The meaning of ibadat changed from signifying “service” to signifying “worship.” 
Salat. The meaning of salat transformed from connection to ritual.
Hawa. The meaning of the term hawa altered from caprice to capricious opinions.  
Jihad. Jihad meant struggle. According to a few, it also referred to fighting in self-defense. 
But hawkish ulama re-interpreted it as fighting a war of aggression to spread Islam by the sword, in a struggle of the dar al-Islam (abode of peace) against the dar al-harb (abode of war).
Qalb: The meaning of the term qalb changed from brain to heart. The Arabic word for heart is “fuad.” 
Mutashabihat: The meaning of mutashabihat changed from signifying allegorical to “unclear.” 
People ask what were the reasons for the fall of the Muslim civilization? It is safe to say that they were the reverse of the reason for its emergence in the first place. 
Muslims rose to prominence because they followed the Book of Allah. They regressed after turning from revelation to follow the traditions of the forefathers, known as the prophetic traditions.  
The rejection of reason resulted in a paralysis of the mind. The paralysis of thought in turn accelerated the turn from revelation to tradition. 
The thought of the umma became paralyzed as a result of repeated and relentless assaults on reason. 
"As a result of reactionary tendencies, reason became the target of attack and even an object of ridicule. It was contended that reason was foreign to religious truths and led only to their distortion and misrepresentation. Con¬sequently, all domains of knowledge were given scant attention and their findings were not properly appreciated. Science was discredited on the plea that it led to materialism, and philosophy was opposed as intellect was debarred from entering the portals of divine knowledge. Science and philosophy condemned, what remained was a fairy tale, very comforting to the ignoramus but extremely injurious to the nation as a whole." As a result:
"The Muslim mind…has remained a prisoner of those concepts and basic approaches that doom it to remain bound by past mistakes and digressions and bereft of the ability to penetrate, distinguish, and amend its own course, or to plumb the depths of the issues confronting it. Thus it is unable to boldly chart a course for the future, for it sits bound and blindfolded in a dusty corner of the distant past."  
Because of the repression of reason: 
"very little ijtihad was applied to questions and issues of politics, economics, and society in general. The result of the repression of ijtihad in these spheres has been that until this day there has been no formulation of these sciences from a purely Islamic perspective."  
With time, matters turned worse.
"As time passed, the crisis in the Muslim mind became more and more difficult to ignore, for the gulf between theory and practice became more exaggerated. Muslim objectives took on the aspect of unattainable hopes and fanciful wishes, and Muslim accomplishments became little more than history and memories of times past. When control of the Ummah passed into the hands of its enemies, the bankruptcy of Muslim society and its political leadership was self-evident. The Muslim intelligentsia also suffered the same fate, and to the same degree, for by that time it was no longer competent when it came to facing the challenges thrown its way by the foreign cultural invasion." 
Taqlid or the unquestioning adherence to tradition became the chief approach. It caused extensive damage to the umma.
"Blind imitation of the past became the hallmark of the Muslims…While the jurists and other religious thinkers never claimed infallibility or finality for their legal and theological decisions, the Muslims thought that the last word had been said on the subject and that amendment or departure amounted to sacrilege. The early thinkers interpreted and applied the tenets of Islam according to the needs and requirements of their time. But to suppose, as the Muslims did, that their solutions were true for all times indicated incapacity to think afresh in accordance with the changing needs of society."  
Scientific enquiry stagnated. 
"Not only was there a dearth of scientific thinking in this period but also an absence of genuine philosophical activity."
The repression of reason and reasoning in Islam corrupted the knowledge of revelation. It enabled the penetration of tradition by unwarranted perceptions:
"traditionalists…did not want to use any type of human reasoning in law and instead preferred to base every single case on the doctrine of tradition, even if it was weak."
"Among the general populace and the semi-educated there has spread a kind of contempt for thought."
"Our honourable scholars are spreading a mentality of conformism which persuades the masses to do what they are told by their religious leaders. They do not want to hear critical questions from their followers and prefer their brains to be completely switched off. They encourage the proliferation of the herd instinct which makes people feel insecure when they are not cuddled into the warmth of group conformity. People behave like sheep who hurry into mainstream (thinking) at the bark of the shepherd’s dogs (the mullahs, Imams, and leaders of sectarian groups). It will require an intellectual revolution to change this mentality of conformity and promote individuality and originality in thought and practice by both the men in the street and the most ordinary sharia student." 
"This intellectual despotism, and the feeling of inferiority pervading our societies, diminished every area of life. The student delegates thinking about himself to his teacher until the educational aspect of the educational and instructional curriculum hardens into blind tradition and the instructional aspect declines to the teacher dictating to the student. Tests become an exercise in rote memorization, not of the understanding of information and how to engage with it, and the foundation of instruction, the instruction of the human being in how to think—since he who can think can also innovate—is ignored. We have been struck with the disease of intellectual laziness under the patronage of that kind of despotism, and we have become those who delegate thinking about ourselves to others, accepting what they say without discussion. For what matters to us is who is speaking, not what he says. Our inherited way of thinking is built on trust in tradition, not intellectual argument."
"It is unfortunate that in the teaching processes in Islamic education in general, rote learning tends to continuously dominate, not only in social sciences and humanities, but also in science teaching…rote learning in educational institutions from basic to higher education of contemporary Muslim world shows that many Muslims still believe that knowledge is something to be acquired rather than discovered and developed; therefore, the attitude of mind is passive and receptive rather than creative and inquisitive. Furthermore, all knowledge comes to be viewed as unchangeable and all books tend to be memorized or even venerated." Therefore, it is now necessary to introduce new methods of teaching in all levels of Islamic education. There are subjects that need to be memorized like the verses of the Qur’an and hadiths. But there are many subjects that need analytical and critical thinking that would be able to develop creativity and innovative imagination among students of Islamic education.  
"The opposition of the Muslim orthodoxy to rational and empirical sciences, in the end created a seemingly unbridgeable gap between the so-called ‘religious sciences’ derived from the ‘signs’ of the Qur’an (‘al-ayat al-Qur’aniyyah’) on the one hand, and ‘non-religious sciences’ derived from the ‘signs of being’ (al-ayat al-kawniyyah) on the other…This dichotomy of sciences is undoubtedly also responsible for the backwardness of science and technology in the Muslim world."
But traditionalism embraced a range of problematic perceptions and practices. 
"However, the traditional approach, in the manner it was presented and applied, did not prevent the Ummah from falling into a state of decline and failure, from which it is still suffering. Likewise, western thought, as it was presented and applied, cannot protect the Ummah from its inherent adverse, harmful, and even disastrous effects…this is conducive to a wide-ranging question: Is the Ummah going through a serious intellectual crisis, and, if so, how can it find its way out?"
"It is vital to answer these questions in order to sort out the mess that the traditional fuqaha’ have left."
It is necessary to ascertain “what went wrong.” There was a breakdown of rationality, referred to as “intellectual suicide.”  
The repression of reasoning corrupted the knowledge of revelation and heralded the emergence of “the tradition of intellectual retardation.” 
Problems were triggered by a collapse of reasoning. Traditionists went on the offensive against the rationalists. The assault upon was justified by the assertion that recourse to reason leads to kufr or unbelief.

text:
Why They Sing: Foreigners, The Internationale, and the Shape of the World to Come
A personal essay with data and reflection

The Scene

There is a moment that keeps appearing on my social media feed, and it never fails to move me. A young man from Europe stands on a street in China — maybe Chengdu, maybe Shanghai — and sings ‘The Internationale’, in Chinese, word by word, until he is in tears. An African visitor does the same in front of Tiananmen. A Latin American traveler hums it on a high-speed train. Since 2020, and more intensely since the great "China Travel" wave that began in 2024, these videos have gone viral — first in China, then around the world, where they provoke astonishment, curiosity, and occasionally discomfort.

Why would foreigners, raised in entirely different political traditions, choose this particular song — the 1871 anthem of the Paris Commune, the hymn of the world's working classes — to express their feelings about China? What is the meaning of this strange tribute? And what does it tell us about the direction of the world?

This essay is my attempt to answer those questions honestly: with data, with comparison, with respect for complexity, and with a personal conviction that development is the most powerful language on earth.

The Root: Zunyi, January 1935
Before a European vlogger weeps on a Chengdu street, before an African traveler raises his voice at Tiananmen, before a Latin American traveler hums it on a high-speed train, there was Zunyi.
It is the night of January 15, 1935, in the old mansion of Bai Huizhang, a Guizhou warlord’s official — a two-story brick house with a carved wooden balcony, taken over without payment when the ragged column marched in. Around a long table sit about twenty men. Their uniforms are in tatters. Some are barefoot. They have walked for three months since breaking out of the Jiangxi Soviet in October 1934; of the 86,000 who set out, perhaps 30,000 remain. The speaker is a forty-one-year-old Hunanese with thinning hair, Mao Zedong. Across from him are Zhou Enlai, precise and exhausted, Zhu De in a faded soldier’s cap, the young staff officers, and the German adviser Otto Braun, who has just lost the argument that cost the army half its strength. For three days they talk. By January 17, the leadership has been quietly remade.
This is the Zunyi Conference. It is not a stage-managed event. It is the moment a broken movement — surrounded, starving, abandoned by its foreign advisors — decides to trust itself.
In the streets below, the rank-and-file do not yet know all this. They know they have walked into a city for the first time in months — a city with tile roofs, with a river, with hot water. They hold mass rallies in the marketplace. They recruit local boys. And in those rallies, between speeches, they sing.
They sing The Internationale.
The Chinese words were written twelve years earlier, in 1923, by Qu Qiubai — a gentle, bookish intellectual, the first translator of the song into Chinese, a man who had walked the Soviet Union on foot and brought back both Marxism and the tune. By January 1935 Qu Qiubai was not there. He was sick with tuberculosis, left behind in the subtropical south when the column moved, captured by Nationalist forces, and on June 18, 1935 — as the Long March was still under way — he was led to a field in Changting, Fujian, sat down cross-legged, and was shot. Witnesses said he sang the song as he died.
So when those ragged soldiers sang The Internationale in Zunyi in the winter of 1935, they were singing it for a comrade who would never finish the march. They were singing it in the language he had made them. They were singing it not as an anthem of state — there was no state, no border they could call their own, no capital, no flag flying over a square — but as the anthem of people who intended, against every military calculation, to build one.
Ninety-one years later, that song is being sung back to China. A European in Chengdu, an African at Tiananmen, a Latin American on a high-speed train. They do not know about Bai Huizhang’s mansion. They may never have heard of Qu Qiubai. But they are singing the same notes, in the same language he translated, because the country that emerged from that Zunyi winter is now the country they have come to see.
That is the circle the rest of this essay tries to understand.
I. Reading the Phenomenon: Why Do They Sing?

The Internationale is not a national anthem. It belongs to no state. Its most famous line — "No savior from on high; no one will deliver us" — is a declaration that ordinary people must make their own history. That is precisely why its use in China is so telling.

First, the singers are not politicians; they are ordinary travelers, students, workers, and vloggers. Their singing is not an endorsement of any single ideology. It is an emotional recognition: here is a country where the labor of ordinary people has visibly produced extraordinary results. The promise embedded in the song's lyrics — that those who toil should inherit the fruits of the earth — appears, in their eyes, to be enacted before them: gleaming high-speed rail, safe streets at midnight, young people from villages holding university degrees, factories turning out world-class products.

Second, the contrast with home is felt, not merely imagined. Many visitors come from societies where upward mobility has stalled — wages stagnated, housing unaffordable, inequality widened, and the future has come to feel like a managed decline. Standing in a Chinese city, they encounter a different texture of life: order, dynamism, opportunity, and a state that seems to be running on behalf of the many rather than the few. The astonishment converts naturally into tribute. And since most of them know only one anthem of the common people, they reach for the Internationale.

Third, there is the information gap finally closing. For years, much of the world was told one story about China through headlines; then visa-free policies were expanded, flights multiplied, and millions of ordinary foreigners boarded planes to see for themselves. What they found — modern infrastructure, clean energy buses, digital payments, courteous public life — often contradicted the caricature so sharply that the experience produced an almost evangelical desire to tell the truth to their own audiences. The Museum of the First National Congress of the CPC in Shanghai alone received nearly 100,000 foreign visitors last year, and its guestbooks fill with words of admiration in dozens of languages.

Fourth — and here I want to be fair, because fairness is what separates analysis from propaganda — part of this is performance. Some videos are click-bait, some are commerce, and some singers are fluent in no Chinese at all. We should not over-read a genre that includes its share of spectacle. But even spectacle is data: people perform what they believe their audience will applaud, and in China the Internationale is applauded because it is understood as a salute to the working people. The sincerity of individual singers varies; the social meaning does not.

II. The Comparison: Two Roads of Modernization

Numbers matter here. Between 1979 and 2023, China's economy grew at an average annual rate of 8.9 percent, contributing 24.8 percent of world growth over that period; by 2023 its GDP reached US$17.8 trillion, about 16.9 percent of the world total. In 2025, with the global economy buffeted by headwinds, China's output crossed 140 trillion yuan with growth of about 5 percent — a rate that kept it at the front of the major economies, and an annual increment roughly the size of a medium-sized economy. In July 2026, the IMF cut its forecast for world growth to 3 percent while raising its forecast for China to 4.6 percent — one downgrade, one upgrade, in the same report.

Most major Western economies have grown at roughly 2 percent or less in recent years. That is not a moral judgment; the West's achievements — mature institutions, research universities, high income levels, the rule of law — are real and I respect them. The point of comparison is different: the two models chose different sequencing. The West industrialized early, offshored manufacturing, and leaned on consumption and finance; China invested first in physical and human infrastructure — roads, grids, schools, skills — and deferred consumption for decades. The results are visible in different ways: Western incomes remain far higher per capita; Chinese living standards have risen faster than almost any large economy in history.

And here fairness cuts both ways again. China's own income inequality remains high, its population is aging, regional gaps persist, and the housing correction of recent years has tested families. No country on earth has solved modernization without costs. What the comparison shows is not perfection, but direction: a developing country that lifted itself without colonizing others, and whose rise lifted a fifth of humanity.

III. The State of the Global Economy and Society

Step back, and the backdrop explains the singing. The world economy in 2026 is a world of paradox: rich on paper, anxious in reality. Global growth has been marked down to about 3 percent by the IMF, weak by historical standards; protectionism has spread; supply chains are being severed for political reasons; and the poorest nations face debt, climate shocks, and shrinking aid.

Within wealthy countries, the decades after the Cold War produced dazzling aggregate wealth and stubborn popular discontent: wages diverged from productivity, housing became inheritance rather than opportunity, and trust in institutions fell. Across the Global South, nearly two-thirds of the UN's Sustainable Development Goals targets were off track even before the recent shocks. The result is a strange global mood — the world is technically richer than ever, yet a growing share of humanity feels that the system is not working for them.

This is the soil in which the Internationale is being sung again. The song's old question — who builds the future, and for whom? — has returned, not because of any party manifesto, but because ordinary people everywhere are comparing systems by outcomes: who feeds their children, who pays them fairly, who gives their young people a future. That is a profound shift in the basis of political legitimacy, and it is global.

IV. China's Development Today

China's current phase — the 15th Five-Year Plan period, Chinese modernization — is best read not as an end-state but as a continuous re-invention. The headline numbers are strong: growth around 5 percent in 2025 on a base of 140 trillion yuan; in the first three quarters of 2026, high-tech manufacturing value-added grew 14.3 percent year on year.

The social ledger is what moves ordinary visitors. From 2012 to 2020, China lifted 98.99 million rural residents out of absolute poverty, removed all 832 poverty-stricken counties and 128,000 villages from the list — an average of more than ten million people a year — and achieved the UN's 2030 poverty goal ten years early. Since reform began, some 770 million rural people have escaped poverty, accounting for more than 70 percent of global poverty reduction measured against the World Bank's international poverty line; China now hosts the world's largest middle-income group, over 400 million people.

The green transition deserves special mention, because it is where China's development most clearly becomes a public good for the planet. In 2025, China added 440 gigawatts of new renewable capacity — roughly 64 percent of the global total — with the world's lowest costs for solar and wind power; pure electric vehicle sales reached 8.2 million, and China's fleet accounts for 58.9 percent of the world's EVs. According to the IEA, China produced about 70 percent of the world's electric vehicles and over 80 percent of battery cells in 2025; statisticians put it simply: of every five new-energy vehicles sold globally, three are made in China. Clean energy now provides 36.8 percent of China's electricity generation.

None of this means China's problems are solved. The demographic cliff, youth employment, local debt, and the psychological weight of a maturing economy are real, and Chinese leaders say so plainly. But the direction — toward quality, innovation, and sustainability — is unmistakable.

V. China's Contribution to the World

China's contribution to global development is not a slogan; it is an arithmetic fact. The IMF's Asia-Pacific director said in October 2026 that China contributes roughly one-third of global growth, and that every percentage point of Chinese growth lifts the whole region. Over the past decade, China's average annual contribution to world growth has stayed around 30 percent — more than any other single economy.

Through the Belt and Road Initiative, launched in 2013, more than 150 countries and 30-plus international organizations have signed cooperation documents; over 4,000 projects have been delivered, pulling in investment of nearly US$1 trillion. Railways in Laos, ports in Pakistan and Greece, digital corridors across Africa, power plants in Latin America — these are not loans on paper but steel, concrete, and electricity in the ground. The World Bank has estimated that BRI transport corridors could significantly cut trade times and costs for participating countries, lifting millions out of poverty over time. (That is the World Bank's analysis, not China's advertisement; I cite it because it is independent.)

China's green industries are likewise a global subsidy to the energy transition: by compressing the cost curve of solar, wind, and batteries, China has made climate action affordable for developing countries that would otherwise be locked out of it. And in the pandemic years, China shipped masks, ventilators, and vaccines to more than 150 countries and international organizations — an act of solidarity that some recipients have already forgotten and history should not.

VI. The Three Global Initiatives: A System of Ideas

What China has offered since 2021 is not only projects but a framework of ideas, and I want to present these carefully, because they deserve to be judged by their content.

The ‘Global Development Initiative’, proposed by President Xi Jinping at the UN General Assembly on 21 September 2021, puts development at the center of the international agenda — a people-first, results-oriented approach covering priority areas from poverty reduction to digital economy and climate. Five years on, more than 130 countries and international organizations support it, nearly 100 have signed cooperation documents, and the "Group of Friends of the GDI" has grown to 88 members.

The ‘Global Security Initiative’, put forward in 2022, begins from a simple proposition: security is indivisible — no country's security should be built at the expense of others'. It advocates common, comprehensive, cooperative, and sustainable security, and explicitly opposes bloc confrontation and zero-sum alliances. The ‘Global Civilization Initiative’, announced in 2023, argues for the equality of civilizations, mutual learning, and respect for the diversity of human development paths.

Taken together with the BRI, they form a coherent worldview: development (GDI), security (GSI), and civilization (GCI) are the three pillars, connectivity (BRI) is the bridge, and the destination is a community with a shared future for mankind. I find this intellectually coherent in a way that the rival doctrine — "you're either with us or against us" — is not. But I must add a note of honesty: initiatives are principles, not guarantees. Their value will be proven only by results on the ground, by the condition of ports and schools and hospitals in partner countries, and by whether the partnerships are genuinely equal. Skeptics are entitled to their doubts; the burden of proof lies with implementation.

VII. Where Is the World Going?

So, to the largest question: where is the world going?

I see two futures on the table. One is a world of blocs — decoupling, friend-shoring, tariffs as weapons, alliances as siege engines — in which the Global South is divided, development is weaponized, and humanity wastes a generation competing over who can sever more links. The other is a world of open cooperation, where multipolarity is managed through rules, where the excluded are seated at the table, and where the great contests of our age — climate, artificial intelligence, demographics, pandemics — are fought as common problems rather than zero-sum games.

The evidence is mixed, and I say this as someone who has spent much of his professional life in diplomacy: the second future is not guaranteed. Protectionism is rising in every region, and even well-meaning industrial policies are hardening into walls. But I am also struck by the deeper current beneath the headlines. The center of economic gravity is shifting to Asia and the Global South; the IMF reports that developing Asia alone accounts for about 60 percent of global growth. When the excluded half of humanity begins to produce, consume, and negotiate, the old architecture of the world economy — built when they were merely markets — must either reform or decay.

My personal conviction is simple: the future belongs to whichever civilization most credibly solves the problem of human dignity, and human dignity begins with development. The Internationale sung on a Chinese street is a small signal of a large shift: ordinary people everywhere are now judging systems by outcomes, not by labels. That is why I also resist triumphalism. China has no interest in exporting its model by force — that would contradict everything it says — and the world does not need a new hegemon; it needs a functioning, fair, plural system. The genius of the three initiatives is precisely their modesty: they are invitations to cooperation, not blueprints imposed on others.

The Last Verse

Let me return to the tears. When a foreign visitor sings the Internationale in China and weeps, what is the weeping for? I think it is not for politics. It is for the recognition that somewhere on earth, the dignity of ordinary labor is being honored in visible, material form — that the world is not condemned to permanent inequality. The Internationale is not a threat to anyone. It is a question posed to every country, including my own: does the world reward honest work? Does the next generation inherit a ladder or a wall?

China's answer, for all its imperfections, has been: development, openness, a shared future. The world's answer is still being written — by every country that chooses cooperation over coercion, dialogue over decoupling, and the patient work of building over the quicker satisfactions of blame. That is the only contest that deserves our seriousness. And if a song helps us remember what is at stake, so be it. It is sung for the people, and the people are listening.
author: zhang_heqing
authorBio: Inspector on X. Retired Cultural Counsellor. Telling China's stories-soft on culture, firm on truth. 🇨🇳 Personal views.

RUST BELT • GARY, 1994 • A City That Could Not Keep Its Promises

👉 Manager Clotilde’s Notice —
This image is from the collection RUST BELT • GARY, 1994 • A City That Could Not Keep Its Promises, now available on our Patreon.
https://t.co/oVJy7WGMpO

RUST BELT • GARY, 1994 • A City That Could Not Keep Its Promises

This collection is a fictional, AI-created photographic story set against the real history of Gary, Indiana, in the autumn of 1994. Its heroine, her personal experiences and the moments portrayed are imaginary, although the historical circumstances behind them are very real.

We have approached this project with considerable care and respect for its historical setting. Nevertheless, individual buildings, locations, architectural details and their condition may differ from how Gary actually appeared in 1994. These images are artistic reconstructions, not archival documentary photographs.

Gary is an American industrial city near Chicago, once built around the enormous steel industry on the southern shore of Lake Michigan. By 1994, decades of industrial restructuring, lost employment and population decline had left deep wounds across parts of the city. Gary had become one of the most painful examples of America's Rust Belt, the former industrial heartland where prosperity had given way to shuttered factories, abandoned buildings and communities struggling to survive.

Our unnamed heroine is a young single mother. The decline of her hometown has fallen heavily upon her life, leaving her burdened by uncertainty, exhaustion and a future she can no longer look toward with confidence.

We follow her through different days of a cold, unforgiving autumn. Her everyday clothing changes, sometimes including the worn leather that has become a familiar part of her appearance. But the sorrow in her eyes remains.

She moves through deserted industrial spaces, neglected downtown streets and residential neighborhoods where houses have lost their inhabitants. She touches boarded windows, examines forgotten objects and pauses before the remains of ordinary lives. Sometimes she seems to be searching for an answer. At other moments, her smallest gesture becomes an act of tenderness toward a city that can no longer care for itself.

Before the monument to Gary's founder, she looks upward with an expression of quiet accusation, as though asking him to witness what has become of the city that bears his name. Elsewhere, she stands before silent machinery or the empty remains of a home, confronting losses far greater than anything she can repair.

Her emotions are not always the same. There is melancholy, bitterness, restrained anger, tenderness, helplessness and the profound fatigue of someone who has lived too long with uncertainty. The gray skies, cold rain, bare trees and deserted streets deepen the oppressive atmosphere.

This is not a story of triumph or miraculous recovery. We offer no comforting promise that everything will eventually be restored.

Our heroine cannot rescue Gary. She knows that. Yet its decline is inseparable from her own life, her memories and her sense of belonging. She suffers with her city, bears witness to its disappearance, and continues to live beneath the weight of everything it has lost.

RUST BELT • GARY, 1994 is not a celebration of beautiful ruins.

It is a story about the human cost of watching a once-prosperous city slowly fall apart.

👉 Notice • Behind the story

If the places our heroine visits have made you wonder what happened to this city, we would like to take you briefly into the history behind our fictional story.

The Rust Belt: When America's Industrial Heartland Began to Rust

The Rust Belt is not a state or an officially defined region. It is the name given to a broad part of the American Midwest and Northeast, particularly around the Great Lakes, where steel mills, automobile factories and heavy industry once formed the foundation of countless communities.

For much of the twentieth century, these industries represented employment, prosperity and the promise of a secure future. Entire cities grew around their factories. Generations of families depended upon the work they provided.

But from the later decades of the century, industrial restructuring, automation, international competition and factory closures transformed much of this landscape. Many communities lost enormous numbers of jobs. As people moved away, shops closed, houses stood empty and local governments struggled with shrinking revenues.

The old industrial heartland gradually acquired a new and sorrowful name: the Rust Belt.

Gary: A City Born from Steel

On the southern shore of Lake Michigan, not far from Chicago, stands Gary, Indiana.

Its history began in 1906, when the United States Steel Corporation established a new industrial city alongside what would become the enormous Gary Works steelmaking complex. The city was named after Elbert H. Gary, a leading figure in U.S. Steel, whose bronze monument appears in our collection.

The steelworks began operating in 1908. What followed was extraordinary growth. Workers arrived from many parts of America and from overseas, including African Americans moving north in search of opportunities during the Great Migration.

Gary became a bustling industrial city. Its Broadway offered department stores, theaters, hotels and restaurants. Neighborhoods grew around schools, churches and everyday local businesses. At its population peak in 1960, the city was home to more than 178,000 people.

Yet even during its prosperous years, Gary was not an uncomplicated American dream. Dangerous industrial work, pollution, racial segregation and unequal access to housing and employment were also part of its history.

When the Prosperity Began to Disappear

Gary's decline did not happen overnight, nor was it caused by one event.

From the 1960s onward, technological change, competition and restructuring drastically reduced the number of workers required in the steel industry. Gary Works continued producing steel, but the vast workforce that had once sustained the city's economy was greatly diminished.

Employment disappeared faster than the city could replace it.

Families began leaving. Among them was a major movement of white residents toward surrounding suburbs, part of the American phenomenon known as "White flight". Racial prejudice, housing discrimination, suburban development and changing economic opportunities all contributed to this transformation. Many Black residents faced additional barriers to obtaining housing and opportunities elsewhere.

Businesses followed departing customers. Properties lost value. Tax revenues declined. The resources available to maintain streets, schools and public services came under increasing pressure.

One empty house became several. A closed shop was followed by another. Some industrial properties became neglected brownfields, while parts of the once-busy downtown lost much of their commercial life.

Gary in 1994: The Setting of Our Story

By the autumn of 1994, the decline had become impossible to ignore.

The city had already lost tens of thousands of inhabitants. Parts of Broadway were lined with closed or boarded businesses. The former Sheraton Hotel stood empty near City Hall, a particularly bitter reminder of unsuccessful attempts to revive downtown.

Abandoned houses, vacant lots, neglected buildings and deteriorating infrastructure had become familiar sights in some neighborhoods. Other streets remained inhabited, but many residents lived beside the visible consequences of years of disinvestment.

Violent crime added another terrible burden. In 1993, Gary recorded 110 homicides and had the highest reported murder rate among American cities with more than 100,000 inhabitants. Newspapers used the grim description “murder capital.” It was a real and devastating chapter in the city's history, not an invention of our story.

Yet Gary was never simply an empty city inhabited by fear. People continued working, raising families, maintaining homes and preserving their communities. The tragedy was that so many had to do so while the city around them was losing the economic foundations upon which it had been built.

And What Became of Gary?

The losses did not end in 1994.

Population decline continued into the following decades. Some famous buildings deteriorated further; others, including the abandoned Sheraton Hotel, were eventually demolished. Empty properties and the costs of neglect remained enormous problems.

Gary Works, however, never entirely fell silent. Steel production continued, although with a far smaller workforce than during the industry's great years.

Today, efforts to remove dangerous structures and redevelop parts of Gary coexist with the lasting consequences of deindustrialization and depopulation. The city remains inhabited, with people whose lives and memories cannot be reduced to images of abandonment.

Our heroine is imaginary. She does not speak for every person who lived in Gary, nor do our photographs claim to reproduce every street exactly as it stood in 1994.

But the history beneath her sorrow is real.

Behind every abandoned house was once an address. Behind every closed factory was once a working day. Behind every empty street were people who had believed that their city would continue to provide a future.

That is the history our collection asks you to remember.

Not merely the buildings that were lost, but the lives that had to continue among them.

text:
India’s iPhone Boom: Subsidy Without Substance  

Ecosystem, Not Handouts, Powers Smartphone Sovereignty  

From Screwdriver to Silicon: Why India Must Go Upstream  

India is celebrating a milestone: one in four iPhones now rolls off assembly lines near Chennai. Tens of thousands of jobs have been created, exports are rising, and policymakers are hailing this as proof that India is finally muscling into global electronics manufacturing.  

But beneath the headlines lies a sobering truth: assembly is not the same as manufacturing. And subsidies are not the same as an ecosystem.

The Mirage of Assembly

When you peel back the layers of India’s iPhone story, what you see is a screwdriver economy. Yes, India has moved beyond simply tightening screws — it now assembles sub‑components like mainboards. But the heart of the smartphone — the memory chips, processors, OLED displays, camera lenses, and lithium batteries — still come from abroad.  

In fact, most of them come from China, South Korea, and Taiwan. India is importing the expensive guts of the phone, adding labor and logistics, and then exporting the finished product. The value India captures is modest. The value it pays out — in subsidies — is not.

The Subsidy Trap

To lure Apple’s contract manufacturers, India offers 4–6% of invoice values as subsidies. That means taxpayers are footing the bill every time an iPhone is shipped. Worse, as global chip prices rise — driven by the AI boom — the subsidy bill automatically balloons.  

This is fiscal fragility disguised as industrial policy. India is narrowing its trade deficit in phones, but at the cost of swelling its fiscal deficit. It’s like paying rent on a house you don’t own: the moment you stop paying, the factory may pack up and leave.

Lessons from East Asia

Contrast this with South Korea. When Samsung and LG built their empires, they didn’t rely on perpetual subsidies. They reinvested profits into R&D, built fabs, and created a vertically integrated ecosystem. Today, Korea controls critical nodes in the supply chain: semiconductors, displays, and batteries.  

Or look at China. Foxconn’s mega‑factories were enabled by provincial governments, but the real story was the ecosystem: Shenzhen’s dense network of suppliers, entrepreneurs, and risk‑takers. China didn’t just assemble; it built the upstream industries that make assembly profitable.

India, by comparison, is subsidizing the downstream without building the upstream. That’s like trying to win a marathon by sprinting the last 100 meters while ignoring the first 42 kilometers.

Ecosystem Depth Is the Real Moat

High‑end consumer electronics like smartphones are unforgiving. The moat is not cheap labor or subsidies. The moat is ecosystem depth.  

- Semiconductors: Without fabs, India will always import the brains of the phone.  
- Displays: OLED panels are capital‑intensive and technologically complex.  
- Batteries: Gigafactories require scale, chemistry expertise, and supply chains for rare earths.  

These are not industries you can conjure with a subsidy scheme. They require decades of patient investment, risk‑taking entrepreneurs, and a state willing to coordinate capital and talent.

A Smarter Path Forward

India should learn from its Asian peers. Instead of pouring billions into subsidies that inflate with chip prices, it should channel resources into:  

- Education and skills: Build a workforce that can design chips, not just assemble boards.  
- R&D investment: Seed labs and startups that can innovate in optics, batteries, and semiconductors.  
- Labor‑intensive industries: Textiles, toys, and other sectors where India has comparative advantage.  
- Design and engineering hubs: Position India as the brain behind devices, even if the guts are made elsewhere.  

This is not to say India should abandon electronics assembly. It creates jobs, builds know‑how, and integrates India into global supply chains. But it should be seen as a stepping stone, not the destination.

The Bottom Line

India’s iPhone factories are a symbol of progress, but they are also a warning. Without ecosystem depth, India risks becoming a subsidy‑dependent assembler, forever paying rent on someone else’s technology.  

The real lesson from Korea and China is simple: ecosystems, not subsidies, build sovereignty in high‑end manufacturing. If India wants to be more than a screwdriver economy, it must invest in the hard, slow work of building upstream industries.  

Otherwise, the iPhones rolling out of Chennai will remain shiny symbols of dependence — not independence.

text:
Golda Meir once said:
“We have a secret weapon in our struggle with the Arabs; we have no place to go”.

Few sentences explain the history of the Arab-Israeli conflict better.

In 1948, when Israel declared independence, neighboring Arab armies invaded. Arab leaders had rejected partition, and some openly threatened the destruction of the emerging Jewish state.

The expectation was that the Jews would collapse.

After all, who were they?
Holocaust survivors, refugees from Arab persecution, immigrants with few possessions, rebuilding a nation after centuries of exile. Many had escaped societies where Jews had historically lived under discriminatory restrictions, including the dhimmi system.

The prevailing contempt for Jewish military capability was about to meet reality.

The Arab armies lost.

And the defeat was so humiliating that Syrian intellectual Constantin Zureiq gave it a name in his 1948 book: The Meaning of the Disaster - al-Nakba.

The later elevation of the Nakba into the central framework for understanding 1948 is not merely a neutral description of Palestinian suffering. It is part of a revisionist project that shifts historical attention away from the attempted destruction of the Jewish state and toward a narrative in which Palestinian victimhood becomes the primary moral and political fact. That framing often treats the consequences of the Arab rejection of partition and invasion as though they were the original cause of the conflict, while minimizing the existential threat faced by Jews who had survived genocide, persecution, and expulsion.

But in realtime, this was about multiple Arab armies who had failed to defeat a state that had barely been born.

Rather than reconsider the premise that Jewish sovereignty must be eliminated, the region’s revolutionary leaders increasingly embraced another strategy.

If Israel could not be destroyed immediately, perhaps it could be exhausted.

Gamal Abdel Nasser built his political project around pan-Arab nationalism, confrontation with Israel, and promises of eventual victory. His catastrophic defeat in 1967 did not end the confrontation. Egypt subsequently launched the War of Attrition.

The underlying calculation was straightforward: Israel was small, surrounded, and dependent on maintaining a functioning society. Its enemies could impose a permanent military and economic burden until the Jewish state became unsustainable.

But something was missing from that calculation.

The Jews had nowhere to go.

The Six-Day War also accelerated an ideological transformation.

Israel, previously portrayed as an artificial and vulnerable state of refugees, was increasingly recast as a powerful Western colonial project.

The Palestinian national movement drew on the Algerian revolutionary model: portray the conflict as indigenous liberation against foreign settlers, sustain armed resistance, and eventually force the colonizer to withdraw.

It was a compelling narrative for international audiences, particularly amid the global wave of decolonization.

But it contained a fundamental contradiction.

The French could leave Algeria and return to France.

Where, exactly, were the Jews supposed to return?

Poland? Germany? Iraq? Yemen? The countries that had murdered, persecuted, or expelled them?

Israel was not a distant imperial possession administered from a European capital. It was the restored national home of a people with an ancient connection to the land, reinforced by generations of refugees who had no other national refuge.

That distinction matters enormously.

A colonial power can calculate that maintaining a colony costs more than abandoning it.

A nation fighting for its survival cannot make the same calculation.

And yet, for decades, Israel’s enemies continued to confuse its attachment to life with an inability to endure suffering.

Hamas turned that misconception into an explicit ideological weapon.

Its leaders repeatedly celebrated martyrdom and contrasted their willingness to sacrifice lives with Israel’s determination to preserve them.

Israel mourned its dead. Hamas glorified death in its propaganda, and intentionally caused civilian deaths for propaganda wins.

Israel negotiated agonizing exchanges to recover its hostages. Hamas exploited those hostages as instruments of psychological warfare.

Israel’s concern for human life was interpreted as a strategic vulnerability.

October 7, 2023, was the culmination of that calculation.

Hamas breached Israel’s defenses, massacred civilians, abducted families, and demonstrated what its vision of destroying Israel meant in practice.

The attack was not simply a protest against borders or settlements. Its victims included peace activists, children, elderly people, and foreign workers.

The brutality was the message.

And Hamas apparently believed the shock would expose Israel’s fragility.

Instead, it exposed something else.
The Jews still had nowhere to go.

For three years, Israelis have endured enormous military, economic, and psychological costs. Reservists left their families and businesses. Communities buried their children. Hostage families fought to bring their loved ones home.

The country has experienced bitter internal disagreements, political failures, and extraordinary grief.

But the fundamental commitment to national survival has not disappeared.

That is the mistake repeated by generations of Israel’s enemies.

They assume that because Jews value life, they will eventually surrender to those who threaten it.

They confuse reluctance to fight with an inability to fight.

History suggests otherwise.

In 1973, Egypt’s Anwar Sadat launched another war against Israel. Four years later, he stood before the Israeli Knesset in Jerusalem. In 1979, Egypt became the first Arab country to sign a peace treaty with Israel.

Not because Jews had finally abandoned their homeland, but because Egypt’s leadership recognized that permanent confrontation was not a viable path to its objectives.

Decades later, the Abraham Accords demonstrated another possibility.

The UAE and Bahrain chose normalization rather than waiting for Israel’s disappearance.

The lesson is that peace requires accepting only one fundamental reality:
Israel is not going anywhere.

And this is where the next phase of the conflict must begin.

The objective cannot simply be to win another war, only to prepare for the next one.

It must be to dismantle the political and educational structures that perpetuate the expectation of Israel’s eventual destruction.

That means fundamentally reforming the Palestinian institutions that have failed to produce accountable governance, ending incitement and the glorification of terrorism, replacing dysfunctional refugee policies with realistic paths to citizenship and dignity, and developing credible alternatives to Hamas rule.

It also means expanding the model of regional cooperation demonstrated by the Emirates: economic integration, shared security interests, and the recognition that prosperity offers more than permanent confrontation.

UNRWA’s uniquely inherited refugee-registration framework must be shut down, as well as its education to terrorism and Martyrdom.

The Palestinian Authority’s corruption and failures, and continues terror support and violation of the Oslo accords must be used as basis to dismantle it, and replace it with local authorities' governance, based on Dr.  Mordechai Kedar’s emirates plan.

And Arab governments have a decisive role to play in ending the political fantasy that Jewish sovereignty is temporary.

They have to become stakeholders in Israel’s continued existence.
Because the strategic calculation that has sustained this conflict for generations is fundamentally flawed.

Jews do not want a forever war.
They have never needed to love death to demonstrate their willingness to defend life.

And when the alternative is national annihilation, they have repeatedly shown that they can endure extraordinary costs.

The sooner the region accepts that, the sooner it can stop preparing for Israel’s destruction and start building a future alongside it.

**Paris curfews after the October 17-18 riots restored one calm night in targeted zones, but the government’s intelligence and deployment failures handed opportunists a platform six months before the 2027 election.**[[1]](https://t.co/irtnU9YCX2)

[Take 11/15 · 𝕏-1]
### 1. The Frame
**What people think this is about:** Spontaneous outrage over rising living costs, underfunded schools, and eroding public services that boiled over into riots and looting, met by necessary but heavy-handed state crackdowns including curfews.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** A centrist government facing fiscal pressure and a fragmented parliament is using localized curfews and blame on “ultra-left” agitators to reassert control and blunt momentum ahead of the presidential vote, while local authorities and opposition exploit the disorder to demand more resources or score political points.

### 2. Observations
- The protests began weeks earlier with high-school students over school conditions and expanded into a broad “convergence of struggles” on October 17 involving unions, climate activists, and revived Yellow Vests; most marches stayed peaceful while masked groups hijacked them for looting and arson.[[2]](https://t.co/qjkxCJ8mVt)
- Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted police “lost control” in several cities despite 60,000 officers deployed, citing intelligence and planning shortfalls; his resignation offer was rejected, but the admission undercuts the government’s narrative of competent response.[[1]](https://t.co/irtnU9YCX2)
- Over 2,400 arrests (roughly 70% adults, many with prior records) and nearly 1,000 police injured show the violence was concentrated and opportunistic rather than purely spontaneous; authorities are already using facial recognition and fast-track prosecutions.[[3]](https://t.co/7aecCNXnGv)
- PM Sébastien Lecornu’s targeted curfews (e.g., specific Paris squares and commercial zones, minors-only in some northern and southern cities) delivered calm on the night of October 19-20 without a nationwide lockdown, but he left the state-of-emergency door open while blaming “ultra-left radical groups” seeking chaos before the 2027 vote.[[4]](https://t.co/aeZbUAyv9I)
- Damage hit thousands of businesses and public buildings (Limoges town hall burned, Marseille municipal building stormed); the government promises recovery funds clawed back from perpetrators, a classic liability-shifting move.
- Similar cost-of-living protests flared in Italy, Spain, and elsewhere, suggesting the French episode is part of a wider European pressure cooker rather than an isolated domestic failure.

### 3. Snapshot
On October 17, 2026, more than half a million people protested nationwide over living costs and public services. Violence and looting erupted in multiple cities that weekend, prompting partial curfews ordered by PM Lecornu on October 19 that took effect that night in targeted zones. By October 20, authorities reported the measures helped keep the peace overnight, with new localized curfews possible and larger protests expected the following Saturday.

### 4. Timeline of material facts
- **Weeks before Oct 17:** High-school blockades over school conditions evolve into broader protests. (IT)
- **Oct 17:** Nationwide demonstrations; >500,000 participants; violence and looting begin in several cities. (LT)
- **Oct 17-18 weekend:** Arson (Limoges town hall), looting of thousands of businesses, clashes; ~2,400+ arrests, ~1,000 police injured. (LT)
- **Oct 19:** Crisis meeting; Interior Minister Nuñez admits loss of control and offers resignation (rejected); Lecornu orders localized curfews and does not rule out state of emergency. (LT)
- **Night of Oct 19-20:** Targeted curfews in Paris (République, Les Halles), Lyon, Nice, Lille area, etc.; reported calm in restricted zones. (IT)
- **Oct 20:** Lecornu states curfews contributed to calm; new ones to be decided locally; Justice Ministry reports ~123-149 jailed so far. (LT)

### 5. Sides
**Government / Macron-Lecornu team (IT/LT mix):**  
Steelman: Legitimate grievances exist, but organized ultra-left and criminal elements hijacked peaceful protests to create chaos ahead of the 2027 election; targeted curfews protect people and property without overreach, and accountability (including recovery of damages) will follow.  
Critique: LT — Curfews were narrow and effective overnight. IT — Blaming “ultra-left networks” while admitting intelligence failures shifts focus from governance shortfalls; election timing amplifies the incentive to project strength.

**Protesters / opposition / local mayors (IT mix):**  
Steelman: Decades of underinvestment in services and squeezed purchasing power are real; the state failed to anticipate or contain violence despite massive deployments, and curfews punish the many for the actions of a few while ignoring root causes.  
Critique: LT — Peaceful majority and legitimate complaints documented. IT — Some organizers and breakaway groups knew or tolerated escalation; demands for compensation and new protests risk further disorder.

**Ultra-left / opportunistic actors (DK on coordination):**  
Steelman: Highlighting systemic failures through direct action.  
Critique: LT — No public evidence of centralized command yet. IT — Masked groups and repeat offenders drove the worst violence and looting; prior records among many arrestees support opportunism over pure ideology.

### 6. Rumsfeld Matrix
**Known Knowns:** Curfews were localized and produced at least one calm night; arrests exceeded 2,400 with significant injuries on both sides; protests started over concrete grievances.  
**Known Unknowns:** Exact coordination or funding behind the most violent groups; full scope of intelligence failures; how many arrestees were opportunistic looters vs. ideological actors.  
**Unknown Knowns:** Police records of many arrestees; existing data on repeat offenders in French urban unrest.  
**Unknown Unknowns:** Whether next weekend’s planned protests escalate again or fizzle; downstream effects on 2027 election dynamics or European contagion.

### 7. Incentives map
- **Government:** Restore order narrative to limit political damage before 2027; curfews are low-cost signaling versus full emergency. Media attention favors violence footage, so containing it protects incumbents.
- **Opposition / locals:** Leverage failures for more central funding or political capital (e.g., Marseille mayor demanding compensation).
- **Media / platforms:** Violence, looting, and “chaos” outperform dry policy coverage; engagement incentives favor escalation framing.
- **Agitators / looters:** Low personal cost in the moment (masks, crowds) with high upside for theft or disruption; prior records suggest many are repeat players.
- **Broader public:** Fear of disorder and property damage pushes tolerance for restrictions; economic pain sustains protest energy.

### 8. Dueling AI advice
**Moral AI Advice:** Map the real grievances (costs, services) against the documented violence and arrest data. Prioritize restoring order while addressing fiscal and service failures; do not let election-year rhetoric substitute for competence on intelligence and deployment. Track whether curfews remain narrow or expand.

**Evil AI Advice:** Milk the unrest for maximum political extraction—blame the other side, promise tough measures that play well on TV, and use recovery funds as patronage. Let the next protest weekend cook if it weakens rivals; position yourself as the only adult in the room.

### 9. Practical takeaway
- Watch whether October 24-25 protests stay contained or repeat the pattern; localized curfews scaling or a state of emergency would signal escalation.
- Scrutinize arrest and prosecution data for repeat offenders vs. first-timers to gauge opportunism.
- Note any shift from targeted curfews to broader measures or troop deployments.
- Track compensation mechanisms and whether they actually claw back from perpetrators.
- Compare French coverage with parallel unrest in Italy and elsewhere for pattern recognition.
- Primary sources (prefecture statements, Justice Ministry releases) over partisan commentary.

### 10. What would falsify this read
- Evidence of large-scale, pre-planned coordination by named ultra-left networks with operational control over the violence.
- Sustained calm through the next protest cycle without further arrests or damage.
- Government data showing the majority of arrestees had no prior records and acted purely on economic grievances.
- Rapid, verifiable improvement in school funding or cost-of-living metrics tied directly to de-escalation.
