text:
When you think about someone who legitimately changed your life, who comes to mind?

About 10 or 11 years ago, my roommate and one of my best friends passed away suddenly in a skiing accident.

But rather than tell you about his death, I want to tell you about the life he lived and why it impacted me so much.

First, I sometimes wonder if he somehow knew his time on Earth would be short.

About six months before he died, a group of us went camping in Joe’s Valley to do some bouldering and enjoy the outdoors.

One night, as we sat around the campfire, he said something I’ll never forget:

“I could die tomorrow and be totally happy.”

And he meant it.

He genuinely loved his life.

Every single day, he woke up with the intention of doing something meaningful. He didn’t waste time. He wanted to experience everything life had to offer.

One afternoon, on a whim, I asked if he wanted to rappel Bridal Veil Falls.

Two hours later, we were standing in Provo Canyon, ropes in hand.

He loved canyoneering.
He loved climbing.
He loved skiing.
He loved cold plunging, long before it became popular.
He loved Nitro Circus.
He even qualified for and competed in World’s Toughest Mudder in Las Vegas.

And he was absolutely fearless. Sometimes to a ridiculous degree.

Once, he decided it would be fun to turn himself into a human torch. He covered himself in Vaseline and gasoline, lit himself on fire, and did a backflip into a lake.

His girlfriend broke up with him over that stunt because she didn’t want to be with someone so reckless.

He wasn’t particularly bothered.

That was him. Always chasing another adventure.

But as much as he loved adventure, he loved his friends and family even more.

He was fiercely loyal and protective of the people he cared about.

And if you asked him whether anyone in the world was more satisfied with their life than he was, he’d tell you absolutely not.

He loved being alive.

The morning of the day he died, he challenged me to complete a bouldering route at our climbing gym that he’d just conquered.

We loved challenging each other, even though he was the better climber.

That evening, I was on my way to the gym when I got the news that he’d died.

I didn’t turn around.

I couldn’t think of a better way to spend that evening than doing exactly what I would have done if he’d been there.

So I climbed.

I cried. I talked with friends. And I climbed.

One of his last social media posts was about how much he loved small cemeteries.

The last picture he took was of the sunset over Utah Lake during an evening run.

Sometimes I think about those little details, and about that night around the campfire.

“I could die tomorrow and be totally happy.”

I don’t know many people who could genuinely say that.

When my first child was born, I named her after him.

I couldn’t think of a better name.

He taught me what it means to live with purpose, to embrace life, and to love the people around you with unwavering loyalty.

And even now, more than a decade later, I sometimes feel his spirit close by.

I believe in guardian angels.

And I believe he’s one of mine.

Till we meet again, brother.

text:
NYC Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels grilled by NYT’s Nikole Hannah-Jones over integration plan

New York City Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels faced a public grilling by New York Times journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones at a school integration town hall Tuesday night over his lack of a detailed plan to address inequality in city public schools, more than 10 months into the new mayoral administration.

The Brooklyn-based civil rights writer recently published a follow-up essay about her choice of a racially segregated school for her daughter, outlining the prior gaps in her child’s education and renewing calls for a citywide school integration plan.

“The people who keep getting told they have to wait for the ‘right time’ are the people who need public schools the most,” Hannah-Jones said at the Washington Irving Campus near Union Square in Manhattan.

“You have to understand the discontent with this. It’s 10 months in,” she told Samuels. “When a timeline can’t be offered, you can understand why people will feel like that means you are just delaying.”

Throughout the contentious town hall, Hannah-Jones urged Samuels to eliminate selective or “screened” admissions, gifted programs, and priority entry in some of the most white and wealthier parts of the city. The chancellor dodged several questions, as the audience of families, teachers, and advocates heckled and jeered. Organizers estimated nearly 800 people were in attendance.

Samuels, meanwhile, insisted their disagreement was not about the need to address the issue, but the “how” to do so. The chancellor has said truly integrated schools are one of the top three priorities of his tenure, and he has started engaging local superintendents and parents in coming up with district-level plans.

“You need to be able to have conversations with communities, rather than pronounce something from on high, for it to actually work and be sustainable,” Samuels said.

“It’s not as though you’re going to remove screens, and it’s going to suddenly have everybody going everywhere, and it’s going to be great,” he added.

Hannah-Jones’s Sept. 20 article wrestles with the impact of the choice she made with her husband Faraji, who sits on the city’s Panel for Educational Policy, to send their daughter, Najya, to predominantly Black, low-income elementary and middle schools.

A decade after the first essay was published, Najya is now a teenager who disagrees with her parents’ choice. Given the chance to select her own high school, Najya picked the type of selective program her mother has spent her career advocating against.

In that school, the shortcomings of her prior education were laid bare as she was forced to catch up to her classmates, she wrote.

In an interview last month, Mayor Mamdani pledged to release a school integration plan, but there’s been little public progress. So far, the chancellor has launched “working groups” to focus on the issue. For now, the task forces are in only five local school districts, with the mayor intending to expand them citywide by 2028.

Meanwhile, Mamdani has largely been quiet or backed away from the sweeping admissions changes that he championed before and on the campaign trail. As a state assemblyman, he called for changes to specialized high schools such as Stuyvesant High School, where only three Black students received offers this year, but has since pledged to keep using a single entrance exam. More recently, he said he supported phasing out gifted programs in kindergarten, but ten months into his term, he has made no such moves.

At the same time, the mayor has explained his selection of Samuels as chancellor was based in part on his record as a local superintendent in integrating schools within his geographic district.

Throughout the town hall, Samuels kept returning to that experience, leaning on the inroads he made in Brooklyn and Manhattan, particularly by merging under-enrolled schools in ways that diversified their student body. By the chancellor’s estimate, there are roughly 30,000 children in schools with low enrollment — and with it, fewer opportunities for advanced coursework and extracurricular activities.

The chancellor also cited pandemic-era reforms, when the realities of school closures forced the system to pause screened middle school admissions policies. Today, there are 80 public schools that consider the grades and essays of applicants, which can lead to less diverse classrooms. Before the pandemic, there were 196 such schools, including in several districts that opted not to reinstate screens.

“I thank you for … your past work furthering integration. You did that as superintendent, and you had to be limited by what the administration would support. But now you are the head of that system,” Hannah-Jones countered. “There is no buck to be passed now. You head the system.”

Students tell their own stories

Beyond the discussion between Samuels and Hannah-Jones, some of the most poignant stories came from students themselves, who described the stakes of unequal schools with varying degrees of access to opportunity.

“I feel like there’s so much beauty in all the different school communities that exist in New York, and all the differences,” said Camilla Spillman, a Manhattan high school senior. Her school, serving grades 6 through 12, has dropped selective admissions since she first applied to middle school, and its student body has become more diverse.

“But I also feel like what school you go to should not so sharply define, like, what opportunities you’ve access to, what you’re going to do, and where you end up going,” she added.

Katelyn Melville attended her zoned elementary school in Queens, but tested into a selective middle school. She estimated she went from seeing “dozens of students who looked like me every day” to 10 or fewer. When it came time to select a high school, she surmised she had to pick between academic rigor and a feeling that she belongs. She went with a predominantly Black and Hispanic school in Brooklyn.

“To this day, I’ve never even taken basic chemistry, because the turnover at my school was so high, we never had a teacher stay long enough to teach it. When it came time to list my extracurriculars and advanced courses on college applications, it hit me: I was entering a race that had begun far before I realized,” said Melville, now a college sophomore.

“I can’t say I made the wrong decision, but I can’t say I made the right one either,” Melville said. “However, what I can say is I shouldn’t have had to make that decision at all.”

Hindu devotees scale back Shanti Mata festival amid airstrike fears

DMG Newsroom

21 October 2026, Kyauktaw

The annual Shanti Mata festival, a Hindu religious observance, was held on a smaller scale in areas controlled by the Arakan Army in Arakan State this year amid fears of military junta airstrikes.

Although the festival is traditionally marked by large public gatherings, local residents said this year's celebrations were held quietly to avoid attracting airstrikes.

"In previous years, the festival was celebrated on a grand scale," said a local festival organizer. "This year, we had to worry about airstrikes. Because junta forces target public gatherings with aerial bombardments, we did not dare hold large scale celebrations. We refrained from inviting outside guests and restricted the event strictly to residents within our own village."

Under normal circumstances, the Shanti Mata festival is celebrated over at least five days each October, with Hindu worshippers gathering for community prayers, traditional drumming and dance performances.

Devotees revere Shanti Mata as a protective deity believed to grant health, wisdom, prosperity and protection from hardship.

In previous years, thousands of worshippers from various townships gathered in Kyauktaw, Buthidaung and Maungdaw to participate in the festival.

"Because of airstrike fears, turnout was very low," a Hindu woman said. "In past years, visitors came from other townships. This time, we intentionally refrained from notifying people to prevent large crowds from forming."

During the festival, devotees offer Shanti Mata scented oils, lamps, flowers and 8 to 10 varieties of fruit, including bananas, grapes, apples and guavas. The observances include vegetarian feasts, devotional recitations by religious leaders, nightly traditional drumming, prayers and sacred dances.

On the final day of the festival, devotees immerse the idol of Shanti Mata in nearby rivers or streams, accompanied by floral offerings and floating lamps.

text:
Tuesday, October 20, 2026 · 11:59 PM ET

Every marquee on Tuesday had a famous name on it. Paul George in green for the first time. LeBron James in a Sixers jersey at Madison Square Garden. Barcelona's teenagers walking into the Parc des Princes. Envoys in Oslo. Earnings from the giants everybody waits for.

And almost every result on Tuesday was decided by somebody who was not on the marquee.

A wing who did not play in the first half. A reserve shooter left open because the defense was staring at the stars. A defender rising for a header. A midfielder chesting down a clearance. Industrial companies and credit bureaus carrying the stock market while the famous tech names went sideways. Working-level officials agreeing on next steps while the headliners talked past each other on television.

The headliner versus the rotation. That was Tuesday.

Monday was adding versus holding, and it gets one echo, and this is it. Monday said a lead is a thing you are doing, not a thing you have. Tuesday showed you who does the adding once the lead starts to shrink. It is almost never the name on the poster. It is the eighth man, the second option, the person nobody bought a ticket to see.

Start in Detroit, because the NBA season started there, in the afternoon, and it wrote the cleanest version of the argument before most people got off work.

The Detroit Pistons beat the Boston Celtics 121–113 at Little Caesars Arena. The league picked the matinee to open its season. It was the first game of the 2026-27 NBA year, and it was a sellout.

The headliner was Paul George. He is 37, in his 17th season, and he was playing his first game for Boston after the Celtics acquired him from Philadelphia in the deal that sent Jaylen Brown the other way.

George was magnificent. He scored 38 points. That is the most ever by a Celtic in his debut. He made 7 of 12 three-pointers. One of them moved him past Kyle Korver into eighth place on the NBA's all-time list for threes made. Early in the third quarter he hit three three-pointers in less than a minute, and Boston led 72–50.

Twenty-two points. On the road. In the second half. With the best player on the floor wearing your jersey.

That is a headliner doing everything a headliner is supposed to do. And it was not enough, because the other side went to its rotation and the rotation did not care who was on the poster.

Look at Javonte Green. He is a former Celtic. He did not play in the first half. JB Bickerstaff sent him in during the third quarter to bring some athleticism and some hustle on the wing, and the NBA's own live blog described it as instant impact.

Green scored 19 points, every one of them after halftime. He made five of his eight three-pointers. He finished plus-21, the best number on either team. A man who did not touch the floor before intermission was the swing of the whole afternoon.

Look at Duncan Robinson. He scored 21 points and made 5 of 9 from three. With Detroit trailing 99–95 and 7:34 to play, he hit a three that forced a Boston timeout. A minute later he drew a foul from Sam Hauser on a three-point attempt off a broken possession that went from Daniss Jenkins to Ausar Thompson to Robinson flying out of the corner. On the next trip, Robinson found Green for another three. Detroit had its first lead since it was 34–33 in the second quarter.

Then the run. Eighteen straight Detroit points. Green made a go-ahead three. Jalen Duren added a three-point play. Robinson connected again. Pistons 107, Celtics 99, with 5:10 to go.

Boston made one more push. Jayson Tatum found George for a three on the break that capped an 11–2 run and cut it to 114–110 with 1:06 left. That was the last time Boston got close. Detroit closed it out.

The quarter-by-quarter tells it. Boston won the first quarter by one and the second by twelve. Detroit won the third 37–30 and the fourth 39–25. Seventy-six points in the second half for the Pistons. The rotation came in, and the scoreboard flipped.

Duren finished with 22 points and nine rebounds. Cade Cunningham had 22 points and eight assists, and he gave the halftime its real summary: "We had a good talk at halftime, and we lit that fire a little bit better."

Ausar Thompson had 11 points, 11 rebounds and five assists. He also produced the highlight of the afternoon in the second quarter, floating through the lane and flipping in a right-handed reverse layup that had the broadcast reaching for figure skating comparisons. Even the highlight came from a role player.

The NBA called it the largest opening-day comeback in 30 years. The last team to come back from 20 or more down on opening day was the Celtics themselves, in 1997, against the Bulls.

Here is the honest part, because a thesis that hides its counterevidence is a slogan. Boston's second headliner had a bad day, and that matters to the story. Jayson Tatum, playing what is set to be his first full season since tearing his Achilles tendon in May 2025, made 6 of 23 shots and scored 13 points. AP noted that a lack of hustle on defense let Green take his time on the fifth three-pointer that put Detroit up 13 with 3:33 left. Tatum did pass for 11 assists, so it was not an empty night. But if the second star had made a few more, George's 38 might have been enough.

That is still the point. A team that needs both headliners to be perfect is a team with a thin rotation. Detroit needed neither of its famous names to be perfect. It needed Green, Robinson, Duren and Thompson to show up, and they did.

The Pistons outscored Boston 44–34 in the paint and 24–16 on second chances. Rotation numbers. Nobody puts a putback on a poster.

Monday's echo, one more time: Boston led by 22 and stopped adding. Detroit never stopped.

Now go to New York, because the second game of the night was built entirely around headliners, and the headliners mostly got outplayed by the people standing next to them.

The Philadelphia 76ers beat the New York Knicks 106–100 at Madison Square Garden. It was Ring Night. The Knicks raised their 2025-26 championship banner, their first title in 53 years, in a pregame ceremony that NBC said ran about 30 minutes. They wore gold-trimmed uniforms. Jalen Brunson wore gold sneakers.

Brunson told the crowd: "The joy that this city had this summer, we would love to replicate that again."

And on the other bench sat the biggest headliner in the sport. LeBron James, beginning an NBA-record 24th season, with his fourth team, in his Sixers debut. Next to him, Jaylen Brown, the 2024 Finals MVP, in his first game since Boston traded him. Joel Embiid. Tyrese Maxey.

You could not build a bigger marquee if you tried. And here is how the night actually went.

James finished with 14 points and nine rebounds. Brown had 19 points, eight rebounds and six assists. Embiid had 13 points and 11 rebounds on 4-of-15 shooting. Good lines. Not the lines that decided the game.

The game was decided by Maxey, who scored 28, made 8 of 9 free throws and opened the season with back-to-back three-pointers. And it was decided, in a very specific way, by Philadelphia's reserves.

AP put it plainly. The Sixers got three three-pointers from Anfernee Simons and two from fellow newcomer Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, "as the reserves took advantage of the open looks they got when the Knicks were caught focusing too much on the bigger names."

That is the essay, written by a wire reporter on deadline. The defense looked at the marquee. The rotation got the shots.

Simons finished with 13. Caldwell-Pope finished with 10. With LeBron on the bench in the third quarter, the NBA's live blog said Simons was the one keeping Philadelphia's offense afloat.

New York's side of the floor told the same story from the other direction. The Knicks' best stretch of the first half came from their bench. Andre Drummond, a former Sixer, crashed the glass against his old team and had 10 points and 12 rebounds by halftime. Jose Alvarado dropped a dime to Drummond, stole the ball from Brown at midcourt and pushed it for a transition three. New York led the bench battle 25–8 at the break.

Drummond said what every rotation player says on opening night: "I'm tired of the preseason. I'm ready for the real thing."

He finished with 12 points and 14 rebounds in about 24 minutes. Karl-Anthony Towns, the starting center, was in foul trouble in the first half and played about the same number of minutes. The backup was the best big man New York had for long stretches.

The Knicks led 58–54 at the half. They led 76–72 with three minutes left in the third quarter after Josh Hart, Brunson and Towns scored 13 straight New York points.

Then Philadelphia closed the quarter on an 11–0 run, finished with a three at the horn, and led 83–76 going into the fourth. Maxey's three-point play early in the fourth made it 87–78.

The Knicks did not fold. They cut it to 96–95 when Towns made a three. Embiid answered with a three of his own. New York got within one twice in the final three minutes and never got over the top.

Brunson scored 21 points on 6-of-19 shooting. Towns had 19 and 12. But Mikal Bridges scored four and OG Anunoby scored 10 on 3-of-12. The Knicks shot 37.2 percent. When half of your starting lineup goes cold and the other side's reserves are hitting open threes, the banner does not play defense.

James, afterward, sounded like a man who understood exactly what had happened. "I think we played exceptionally well, especially defensively," he said. "Didn't shoot the ball well, but we have capable shooters."

The biggest name in the building talked about defense and shooters. That is a headliner telling you the rotation won the game.

He was asked if he liked winning on another team's Ring Night. "Yeah, I do," he said.

One more piece of honesty. This was one game. The Knicks swept Philadelphia in the second round last spring, and AP noted they finished their title run 16–3 with the highest point differential in NBA postseason history. One October loss does not undo that. But it does tell you how the Sixers plan to beat people. Not with four stars taking turns. With four stars pulling the defense so the fifth and sixth guys get clean looks.

The night's third game, Thunder at Spurs, was still being played as this was written, so it stays out. Finished nouns only.

Now cross the Atlantic, because European football spent Tuesday night making the same argument at a much louder volume.

Paris Saint-Germain beat Barcelona 4–2 at the Parc des Princes in the Champions League. It was Barcelona's first defeat of the season. Sky Sports counted 40 attempts on goal between the two sides. The attendance was 47,421.

Look at the marquee first. PSG are the holders. Ousmane Dembélé is the Ballon d'Or holder. Lamine Yamal wears Barcelona's number 10.

Dembélé came off in the 19th minute with a suspected hamstring problem. The headliner was gone before the first half was even halfway done. And PSG went to the rotation.

Ferran Torres, who replaced him, was denied twice by Barcelona goalkeeper Joan García before the break and later hit the post. He did not score. But PSG kept arriving.

Désiré Doué opened the scoring in the 38th minute after an interception, driving to the edge of the box and rifling a low shot into the corner. BBC noted Doué had failed to score in his first seven games of the season and has now scored in each of his last three. He was named player of the match.

Barcelona answered through a 19-year-old full-back. Xavi Espart burst into the box ten minutes into the second half and beat Matvey Safonov at the near post. Fermín López made the assist. 1–1.

Read the Barcelona scorer one more time. Not Yamal. Not Raphinha. A teenage full-back. Even the visitors' rotation was doing the work.

Then PSG scored from a corner. Lucas Hernández, a defender, powered in a header in the 72nd minute. 2–1.

Then the headliner finally delivered. Yamal turned Warren Zaire-Emery, sprinted into the box and squeezed a shot between Safonov and the post from a tight angle in the 79th minute. 2–2. For about two minutes, the marquee had its moment.

Less than two minutes later, Vitinha controlled a clearance on his chest and volleyed it into the bottom corner. 3–2.

Five minutes after that, Fabián Ruiz tapped in Achraf Hakimi's low cross at the back post. 4–2.

Barcelona's best player produced a goal of genuine genius and lost. PSG's best player left injured and they won. That is the headliner versus the rotation in one match.

PSG are now three for three in the league phase with nine points. Barcelona stay on six. And Sky Sports pointed out the timing: Barcelona play Real Madrid at the Bernabéu in the first Clásico of the season in five days.

The rest of the Champions League night kept piling evidence on top.

Liverpool came from 2–0 down to beat Villarreal 4–3 at Anfield and stay perfect. Georges Mikautadze and Sergi Cardona put Villarreal up early. Then Alexis Mac Allister headed one in from a corner. Ronald Araújo headed in another to make it 2–2. Mac Allister scored again, and Florian Wirtz scored what proved to be the winner. Tani Oluwaseyi's late goal for Villarreal was not enough.

And UEFA's player of the match at Anfield was not Mac Allister with two goals or Wirtz with the winner. It was Rio Ngumoha.

In Istanbul, Fenerbahçe led Slavia Prague 2–0 inside 11 minutes through Oğuz Aydın and Mason Greenwood. Slavia came back. Lukáš Provod pulled one back, and in the 90th minute a 20-year-old substitute named Pavel Kačor hit an acrobatic volley to make it 2–2. A bench player scored Slavia's first point of the league phase.

In Stuttgart, the home side dominated the first half and led through Jamie Leweling. Atlético Madrid sent on Ademola Lookman at halftime. Within a minute of the restart, Lookman picked out Julián Alvarez, who swept it into the top corner. A halftime substitute changed the result inside 60 seconds. Atlético held on for a 1–1 draw with ten men after Morten Hjulmand was sent off.

Not every result fit the thesis, and the ones that did not deserve their own line. Manchester City beat AEK Athens 5–1 and Phil Foden scored a hat-trick, which is a headliner doing headliner things. In Baku, Serhou Guirassy scored both goals in Dortmund's 2–1 win over Sabah, his 21st in 27 Champions League appearances.

Foden and Guirassy are the reminder that stars still win games. The rest of the night is the reminder of what happens when the star is hurt, marked, or tired. Then the question becomes who else you have.

Now leave the stadiums, because the rest of Tuesday ran on the same rule, and in places where the stakes are much higher than a league table.

Start in Oslo.

Steve Witkoff, President Trump's special envoy, met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in the Norwegian capital on Tuesday. Jared Kushner joined by video link. Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre took part.

This followed weeks in which, as BBC put it, relations between Kyiv and Washington had soured to the point that Trump had said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president. Kyiv had accused the US of withholding key intelligence. Washington called that claim "scandalous."

Now watch who said what on Tuesday.

The headliners stayed in their positions. Speaking after Zelensky's news conference, Trump told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal," that Russia would like to "get it done," and that it was "time for Ukraine to end this war." In Moscow, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov had said the Kremlin would listen to what Witkoff offered while ruling out "any political concessions."

Witkoff himself was not at the joint press conference after the talks.

But below the headline level, something moved. A US official described the talks as "very productive and constructive" and said there was "strong alignment at the working level" among the US, Ukraine and Europe on "the next steps."

The working level. That is the rotation, in diplomatic language.

And the most concrete result of the day was not a peace plan. It was a piece of plumbing. Zelensky said intelligence sharing with the US on Russian missile attacks "works now." He spelled out why it mattered: "Speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, our children, adults, civilians because we can hear when ballistic is coming."

Early warning is not a headline. It is a feed of data that tells a family in Kyiv to get to the shelter a few minutes sooner. It was the most important thing restored on Tuesday, and almost nobody will remember the name of the official who restored it.

Stubb said "genuine progress" had been made but gave no details and warned that patience would be needed. Zelensky said Ukraine was "ready for negotiations," and added: "Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people because Russia attacks."

The cost of the gap between the headliners and the working level was counted in the same news cycle. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed in Russian drone attacks on Tuesday: four in Kyiv and the capital region, four in the Donetsk region, and two in Dnipro.

Witkoff is due to meet Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, with Kushner again joining virtually. That is the next marquee. What matters is whether the working-level alignment from Oslo survives contact with it.

Now go south, to the Strait of Hormuz, where the headliners spent Tuesday trading threats and the people paying for it were the crews.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard said tankers had struck mines its navy had laid in the strait and been set on fire. The IRGC said the vessels had tried to use what Iran unilaterally calls an unauthorized route through the southern part of the strait, near the Omani coast.

The IRGC statement, as reported by Euronews: "With the explosion of mines laid by the IRGC Navy in the illegal passage south of the Strait of Hormuz, two offending tankers were set on fire and brought to a standstill." The vessels were not named and the precise location was not disclosed. Other outlets reported a different number of ships, so this essay sticks to the IRGC's own words and makes no count of its own.

Euronews also noted the legal reality: Tehran has no recognized authority under international maritime law to restrict or authorize passage through the strait, which is subject to the right of transit passage under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. The claim is Iran's. The control is contested.

The headliners did what headliners do. Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, said Tehran would retaliate against any US attack. "In practice we have shown that we absolutely do not leave any blow unanswered," he said.

And then a detail that fits this essay almost too well. The IRGC-affiliated Tasnim agency quoted an unnamed Iranian security source saying that uncertainty over who holds decision-making authority in Washington was complicating negotiations. It named Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and negotiators Witkoff and Kushner as figures whose respective roles remained unclear to Iranian officials.

Read that carefully, and as a claim from one side, not a verdict. Tehran's complaint is not that there is no headliner. It is that there are too many, and nobody can tell which one is actually running the play.

Now the rotation. Arsenio Dominguez, secretary-general of the International Maritime Organization, said about 6,000 seafarers have been stranded in the strait since the war began. He criticized shipowners for continuing to send crews into the area.

Six thousand people. Nobody knows their names. They are not on any marquee. They are cooks and engineers and deckhands standing on ships that cannot move, while the famous names on both sides argue about routes and retaliation.

Now go to Wall Street, where the market made the headliner-versus-rotation argument with actual money.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 529.85 points, or 1.02 percent, to 52,495.88 on Tuesday. The S&P 500 rose 21.84 points, or 0.28 percent, to 7,712.57. The Nasdaq Composite fell 6.07 points, or 0.02 percent, to 26,424.82.

Look at the shape of that. The Dow, full of old-line industrial and financial names, jumped more than one percent. The Nasdaq, home of the famous growth names, went nowhere.

Reuters reported that 3M shot up 5.8 percent after saying it was expanding its data-center partnership with Amazon and raising its full-year profit forecast. CNBC reported Equifax, the credit bureau, leapt almost 12 percent at midday after beating earnings estimates. Hasbro, the toymaker, gained more than 5 percent after better-than-expected results and a raised revenue outlook. Northrop Grumman jumped nearly 5 percent after its quarterly report.

A sticky-note company. A credit bureau. A toymaker. That was the rotation that lifted the market on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, the headliners waited. Reuters quoted Bruce Zaro of Granite Wealth Management: "Investors really are waiting for the growth companies to report." Meta reports Wednesday. Netflix fell in after-hours trading after giving a disappointing quarterly forecast.

Not every name on the board cooperated. CNBC reported General Motors fell nearly 7 percent at midday even though its third-quarter numbers beat expectations and it announced a new $20 billion buyback. A beat is not always enough when the market wants something else.

The background mattered too. Brent crude touched $111.99 during the session, a five-month high, then settled down 76 cents at $108.79. The 10-year Treasury yield slipped to 5.121 percent. Jake Dollarhide of Longbow Asset Management called it "a market relieved that rates have come down, relieved that there's less volatility in oil prices, even though they remain elevated."

Oil near $110 is the Hormuz story showing up on a price screen. The seafarers in the strait and the traders on Wall Street were looking at the same war on Tuesday from opposite ends.

So here is Tuesday, laid out side by side.

In Detroit, the headliner scored 38, the most ever by a Celtic in a debut, and lost to a wing who did not play in the first half.

In New York, the most famous player in the sport scored 14 in his debut and won, because the defense was staring at him while his reserves hit open threes.

In Paris, the Ballon d'Or holder left in the 19th minute, Barcelona's number 10 scored a goal of genius, and the match was won by a defender's header and two midfielders in the last ten minutes.

In Liverpool, Stuttgart and Istanbul, the result turned on headers from corners, a halftime substitute and a 20-year-old off the bench in the 90th minute.

In Oslo, the headliners repeated their positions, and the working level restored the early-warning feed that tells Ukrainian families when the missiles are coming.

In the Gulf, the spokesmen traded threats, and 6,000 unnamed seafarers stayed stranded.

On Wall Street, the famous growth names went sideways, and a credit bureau, a toymaker and an industrial company carried the Dow up more than 500 points.

Here is the lesson, and it is the same in every room. The headliner gets you into the building. The rotation decides what happens once you are inside.

Headliners draw the defense, the cameras, the security guarantees and the analyst coverage. That attention is real and it is valuable. But attention is also a cost. Every defender looking at LeBron is a defender not looking at Simons. Every minute the world spends on the envoy's flight path is a minute it does not spend on the early-warning feed.

The teams that won on Tuesday understood that. Detroit did not try to out-George Paul George. It let him have his 38 and won the minutes he was not on the ball. Philadelphia let the Knicks chase its stars and took the open shots. PSG lost its biggest name before the 20th minute and never looked like a team that missed him.

Monday said keep adding. Tuesday told you who does the adding. Not the poster. The rotation.

Season openers are the one night of the year when every marquee is lit at once. Remember who actually won them.

The headliner versus the rotation. Know who is on your bench.

Ethiopia’s pursuit of sea access is not an attempt to challenge Eritrea’s sovereignty or lay claim to its territory. It is a matter of Ethiopia’s legitimate national interest and strategic necessity, one that can be addressed through peaceful negotiations and mutually beneficial arrangements.
When Ethiopia reached an agreement with Somaliland to secure access to the sea, Eritrea opposed it. Its position on Red Sea affairs, including its insistence that governance of the Red Sea should be restricted to coastal states, raises a fundamental question: On what principle does Eritrea oppose Ethiopia’s legitimate aspiration to secure sea access?
If Eritrea’s position offers no viable alternative for Ethiopia and instead focuses on preventing Ethiopia from securing access to the sea through peaceful means, such a stance contradicts the principles of good neighbourliness, regional cooperation, and shared development.
Ethiopia’s pursuit of sea access should not be treated as a justification for territorial conflict with Eritrea. However, just as Eritrea expects its own sovereignty to be respected, it must also refrain from policies that undermine Ethiopia’s legitimate national interests. The future stability of the region will not be secured by one country denying another its legitimate interests, but by pursuing solutions through dialogue, mutual understanding, and mutually beneficial cooperation.

URANIUM SENTIMENT & STOCK TRACKER

Wednesday, 21 October 2026

Uranium stocks barely moved on Tuesday in another quiet, low-volume session. But beneath the calm, Cameco and URA slipped to fresh lows.

Sentiment on X weakened again. Junior-miner investors sound close to giving up, while Cameco and physical uranium trust holders remain relatively calm.

SENTIMENT ON X

🔴 3.9/10 Cautious ▼

Previous 4.1 | 7d ago 3.8 | 30d ago 5.0
Confidence: Medium-low

- Junior-miner sentiment is approaching despair, with talk of stocks "going to zero," tax-loss selling and "pain only."
- A few investors are buying small dips, but even they admit they have little confidence that the bottom is in.
- Cameco holders remain relatively calm, mostly holding or adding ahead of the 30 October results.
- Physical uranium trust holders increasingly see the discounts as an opportunity, while some contrarians view the weakness in uranium stocks as a potential buying signal.

Signal: Sentiment remains gloomy and is drifting lower. There is little evidence of buyers stepping in with conviction.

URANIUM STOCKS

🔴 2.8/10 Oversold ▬

Previous 2.8 | 7d ago 2.8 | 30d ago 3.0
Confidence: High

- Energy Fuels: +0.61%, stabilising just above Monday's one-year low.
- Sprott Physical Uranium Trust: +0.43%.
- URNM: +0.33% to $43.19 on light volume, still above last week's low.
- Denison: 0.00%, unchanged.
- Cameco: -0.24% to $80.51, its lowest close since November 2025.
- URA: -0.26%, its lowest close in a year.
- Uranium Energy: -0.76%.
- Ur-Energy: -1.20%, the weakest performer, with no fresh company news identified.

Breadth: 3 up | 4 down | 1 unchanged

Every move was small. This looked more like a market drifting lower than investors rushing for the exits.

Signal: Uranium shares remain deeply oversold and are holding near their lows, but there is still no convincing rebound.

PHYSICAL URANIUM

Spot: ~$90.13/lb ▬
Unchanged for several days.

Long-term price: $96.50/lb ▬
Unchanged since the last monthly update. Spot remains roughly 7% below it.

Sprott Physical Uranium Trust: 12.59% discount to NAV (20 Oct), narrowing from 13.19%. No additional uranium purchased.

Yellow Cake: 22.02% discount to NAV, widening from 21.69%. Last confirmed share close: 525.0p (19 Oct).

Signal: The uranium price is holding firm while the vehicles owning the physical metal continue to trade at substantial discounts to the value of their holdings.

COMBINED SIGNAL

A gloomy crowd. Deeply oversold shares. And a uranium price that refuses to follow stocks lower.

It's essentially the same washed-out setup as last week, only quieter.

Selling pressure appears to be easing, but buyers aren't showing much conviction either.

That leaves room for a bottom to form, although it may take longer than investors hope.

BOTTOM LINE

Lean buy, but be patient.

When junior-miner sentiment approaches despair while the underlying commodity holds firm, opportunities can emerge for patient investors.

But poor sentiment alone doesn't mean the bottom is in.

I'd favour gradual accumulation over aggressive buying, keeping enough cash available in case the weakness continues.

The physical uranium trusts offer a way to gain exposure to the metal at substantial discounts, although those discounts could persist.

Cameco's 30 October results are the next important test of whether confidence among producer investors holds up.

What I'm watching: Whether Cameco and URA can defend their lows, whether the Sprott trust's discount continues to narrow, and whether sentiment finally begins to recover.

OIL, TRADE AND GEOPOLITICS: IS INDIA'S ENERGY POLICY BECOMING A BARGAINING CHIP?

🇮🇳 INDIA'S ENERGY SECURITY MUST COME BEFORE GREAT-POWER PRESSURE.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's October 20, 2026, remarks in Mumbai have raised important questions about India's oil imports, its relationship with Russia, and the growing role of the United States in India's energy choices.

According to media reports, Washington wants to explore cooperation with Reliance Industries on Venezuelan oil, including refining Venezuelan crude and potentially expanding oil production there. Rubio also acknowledged India's progress in diversifying its energy supplies.

But the larger question is this: Who ultimately benefits when energy purchases become part of trade negotiations and geopolitical pressure?

India imports a substantial share of its crude oil requirements. Its decisions affect fuel prices, inflation, transport costs and the daily lives of millions of ordinary citizens.

Russia has been an important source of relatively competitive crude for Indian refiners. Diversification can strengthen energy security, but replacing one supplier with another should be guided by transparent economic calculations—not simply by pressure from a powerful foreign partner.

The United States, meanwhile, has its own strategic and commercial interests. Its interest in Venezuelan oil and greater energy trade with India deserves scrutiny alongside India's national interests.

QUESTIONS THE PUBLIC DESERVES ANSWERS TO

• Will alternative oil supplies offer India genuinely competitive prices after accounting for transport, refining and other costs?

• Will any shift in imports increase or reduce the burden on Indian consumers?

• Are India's energy decisions being made independently, in India's economic interest?

• Will trade negotiations protect India's strategic autonomy and its freedom to maintain relations with multiple countries?

• Will the government disclose enough information for Parliament and the public to assess the economic consequences?

This is not a question of choosing Russia over America—or America over Russia. It is about ensuring that India's foreign policy serves its people.

A DEMOCRATIC GOVERNMENT MUST BE ACCOUNTABLE FOR THE ECONOMIC CONSEQUENCES OF ITS DECISIONS. Energy security, affordable fuel, transparency and strategic independence must remain central to India's national interest.

#DimaagiNaxal #Resistance #UnitedResistance

SOURCE — THE HINDU:

SUPPORTING REPORTS

1. The Indian Express — Trade deal close; Rubio urges India to boost US energy and technology purchases.

2. Hindustan Times — Rubio backs India's energy diversification amid Russian oil purchases.

3. Reuters — Rubio's India visit, the trade deal and Russian oil purchases.

text:
1 AM Top-of-the-Hour News

The Wall Street Journal is reporting that Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of a military grade version of his Starlink internet service that Ukraine relies on to operate its drone program in the ongoing conflict with Russia. Speaking to reporters while in Mumbai, India, Secretary of state Marco Rubio insists that the United States did not direct those actions "in any way:": “The president has made clear, at no point did he say deny them the use of this system because I'm trying to punish them or teach them a lesson. ”
Rubio also said it is not accurate that th US had foreknowledge or anything to do with the slowdown.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the slowdown hampered Ukraine's ability to defend itself against Russian drone strikes that caused serious damage and claimed lives, including those of civilians. Zelensky says the warning system is back up and running.

The FEMA administrator is urging states to prepare to handle their own disasters - without federal assistance. Politico reports Cameron Hamilton said this at a conference of emergency officials in Little Rock, Arkansas. Hamilton suggested every state should have the appropriate financial reserves. Hamilton speaking during an interview with Spectrum News.: “How do we reduce those time frames? How do we cut bureaucracy, get back to good common sense, good sound business practices to ensure that the state and local counterparts can be fully empowered to make decisions. ”
Hamilton did not specify a timetable for rolling out these changes. It comes less than a week after FEMA issued a report - noting state disaster agencies are "typically understaffed and underfunded." FEMA did not provide any comment.

The USS Abraham Lincoln is heading to a new home port. The Navy carrier recently returned after a near-record deployment in the Middle East. It will relocate permanently to Bremerton, Washington later this year to undergo a maintenance period.

Parisians are voicing mixed views on a second night of partial curfews. Police patrolled the capital after weekend riots and looting plunged France into one of its worst periods of unrest in years. This man - speaking here by way of an interpreter - does not think the peace will last.: “Imposing an 11:00 p.m. curfew isn't going to put an end to the looting. Generally, looting takes place during the day when unfortunately, all the shops are open and so on. I find it truly unfortunate and once again, I don't believe this is something that will actually stop the violence. ”
France's prime minister plans to meet unions today  to discuss security and has vowed a "massive" police deployment at protests going forward

The man who allegedly rammed his car into Australian lawmaker Helen Haines appeared in court and was charged with three offenses. Officials say he was charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a public official.
Doctors say they had to amputate one of Haines' legs after being struck twice. The suspect was restrained by members of the public before being arrested.

Nearly a decade after Boeing unveiled its largest 737 Max jet, the Federal Aviation Administration approved the Max 10 for passenger service, ending years of delays.: “Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says the certification followed extensive safety reviews, including thousands of hours of test flights and called it a major win for American manufacturing. 210,000 jobs across Boeing. That 80% of this aircraft is made in America. It's an American product. For airlines, the larger plane offers a way to carry more passengers on a single flight, potentially lowering costs per seat. For travelers, it could eventually mean more seats on popular routes, Spencer Rain, Worldwide News Network. ”

Sjoe! The 47th Presidency🇺🇲 Meets the 47% Problem🇿🇦: Leverage Is Not the Same as Delivery 🌍📉 ~ The Window Won't Stay Open Forever: South Africa's Race Against Its Own Failures 🚪⏳ ~ The Politics of Pressure: Washington Pushes, Pretoria Must Prove It Can Deliver ⚖️💧
Before the Threshold Hardens: A Middle-Income Democracy and the 47th PresidencySjoe. Nearly half the young people who want work cannot find it. Nearly half the treated water never reaches a paying tap. Nearly half the world’s adults endorse enough classic antisemitic tropes to register on the highest global index yet recorded. 

And the 47th President of the United States has already cut aid, excluded South Africa from the next G20, restricted visas for officials linked to certain land and race policies, and offered a refugee pathway for some of those who say they no longer feel safe. 

The claim is plain and testable: external leverage can raise the price of the status quo and legally existing instruments can be redirected toward litres delivered, formal jobs created and primary data elevated, yet residual operational capacity remains the binding constraint. 

Ideology does not raise water pressure. The window is still open.

Context: What the Numbers Actually Measure

Non-revenue water at 47.3 percent means roughly half the volume that leaves a treatment works never generates revenue—lost to leaks, theft, metering error or unbilled use (Department of Water and Sanitation, 2025/2026). The figure has held steady for years while bulk storage in some systems remains relatively high. 

Youth unemployment for ages 15–34 stood at 47.4 percent in the second quarter of 2026 (Statistics South Africa, 2026). 

The Anti-Defamation League’s Global 100 Index recorded 46 percent of adults worldwide holding deeply entrenched antisemitic attitudes—the highest level since systematic tracking began and roughly double the figure of a decade earlier (Anti-Defamation League, 2025). 

Cross-national studies place the statistical trough of the U-shaped well-being curve near age 47 (Blanchflower, 2021). 

Refining capacity has fallen from more than 720 000 barrels per day to roughly 250 000; imports now supply about 61 percent of demand and a finished-product premium of roughly R19 billion a year sits inside the Basic Fuel Price (South African Reserve Bank, 2026).

These series are independent. Their simultaneous proximity supplies an observational index of concurrent limits rather than evidence of design. 

Path dependence matters here: the Commissions Act 8 of 1947 still supplies the coercive powers for presidential inquiries, while educational legacies traceable to the 1953 statute continue to appear in labour-market outcomes. 

Institutional incentives favour processes that generate dense documentation over capacity utilisation. Filing is easier to count than residual chlorine. 

The Equity Equivalent Investment Programme already lets qualifying multinationals meet ownership-scorecard points by investing equivalent value in skills, enterprise development or infrastructure instead of selling shares (Department of Trade, Industry and Competition, n.d.). 

The practical question is whether any of these instruments will be scoped to residual chlorine logs, litres actually delivered and verified job absorption before the climate clock and the attitude index both move further.

Sjoe!
A full dam above a leaking network is less a reservoir than an expensive fountain that never reaches the garden.

Stirring Questions:
Does a system that loses nearly half its treated water retain any meaningful operational margin once evaporative demand rises?
If the 47.3 percent figure has been stable for years, what measurable change in physical losses would constitute evidence that the margin has been restored?

What these questions together illuminate is the difference between bulk hydrology and residual operational capacity. Without that distinction, preparedness remains weather commentary rather than engineering. 

The Pacific does not negotiate with supplier contracts.

1. The Index That Is Not a Cause

The recurring integer marks coincidence of strain rather than causation. An excluded 15–34 cohort enters the labour market at 47.4 percent and will later reach the mid-life well-being trough with thinner skills, thinner savings and thinner networks. 

A distribution network already discards 47.3 percent of treated volume. Critical wastewater systems have risen to 47 percent. 

The global attitude measure sits at 46 percent. No single source causes the others. 

Together they remove sequential room for correction.

Longitudinal tracking of the present youth cohort would reveal how early exclusion compounds into later vulnerability; without it the full cost appears only after cheaper intervention has closed. 

Governance scholars note that societies struggle to maintain simultaneous focus on slow-moving structural failures and more dramatic external signals. 

A recurring integer can function as a crude attentional device provided it is treated as a prompt for measurement rather than as proof of hidden design (Statistics South Africa, 2026; Department of Water and Sanitation, 2025/2026; Blanchflower, 2021; Anti-Defamation League, 2025).

Sjoe!
A number that keeps arriving at the scene of the strain is at least worth interviewing.

Stirring Questions:
Why does the same integer keep landing on moments of maximum strain across otherwise unrelated domains?
What would systematic tracking of the present 15–34 cohort reveal about their well-being and economic security at age 47?

What these questions together test is whether a society can convert numerical coincidence into better data infrastructure rather than into another round of expressive politics. 

The answer determines whether the next generation inherits measurement or merely another set of unresolved pressures.

2. The Cost That Cannot Seal a Joint

In February 2025 the White House issued an executive order suspending aid, directing prioritisation of resettlement for Afrikaners and other minorities facing race-based discrimination, and citing the Expropriation Act, farm attacks and certain foreign-policy alignments (The White House, 2025). 

South Africa was later disinvited from the 2026 G20. Visa restrictions followed for foreign nationals linked to policies enabling uncompensated land seizures, race-based discrimination or incitement. 

These steps impose concrete costs and alter relative incentives for decision-makers. They do not seal a joint or chlorinate a works. A full dam upstream of a network losing 47.3 percent does not raise pressure at the tap. 

Bronkhorstspruit supplied unchlorinated water for three weeks after a supplier dispute and recorded 408 gastrointestinal cases (author's note, the 'government of inefficiency throwing away text books rings a bell), mostly children under four. 

The climate clock does not pause for procurement cycles. 

Reciprocal openings in trade or technology become usable only if domestic institutions can absorb capital and performance contracts. External signals remain weather commentary until residual capacity moves. 

Cities that reduced non-revenue water below 25 percent before earlier strong El Niño events experienced shorter interruptions; the physics of leakage does not change with latitude (Department of Water and Sanitation, 2025/2026).

Sjoe!
The Pacific does not negotiate with supplier contracts. It simply raises the temperature and waits.

Stirring Questions:
How permanent is the shift in fuel-sourcing patterns once distant disruptions moderate?
What residual-chlorine and pressure-management standards would have to be met, and verified independently, before a works already losing half its product can be considered to have re-acquired buffer?

What these questions together force is a separation between climatic or diplomatic scale and operational readiness. The former is measured in degrees or statements; the latter is measured in residual chlorine logs and litres actually delivered.

3. The Pathway Already on the Statute Book

The Equity Equivalent Investment Programme allows multinationals that do not dilute equity globally to claim ownership points by investing equivalent value—commonly 25 percent of South African operations value or 4 percent of local turnover—into skills, enterprise development, suppliers or infrastructure. 

Cumulative commitments have reached at least R12.8 billion across firms including Microsoft, IBM, HP and automotive manufacturers, with documented job induction. Applied to refining, an EEIP vehicle could fund construction skills, local fabrication SMMEs and process-water efficiency while restoring domestic processing that has fallen from more than 720 000 barrels per day to roughly 250 000 and cutting the finished-product premium. 

The Central Energy Fund has outlined plans to revive the Sapref site toward 400 000 barrels daily, scalable higher subject to investment. Binding the spend to measurable absorption of the 15–34 cohort and reductions in non-revenue water converts compliance into capacity. 

Institutional incentives that elevate process and loyalty metrics over measured outcomes lengthen the interval between a proven technique and its deployment. 

The legal pathway exists; the open variable is whether terms of reference prioritise litres processed, jobs created and litres delivered (Department of Trade, Industry and Competition, n.d.; South African Reserve Bank, 2026; Central Energy Fund, 2026).

Sjoe!
Owning the minerals while renting the refining is a particular kind of national specialisation. It has the virtue of clarity, if not of comfort.

Stirring Questions:
Can technical partnerships that demonstrably reduce physical losses and disease risk be evaluated primarily on engineering outcomes rather than on diplomatic posture?
What concrete, time-bound metrics would demonstrate that any such partnership has altered the 47.3 percent figure rather than generated announcements?

What these questions together identify is a friction that operates on the same timeline as the climate and attitude clocks. 

Every month spent resolving annotation is a month the leakage rate remains uncorrected.

4. The Signal Before the Threshold

The Commissions Act 8 of 1947 remains the operative source of subpoena, document-production and oath powers. Activating it while the global antisemitism index sits at 46 percent—to elevate primary attitude and incident data, examine the documented antisemitic elements of the 2001 Durban NGO Forum (circulation of materials including The Protocols of the Elders of Zion and revival of “Zionism is racism” language that prompted U.S. and Israeli withdrawal), and impose short public timelines—would convert observation into preventive governance before the measure hardens at 47. 

Projecting that record outward demonstrates willingness to treat the index as an action trigger on an axis the United States already prioritises. The signal does not erase other bilateral disputes; it reduces friction on one and models early measurement. 

Low opening thresholds generate visibility; high closing thresholds keep decisive outcomes distant. Design discipline—public timelines, mandatory data protocols, clear implementation pathways—is the difference between a stage with excellent lighting and an instrument that reduces risk. 

Success is testable by improved visibility and incident response versus another unfinished stage (Anti-Defamation League, 2025; contemporary accounts of the 2001 conference).

Sjoe!
An open door is only a problem if the room behind it is never cleaned.

Stirring Questions:
What precise terms of reference, timelines and implementation mechanisms would keep such a commission from joining the list of unfinished stages?
How would elevating primary data to parity with high-status frames change public understanding and policy calibration?

What these questions together test is whether institutional design can move from oxygen extraction to measurable risk reduction. 

The answer determines whether the next commission is remembered as precedent or as performance.

5. The Test That Ideology Cannot Pass

Every pathway returns to the same series. Sustained, independently verified declines in non-revenue water below 30 percent with residual-chlorine compliance above 95 percent at previously critical works; measurable absorption of the current 15–34 cohort into formal employment or enterprise; and movement or non-movement in attitude and incident indices. 

Cities that reduced losses before prior strong El Niño events experienced shorter interruptions and lower disease spikes. The physics of leakage does not vary by political system. The integer organises attention; it does not alter the arithmetic of youth exclusion or the revenue loop that under-funds maintenance. 

Cumulative evidence from labour statistics, water audits, trade data and attitude surveys converges on residual operational capacity as the binding constraint. 

Economic incentives reinforce the pattern: municipalities that lose nearly half their treated water also lose the revenue that would fund maintenance, lengthening the next repair cycle. 

The loop is self-reinforcing until an external shock makes the shortfall visible in hospital admissions rather than balance sheets (Department of Water and Sanitation, 2025/2026; Statistics South Africa, 2026; South African Reserve Bank, 2026).

Sjoe!
The evidence does not require a miracle. It requires the decision to treat water as an engineering problem at the speed the climate clock now sets.

Stirring Question:
What ring-fenced maintenance budgets and technical-appointment rules would have to be in place, and audited quarterly, before the 47.3 percent figure can be treated as temporary rather than structural?
If comparative experience shows shorter disruptions where losses were reduced first, what prevents the same sequence here?

What these questions together convert is the cumulative evidence into an operational test. Either the physics of leakage and chlorination can be altered at the required speed, or the language of a miracle of execution remains the accurate description of the gap.

Synthesis

Independent lines of evidence converge. Official labour statistics, water audits, Reserve Bank analyses of refining capacity, the statute book, and the most comprehensive global attitude survey available all land on or near the same integer without requiring coordinated design. 

The pattern does not prove hidden causation; it supplies an organising observation that becomes useful only when converted into measurement and timed action. 

External costs already imposed by the 47th presidency raise the price of delay. EEIP and the 1947 Act already exist as vehicles that can be scoped to litres, jobs and primary data. 

Multiple independent observations—budget classifications that weight process over capacity, manufacturing shares that stabilised near 12 percent of GDP after foundational statutes existed, and peer industrialisers that improved rankings through infrastructure execution rather than further legal volume—point to the same residual. 

The argument is falsifiable: a sustained, independently verified decline in non-revenue water below 30 percent, accompanied by residual-chlorine compliance and measurable youth absorption, would constitute disconfirmation of the residual-capacity claim. 

Until that occurs, the practical distance remains large enough that only unusually rapid restoration of maintenance and proven tools can close it. 

The stakes are measurable in litres delivered and admissions avoided.

Sjoe!
The map improves when every relevant data point is given the same light. The window is still open.

Stirring Questions:
What would constitute falsifying evidence for the claim that early intervention at the 46 percent mark is higher-value than waiting?
How does a society distinguish genuine preventive urgency from the political utility of prolonged process?

What these questions together keep is the entire argument testable and focused on timing rather than on permanent moral positioning. 

Testability is the difference between a useful framework and an unfalsifiable story.Objections

Objections Addressed

Some will argue that focusing on a number risks superstition. The number is treated as an index, not a cause; the underlying phenomena are examined on their own evidence. 

Others will contend that a new commission will simply become another unfinished stage. Design-specific replies—tight terms of reference, public timelines, mandatory elevation of primary data—mark the operational difference between process and precedent. 

A third view holds that antisemitism concerns or refining capacity are secondary to other priorities. Youth unemployment at 47.4 percent, non-revenue water at 47.3 percent and global attitudes at 46 percent are all measurable; all respond better to early than to delayed attention. 

Trade-offs exist; invisibility is not a neutral trade-off. External pressure cannot replace domestic engineers; it can only alter the relative price of employing them. 

Absolute justice resources remain necessary; the data record relative weight after foundational statutes existed and the concurrent industrial outcome.

Sjoe!
History can be taught at any resolution. Residual chlorine cannot.Stirring Questions

When a treatment works operates without chlorination for three weeks and produces a multi-pathogen outbreak, what independent verification of supplier contracts and residual chlorine logs is required before the plant is declared safe again?
How is that verification scaled nationally when 47 percent of wastewater systems are already rated critical?

What these questions together convert is an incident report into a diagnostic of residual capacity. If the system cannot maintain chlorination under current load, the probability of simultaneous failures rises with every additional degree and every additional dry week.

Conclusion

The 47th presidency arrives while an observational index still marks an open window. External costs have already been imposed. Legally existing instruments can be redirected toward litres delivered, formal jobs created and primary data elevated. 

Residual operational capacity remains the binding constraint. 

Ideology does not raise water pressure. The remaining non-miraculous path is accelerated competence measured in litres delivered and admissions avoided. 

After the statutes that dismantled exclusion were written, the marginal return lay in reliable energy, functioning logistics, higher fixed investment and compounding skills. Measurable capacity outweighs additional exclusive instruments. 

The window is still open. 

The only remaining question is whether terms of reference and verification protocols will treat the series as the operative tests while it can still be opened from the inside.

Sjoe!
The factory floor does not file. It builds.

PAKISTAN WAS CREATED IN 1947. TWO NATIONS CANNOT HAVE FOUGHT EACH OTHER FOR CENTURIES WHEN ONE DID NOT EXIST.

Religions Addressed in John 3:16

“John 3:16 addresses a number of ‘isms.’ The phrase ‘For God’ responds to atheism, which claims there is no God. The phrase ‘so loved’ responds to fatalism, which asserts God is an impersonal force. The phrase ‘the world’ responds to nationalism, which says God loves only one group of people. The phrase ‘that He gave’ responds to materialism, which says it is more blessed to receive than to give. The phrase ‘His only begotten Son’ responds to Mohammedism, which says God has no Son. The phrase ‘that whosoever believes’ responds to five-point Calvinism, which says Christ died only for the elect. The phrase ‘in Him’ responds to pluralism, which says all religions are equal. The phrase ‘should not perish’ responds to annihilationism, which says there is no hell. The phrase ‘but have everlasting life’ responds to Arminianism, which says God only gives life conditionally. John 3:16 is a simple biblicism which reveals the mind, the heart, and the will of God.”

Source: Whosoever Will, David Allen and Steve Lemke quoting Jerry Vines

text:
An investor publicly talking shit about a founder like this is an instant blackballing in my book.

Delaware corporate law has something called the business judgment rule. Courts generally presume that directors act in good faith, on an informed basis, and in the honest belief that their decisions serve the company’s best interests. Courts won’t ordinarily second-guess the commercial wisdom of those decisions.

There’s even Delaware case law involving the use of corporate jets (Conte v. Greenberg, 2024).

Likewise, company-paid accommodation is perfectly normal in the startup world. It can be part of a founder’s compensation, serve legitimate business purposes, and, in certain circumstances, offer tax advantages. None of that is inherently improper, let alone fraudulent. Literally every YC founder I have ever met did this at the time of founding their companies for example.

Outsiders do not have complete information, and to allege fraud on incomplete information is the height of stupidity and ignorance.

text:
A close friend of mine from over 20 years ago lives in South Carolina. 

I told him, "Bro, you have to experience this," so he drove down two hours from Charleston to join us. 

We were told there was no parking at Beeple’s studio, so he parked his car in a nearby lot and we grabbed an Uber.

When we got into line at the venue, my buddy checked his pockets and realized his car keys were gone.

Luckily, he has an AirTag on his keychain. We checked the tracker and saw the keys were moving, so we knew right away they were still in the Uber. I tried contacting Uber Support, sent messages, and even used AI to translate text messages into Spanish for the driver, but got nothing back. 

Every time I tried calling the driver's direct number, it rang and he immediately hung up.

I bought my buddy a hotel room after the event so he could get some rest while we figured it out.

Watching the AirTag, we noticed the keys had been sitting at an apartment complex for a few hours. 

Assuming it was the driver’s home, we grabbed another Uber and headed over there. I told my friend, "Let me do the talking just in case things get sketchy."

Just as we pulled up about 1,000 feet from the complex, we watched the AirTag start moving in the opposite direction on the map. 

The apartment area was pretty rugged, and when I showed a picture of the driver to a local woman outside to ask if she recognized him, she gave me a sharp look like I was an undercover cop, and said “I don’t know him.”

Our cool Uber driver offered to take us back to our hotel for cash so we could keep tracking them.

text:
Christian Okoye had never played a single down of football when he walked into his college coach's office and asked to try out.

He picked running back for one reason. He had seen Marcus Allen make one great run in a Super Bowl on TV.

Within five years, he led the entire NFL in rushing.

Here is the whole thing.

He grew up in Enugu, Nigeria, one of seven kids. He was a small boy when the fighting tore through the country, and he has said his family was extremely poor.

"If you haven't been around war count your blessings because it wasn't pretty."

He played soccer until he got too big for it. So he started throwing things. The discus. The hammer. The heavy iron ball.

He was good enough to represent Nigeria at the African Games. A friend in California got in touch with the track coach at Azusa Pacific, a small school outside Los Angeles, and the coach offered him a scholarship.

He came to America to throw the discus in the Olympics. The Los Angeles Olympics were a short drive away.

He had the marks. Nigeria left him off the team anyway.

"For some reason, Nigeria left me off the team."

He called it a big blow. So he went to his coach's office and said he wanted to play football. He was 23.

He did not like getting hit. He thought about quitting. The coaches and his friends talked him out of it.

The first time he scored a touchdown, he did not know what to do. He just stood in the end zone holding the ball until a referee came over and asked for it.

By his last season at Azusa Pacific he was leading the country in rushing yards per game. He was 6 foot 1, about 260 pounds, and he ran a 4.45 forty for the Kansas City Chiefs.

They took him in the second round.

A teammate started calling him the Nigerian Nightmare. It stuck.

In his third season he led the NFL with 1,480 rushing yards, made the Pro Bowl and was named first team All-Pro.

After his rookie year, his father came to America to see it.

"I'm so glad that my dad was able to come out here after my rookie year."

Here is the honest part. It did not last long. Both knees needed surgery, and after six seasons the Chiefs released him with an injury settlement. He has said he was ready.

"I was actually happy to leave."

But he never really left the kids.

In 1990, while he was still playing, he started a foundation. Its motto is education through sports. He runs free athletic clinics, and he goes back to Nigeria to check on the children his foundation works with there.

He has been working to bring football to Nigeria, starting with flag football because pads cost too much.

The country that left him off its Olympic team is the one he keeps going back to.

Most people don’t hate spending money on good tools. They hate the quiet feeling that their money is being wasted.

If you run an online store or draft marketing campaigns for a living, you know this feeling intimately. You open your billing dashboard, see a stack of heavy technical features and untouched credits sitting right there, and a small part of your brain whispers: Why am I paying for all of this?

You don’t need a full developer's engine room just to rewrite a headline, polish a customer email, or throw together a quick visual for a product offer. You just need a practical assistant that works when you need it, without forcing you to pay for features you’ll never touch.

That’s the silent fatigue a lot of creators and business owners are carrying right now. We end up paying full price for complex tech infrastructure when all we really want is a lean, reliable tool to get daily work done.

Finding a way to strip away that extra bloat and keep your access for less than $15 over three months isn't just a clever budget move - it’s peace of mind. It’s taking back control of your monthly overhead so that cash stays where it belongs: in your ad spend, your inventory, or your bottom line.

If your daily workflow centers on clear copy, sharp communication, and simple product visuals, stop letting heavy tech pricing quietly drain your margins.
This is spot on. Keep your software stack lean, protect your cash flow, and stop paying for power you don't use.

text:
My thoughts on Dr. Lisa Cook and Reparations

Dr. Lisa Cook made history as the first Black woman to sit on the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, sworn in after President Joe Biden nominated her in 2022. She built an impressive academic foundation for the role: a bachelor's degree in philosophy and economics from Spelman College, earned magna cum laude, a Marshall Scholarship that took her to Oxford University for a master's degree in economics, and a PhD in economics from the University of California, Berkeley.

Dr. Cook has expressed support for reparations for Black Americans to address the long-term economic damage caused by slavery and systemic discrimination. Her academic commentary and public statements from 2020 and 2021, before her confirmation, document this stance clearly. She endorsed legislative action on the issue, laid out justification for targeted relief, and offered a direct economic assessment. During a September 2020 appearance on the EconTalk podcast, she said "everybody benefited from slavery" and that the United States "absolutely needs some sort of reckoning with that." She argued that economic proposals around reparations deserve serious consideration. Republican lawmakers made these positions a major focal point during her 2022 confirmation hearings, questioning whether her advocacy aligned with the Federal Reserve's neutral mandate.

Her 14-year term as a Board of Governors member gives her a powerful seat at the table. A Federal Reserve Governor carries three primary responsibilities:

Setting monetary policy
Regulating and supervising banks
Overseeing the Federal Reserve System

A Black American holding this role carries weight across several institutional and economic pathways that economists and policymakers often highlight:

Influencing monetary policy through an inclusive lens
Shaping banking regulation and community reinvestment
Advancing economic research on inequality
Building representation and institutional trust

Could this help build the case for reparations?

Absolutely. Representation of Black Americans in high-level economic positions, combined with the rigorous economic data the Federal Reserve produces, strengthens the case for reparations. Advocates regularly draw on the Fed's research and structural insights to back their claims through:

Quantifying the wealth gap with Fed data
Drawing academic credibility from Black leadership in these roles
Using Fed modeling to project wealth transfers

Since returning to office, Trump has pushed to remove Dr. Cook from her post. Her background, her seat at this powerful table, her 14-year term, her economic education, and her public support for reparations line up as a striking coincidence worth sitting with.
