Trump touted the deal at his North Carolina rally this week: 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘋𝘦𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘞𝘢𝘳 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘣𝘦 𝘪𝘯𝘷𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 $1.5 𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘵𝘰 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘥𝘶𝘤𝘦 𝘤𝘶𝘵𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨-𝘦𝘥𝘨𝘦 𝘴𝘦𝘮𝘪𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘥𝘶𝘤𝘵𝘰𝘳 𝘤𝘩𝘪𝘱𝘴 𝘳𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘪𝘯 𝘕𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘩 𝘊𝘢𝘳𝘰𝘭𝘪𝘯𝘢 𝘢𝘭𝘴𝘰. 𝘐𝘵’𝘴 𝘣𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘯𝘦𝘸𝘴.

The chips in question aren't the kind that run a laptop. Wolfspeed makes 𝐬𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐚𝐫𝐛𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐠𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐮𝐦 𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐝𝐞 semiconductors — the hardened components used in drones, radar systems, missile defense, and electronic warfare, exactly the hardware America can't afford to source from a rival. Wolfspeed's largest U.S. footprint runs through North Carolina, where the administration wants that production anchored for good.

The timing matters. Wolfspeed filed for bankruptcy protection barely a year ago. Instead of watching a strategic chip supplier go under or get bought out from overseas, the Pentagon is betting taxpayer-backed capital on keeping the production — and the jobs — on American soil.

Every dollar of defense-chip capacity built here is a dollar China and Taiwan's supply chain no longer control.

text:
The Mind Illuminated - A Complete Meditation Guide Integrating Buddhist Wisdom and Brain Science.pdf

CULADASA (JOHN YATES, PH.D.) AND MATTHEW IMMERGUT, PH.D. WITH JEREMY GRAVES

THE MIND ILLUMINATED 

A COMPLETE MEDITATION GUIDE INTEGRATING BUDDHIST WISDOM AND BRAIN SCIENCE (Cont.)

pg. 438-443

STAGE EIGHT

Mental Pliancy and Pacifying the Senses

The goal of Stage Eight is complete pacification of the senses and the full arising of meditative joy. Simply continue to practice, using skills that are now completely effortless. Effortlessly sustained exclusive attention will produce mental and physical pliancy, pleasure, and joy.

Stage Eight: The meditator leads, and the elephant obediently follows. The mind has been tamed. The monkey and the rabbit are gone: scattering of attention and dullness are no longer a threat.

• The elephant has become completely white as the hindrances of Ill-will and Agitation Due to Worry and Remorse are replaced by the blisses of physical and mental pliancy.

• There is no flame, because meditation is effortless. 

PRACTICE GOALS FOR STAGE EIGHT

You begin Stage Eight as an adept practitioner. You can consistently pacify the discriminating mind and enter a state of mental pliancy. In other words, you have effortlessly stable attention and powerful mindfulness. Each sit, it can take a while to reach effortlessness, and sometimes you’ll stay at Stage Six or Seven the whole time. But you should be able to reach mental pliancy fairly regularly and remain there for the rest of the sit.

Much of the practice at this Stage simply involves exercising your newly compliant mind’s abilities to explore.

Think of your mind as an unknown territory where no one else has been, and no one but you can go. You alone are responsible for how you proceed, and how you use your skills and develop your mind.

You have two goals for this Stage. As an adept meditator—with a highly compliant mind due to a complete pacification in Stage Seven—your first goal is to exercise this mind, explore its nature, and discover and develop its inherent abilities. Think of your mind as an unknown territory where no one else has been, and no one but you can go. A spiritual teacher can point you in certain directions, make suggestions based on their own experience, and offer valuable methods developed by other meditators in the past. After all, one human mind isn’t so different from another. But it’s your own needs and interests that will determine how you actually proceed. Follow wherever they take you. I promise, you will go places and do things with your mind that are pointless to describe or discuss with anyone who hasn’t made this journey for themself.

The second major goal is complete pacification of the senses, which produces physical pliancy and fully developed meditative joy. Since both pacification of the senses and meditative joy result from the same unification process, we treat them as two parts of a single goal. To pacify the senses, you will exclude all sense objects from attention while sustaining metacognitive awareness. To cultivate meditative joy, you don’t need to do anything different or special, just keep practicing. It will arise naturally once the sensory minds grow quiet and the mind as a whole becomes sufficiently unified.

You’ve mastered Stage Eight when your eyes perceive only an inner light, your ears perceive only an inner sound, your body is suffused with pleasure and comfort, and your mental state is one of intense joy. 

EXERCISING THE NEWLY COMPLIANT MIND

Your first goal is to exercise the skills you’ve already mastered in order to explore the nature of the mind and fully develop its inherent abilities. Mental pliancy gives you effortlessly stable attention and sustained, powerful mindfulness, particularly in the form of metacognitive introspective awareness. The practices in the next section will help you experiment with attention.

text:
What did a woman’s work in an Egyptian temple look like? This painted figure offers a glimpse, with a rattle held upright in her hand.

Dating to about 1250–1200 BCE, this fragment of a tomb painting from Deir el-Medina shows a woman holding a sistrum: a rattle that women often played in temple ceremonies. Her image survives in paint applied to plaster over mud. The damaged inscription includes a reference to Amun, leading the Walters Art Museum to suggest that she may have belonged to his temple staff. The instrument makes her religious activity visible, even though the surviving words cannot tell us her complete story. Music could be part of the work of worship.

That is a small but vivid glimpse of a woman’s religious role. Also, an excellent assignment for anyone whose family has complained that they make too much noise. 😹🎶

Photo: The Walters Art Museum, 32.9, CC0; square detail crop.

ちなみに、「君の名」（５３）の大庭秀雄監督は、横浜映画学校１年の時の「演出」の授業をお持ちだった。監督作の大阪同郷のバタヤンこと川端康成原作「雪国」（６５）の演出とシナリオの違いを概説なさる半期授業だった。
　カントを大阪下町人にしたように超まじめな私は、「雪国」の原作をばらばらにして、シナリオの該当箇所にファイルアップして、授業開始を待ち、１度目は出たところ、その２ヶ月ほど前、日比谷東劇でテオ・アンゲロプロスの２３０分の「旅芸人の記録」（７５）を１日に２回見た※１記録をもっていた私に、いや授業の中で、「あんなの、パンフ見なけりゃわからんもんなど映画なんかじゃない！※２」と言われ……。
　去年、１年先輩の三池崇史監督のウィキペディアを読んだら、大庭監督の意見とくいちがいがあり、映画学校の授業に出なくなった、みたいなこと書いてあるのに、驚き……。私は、（城戸賞受賞することになる）２時間シナリオ提出したあとの二学期からはほとんど出ている。
　が、たしかに「君の名は」（５３）の監督とは学校パンフで知ってはいたし、ラジオドラマ放送の時は女湯がカラになったというような都市伝説も知ってはいたけれど、で、バタヤンの小説も好きくなかったし、（また、６０にもなって、判り始めてきたなどと書くと、この変態じじいがと誤解もされるのもシャクだしで。南無）
　大庭先生の授業だけでなく、１学期の授業は、夏休み終わりまで提出の２時間用映画のシナリオ作りに執心した。３時起きの新聞奨学生で、とくに午前中はヤタラ眠いし、学割きかない「映画スクール」だったので、定期など買ったことなく、交通費の削減にもなったりで。
　が、ある時、大庭監督の方から「キン君、なぜ授業でないの」と、不意に声をかけていただき、私の名を知っているなどないともおもっていて、まるで返事にならないアワアワとなったが……当時はビデオというものが、大金持ちか電器メーカーの家（注１）にしかない時代で、大庭監督の映画を見るわけにも行かず、だから授業で「雪国」をといういまだ内容つかめない小説にも興味わかずで……。
　だが、映画学校を卒業して２０年はたったあと、その２６の時の、第一回監督作品川島雄三「還ってきた男」（４６）の陣中見舞いを大阪から大船撮影所にしたとき、なんと３ショットの写真を撮られていたことを知って。あに図らんや、覆水盆に返らず、こぼれたミルクもグラスにもどらず……（哀）オー！マイゴッド！
　とくに、織田作之助の声一つこの世に残っておらず（ラジオに２．３度出たはずなのに、NHKも消失💢）
　その笑い方一つだけ大庭監督にきかせていただいても恩人となるはずだったのに。ネットなき時代が、にくい。

※１　当時は、まだ入れ替え制ではなかった。
※２　私も、総論は反対だけど、３時間ものなぜ原爆作った化粧品会社の名前みたいな者の映画見る必要など、ない、映画じゃない、などと、その各論には今なら、鋭意、同意賛成できる。
注１なぜ、「家」にあるか――ほぼＶＨＳシステムだったのに、ソニーのみが、他システムのベーターだったので、その（駆逐するためなどの？弱点）モニタリング仕事もあったりで。
Incidentally, Hideo Oba—director of *Your Name* (1953)—taught a "Directing" course during my first year at the Yokohama Film School. It was a semester-long class in which he outlined the differences between the original novel *Snow Country*—written by his fellow Osaka native, Yasunari Kawabata—and the screenplay for his own film adaptation (1965).
Being an incredibly earnest student—much like the "Osaka working-class" version of Kant—I took the original *Snow Country* apart, organized the text to correspond with specific sections of the screenplay, and waited for the class to begin. I attended the first session, but when I mentioned that I had watched Theo Angelopoulos’s 230-minute *The Travelling Players* (1975) twice in a single day at the Hibiya Togeki theater about two months prior, Oba-sensei remarked, "A film that you can't understand without reading the program pamphlet isn't a film at all!"
Last year, I was surprised to read on the Wikipedia page for director Takashi Miike—who was one year ahead of me—that he stopped attending classes at the film school because he disagreed with Oba-sensei’s views. As for me, I attended almost every class from the second semester onward, after I had submitted a two-hour screenplay (which would go on to win the Kido Award).
To be fair, I was aware from the school brochure that he was the director of *Your Name* (1953), and I knew the urban legend that public bathhouses for women would empty out whenever the radio drama version was broadcast. Furthermore, I wasn't particularly fond of Kawabata’s novel. (And I’d rather not write about how I’ve only begun to truly grasp it now that I’m sixty—lest I be misunderstood as some sort of "perverted old geezer." *Namu*.)
Beyond just Oba-sensei’s course, I spent the entire first semester—right up until the end of summer vacation—devoted to crafting a two-hour feature film screenplay. As a "newspaper scholarship student" who had to wake up at 3:00 a.m., I was perpetually sleepy—especially in the mornings. Since my "film school" didn't offer student discounts, I never bothered buying a commuter pass; not having one actually helped me save on travel costs.
One day, Director Oba suddenly asked me, "Kin-kun, why aren't you attending class?" I hadn't imagined he even knew my name, so I was completely flustered and couldn't manage a coherent response. Back then, video players were luxuries found only in the homes of the ultra-wealthy or families connected to electronics manufacturers—so watching Director Oba’s films was out of the question. Furthermore, I had no interest in the novel *Snow Country* (Yukiguni), which was the subject of our class—I couldn't even grasp what it was about.
Twenty years after graduating from film school, I visited the Ofuna Studios from Osaka to offer some encouragement during the production of *The Man Who Returned* (1946)—the directorial debut of Yuzo Kawashima. To my surprise, I discovered that a three-person photograph had been taken of us back when I was twenty-six. Alas—what’s done is done; spilled milk cannot be put back into the glass... (Sigh) Oh, my God!
It’s particularly painful because not a single recording of Sakunosuke Oda’s voice remains in this world—even though he appeared on the radio a few times, those recordings have been lost by NHK! 💢
If only I could have asked Director Oba about the way Oda laughed—that alone would have made him a true benefactor to me. I despise the fact that we lived in an era before the internet.

*Note 1: At the time, theaters did not yet use a "rotating" (fixed-session) screening system.*
*Note 2: While I might disagree with the general premise, I can now wholeheartedly agree with the specific arguments—such as the idea that there’s no need to sit through a three-hour film by someone whose name sounds like a cosmetics company that manufactured atomic bombs, or that such a work doesn't even qualify as "cinema" in the first place.* Note 1: Why was it in the "home"? Given that the VHS system was the dominant standard, Sony’s use of a different system—Betamax—meant that there was a need to monitor it (perhaps to facilitate its elimination from the market?).

text:
The Echoes of Her Wings
She walks the world as light walks water—
soft, and yet the surface never stays the same.
A beautiful woman, and in her wake the air
remembers. A glance becomes a turning.
A quiet word, offered like bread,
finds its way into another’s hunger
years later, in a room she will never enter.
This is the oldest truth the mystics knew:
nothing small remains small.
The butterfly does not measure the wind
it starts; it simply opens.
So does she.
Her kindness is not loud enough
to be called a sermon,
yet somewhere a life changes course
because she once stayed when leaving
would have been easier.
The echoes are not always sound.
Sometimes they are the courage
another person finds at midnight
and does not know why.
Sometimes they are the gentleness
passed from hand to hand
like a cup that has never been empty.
We think we leave footprints.
What we leave are currents.
What we leave is the way the light
leans differently after we have passed.
She does not see most of what she moves.
That is the mercy of it.
The soul is not asked to carry
every consequence it sets in motion—
only to move with care,
only to open its wings
and trust the larger air.
Long after her name has softened
into the stories people tell
when they are trying to explain
why they became kinder,
the ripples will still be traveling.
Somewhere a stranger will choose mercy
instead of the harder thing,
and will not know
that the choice began
with a beautiful woman
who once looked at the world
as if it were already holy
and then, without announcement,
made it so.

text:
When we had our first 10 customers at Octolens, I knew every name and what they were building. At 100, I kept up pretty well, but some were off my radar. Now at many hundreds, the blind spot keeps growing.

Keeping this blind spot as small as possible is my #1 priority.

Here are the things I do every day to work against it and keep customer obsession alive, because I'm convinced it's what got us this far:

1. I still own customer support

A few weeks ago, I allowed myself to add AI replies based on our docs for nights and weekends, but otherwise it's all me, and I check every AI response in the morning.

We also now offer a Slack Connect channel to every customer who converts, and it's GREAT for feedback.

2. I use Octolens for social listening daily

At this point, we get a good amount of brand mentions ourselves to learn from. On top of that, we track competitors and industry terms to get even more feedback. People are definitely honest on Reddit and X.

Everything is routed either to a Slack channel for me to see or to a scheduled task in Claude for analysis.

3. I look at every qualified trial signup

Completed onboarding → Slack notification → I qualify → goes to Attio for an outreach flow where I help and offer a call

4. I watch PostHog recordings and run through onboarding every week

We're constantly tuning onboarding, and I try to put myself in the shoes of someone who's never seen Octolens or a social listening tool before.

Sometimes I can hardly watch a session recording, because UX I thought was great turns out to be really unintuitive.

5. I offer 15-minute demos in the app and in every email

There's literally a little picture of me in the app and a button to book a demo call that anyone can use.

__

What's tricky is that the blind spot is a result of things going well. The more you grow and the more customers you have, the further you naturally drift from the people using your product.

It doesn't fix itself, so you need to actively work against it.

text:
Regional Real Estate Roundup

There's never a dull moment in South Baldwin County commercial real estate! From a million-dollar land sale in Orange Beach to new businesses, exciting development plans and major investments in infrastructure, there's plenty happening across our coastal communities.

Here's a look at what's making headlines in Orange Beach, Gulf Shores, Foley and Robertsdale!

Orange Beach: A Million-Dollar Deal on Canal Road!

Let's start with a big one! The west lot of Pelican Plaza, located next to Melanie Martin Interiors and Blalock Seafood on Canal Road, recently sold for an impressive $1 million!

The 1.32-acre parcel brought approximately $757,576 per acre, or $17.39 per square foot, believed to be the highest price per acre achieved for a land sale along Canal Road.

Heather Harp of RE/MAX of Orange Beach represented the seller, while Tim Arant of RE/MAX Gulf Shores represented the buyer.

It's another exciting transaction highlighting the value of prime commercial property along one of Orange Beach's most established business corridors. Location continues to be a major factor in the commercial market, and this sale certainly gives property owners and investors something to talk about!

Baldwin County: A 180-Day Pause on Certain Rezoning Requests

One of the biggest topics in local development news is Baldwin County's recently approved 180-day rezoning moratorium.

On October 6, the Baldwin County Commission approved a temporary pause on certain rezoning applications within areas governed by county zoning regulations. The measure also includes restrictions involving new data center and renewable energy projects.

But don't mistake this for a halt to growth! The moratorium does not stop all construction or commercial development, and it does not automatically apply within the city limits of Orange Beach, Gulf Shores, Foley or Robertsdale.

The goal is to give county officials time to review land-use regulations and plan for future growth.

For commercial investors and developers, it's an important reminder that knowing a property's zoning and permitted uses before purchasing can make all the difference!

Gulf Shores: Coffee, Anyone? PJ's Coffee Plans New Location!

Coffee lovers may soon have another stop along the Foley Beach Express!

A new PJ's Coffee drive-through is proposed just south of Coastal Gateway Boulevard, near the new Gulf Shores High School.

The Baldwin County Planning and Zoning Commission approved the site plan October 1 for the approximately 511-square-foot building on 0.87 acre.  It's another example of how commercial businesses are looking toward growing traffic corridors and expanding neighborhoods for their next locations.

Gulf Shores: Waterway Village Keeps Getting Better!

There's more activity happening around Gulf Shores' Waterway Village!

The city continues working toward public plaza improvements surrounding the pedestrian bridge over the Intracoastal Waterway.

At the October 19 City Council meeting, officials were scheduled to consider construction agreements and approximately $1.2 million in additional funding for the improvements.

The vision is to create better pedestrian connections and welcoming public spaces that could bring additional activity to nearby restaurants, shops and businesses.

Waterway Village is definitely an area to keep an eye on as these improvements take shape!

Foley: What's Next for Magnolia Walk?

Foley continues to grow, and Magnolia Walk is another development worth watching!

Located near OWA along the Foley Beach Express and Miflin Road, the approximately 99-acre mixed-use development is part of the ongoing investment activity in one of South Baldwin County's growing commercial corridors.

At its October 19 meeting, the Foley City Council was scheduled to consider additional economic development and project financing agreements involving SCP/BPG Magnolia Holdings LLC.

While specific tenants and future businesses have not yet been confirmed, the project represents another opportunity for commercial investment and development in Foley.

With so much activity along the Foley Beach Express, it'll be interesting to see what takes shape next!

Foley: Making Room for More Industry!

Foley isn't just growing in retail and restaurants. Industrial development is getting attention, too!

On October 5, city officials considered rezoning approximately 121 acres near North Juniper Street and Foley Beach Express for the proposed North Foley Industrial Park. The planned industrial park could create opportunities for manufacturing, warehousing, distribution and other businesses looking to establish a presence in Baldwin County.

More industrial development means the potential for additional jobs, business investment and economic activity throughout the area.

Robertsdale: More Commercial Development on the Horizon!

Robertsdale is getting in on the action, too! A construction project listing published in early October outlines plans for a 5,479-square-foot retail building and a 3,936-square-foot service station/car wash facility.

The proposed project carries an estimated construction value of approximately $1.52 million and was listed in the post-bid stage. Its exact location and construction timeline have not yet been confirmed.

With its central location and convenient access to Highway 59 and Highway 90, Robertsdale continues to offer opportunities for businesses serving Baldwin County's growing population.

Until Next Time

Whether you welcome the ongoing development or view it with a cautious eye, staying informed is essential as our coastal communities evolve. The goal of the Real Estate Roundup is to bring you clear, objective updates on the projects, decisions, and changes shaping South Baldwin County—ensuring you always know what is happening in your own backyard.

About the Author

Heather Harp is a commercial and residential real estate professional with RE/MAX of Orange Beach, specializing in commercial investment properties, land sales, development opportunities and business transactions throughout Baldwin County and the Gulf Coast.

text:
The Evolution of the Guitar Volume Pedal, 1930s–2026

The volume pedal allows amplified guitar control without interrupting playing. Hawaiian and lap-steel musicians used foot controls before World War II to soften attacks and extend perceived sustain. Unlike tremolo, a volume pedal provides continuous amplitude control.

By 1948, Rowe Industries of Toledo, Ohio, offered the DeArmond Model 600. Its rocking metal treadle mechanically operated a potentiometer, changing output without external power. The foot effectively replaced the hand on the guitar’s volume knob.

During the 1950s, Paul Bigsby developed a combined volume-and-tone pedal. Forward-and-back movement controlled volume, while side-to-side movement adjusted tone. Fender introduced its own volume pedal in 1954, followed by the dual-axis Volume Tone in 1958. Both remained in Fender’s catalog until 1984.

Pedal-steel players demanded smooth, repeatable control. Goodrich Sound, founded by Philip Goodrich in 1965, specialized in this market. Its cord-operated models, including the later H-120 family, translated treadle movement into potentiometer rotation. The founding date is not the Model 120’s introduction date.

The next important change was optical control. Tel-Ray/Morley pedals became prominent during the 1970s, using a lamp, movable shutter and photosensitive component instead of a mechanically driven audio potentiometer. DeArmond also produced an optical model, the 1630. Optical designs reduced potentiometer contact wear, although their light sources and electronic components still required maintenance.

Ernie Ball introduced its volume pedal in 1977. An aluminum treadle and cord-driven potentiometer offered a straightforward, unpowered design. Later versions accommodated different source impedances, and its familiar mechanism became a pedalboard standard.

As rack processors and electronic instruments proliferated, BOSS expanded the category with FV-series pedals. The later FV-500H and FV-500L offered high-impedance mono and low-impedance stereo versions, respectively, plus expression outputs.

Active and contactless designs further changed the technology. Hilton developed infrared-controlled pedals; Telonics introduced digitally selectable response tapers while preserving an analog audio path. Lehle’s Mono Volume, introduced in 2015, used a Hall-effect magnetic sensor to control an analog voltage-controlled amplifier, avoiding a conventional audio potentiometer. The smaller Mono Volume S followed in 2022, adding USB MIDI capabilities.

Ernie Ball’s 2020 VPJR Tuner integrated active volume control and a digital tuning display. By 2026, pedals could attenuate audio directly or transmit expression and MIDI control data to another device.

Passive pedals can load high-impedance pickups and change treble response, particularly with long cables. Buffered or active designs help manage impedance, while expression pedals generally carry control voltages rather than guitar audio.

Placement remains fundamental. Before overdrive, a volume pedal changes the signal driving distortion; afterward, it changes the distorted signal’s level. Positioned before delay or reverb, it can silence new notes while existing repeats and reverberation decay. The underlying purpose has not changed: precise musical dynamics underfoot.

M/I Homes sold fewer homes at lower prices and kept less of each sale, so profit fell much faster than revenue. Revenue slipped 5% to $1.1 billion, and profit per share before write-downs fell by about a third. Orders dipped after three quarters of growth, and chief executive Robert Schottenstein blamed higher mortgage rates and weaker demand. The company gave no view on the fourth quarter.

• Revenue: $𝟭.𝟬𝟴𝗕 (−5% from a year ago)
• Profit per share, before inventory write-downs: $𝟮.𝟳𝟬 ($4.14 a year ago)
• Gross margin, before inventory write-downs: 𝟮𝟭.𝟯% (24.5% a year ago)
• Outlook: 𝗡𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗴𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗻 (the company issues no revenue or profit targets)

⚖️ 𝗩𝗲𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because the margin fell further instead of finding a bottom, and the order recovery stalled in the same quarter. Overhead also took a bigger share of a smaller revenue. The good news: record equity, no bank borrowing and another $50 million of buybacks, and the Midwest business keeps adding land while the South shrinks.

The question now is whether this quarter is a pause or the start of a second leg down. One view: orders dipped only against a record spring, and the Midwest pipeline carries the builder until mortgage rates ease. The other: each order now costs more in rate buydowns, so every sale brings a thinner margin. Fourth-quarter orders against 1,921 a year ago, and the margin before write-downs, will tell.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝗕𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲

🟢 𝗠/𝗜 𝗛𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗞𝗲𝗲𝗽𝘀 𝗔𝗱𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗶𝗱𝘄𝗲𝘀𝘁
M/I Homes reports two regions. Northern covers its Midwest markets such as Columbus, Chicago and Minneapolis; Southern covers Florida, Texas, the Carolinas and Tennessee. For more than a year the builder has been signing up new lots in the north while letting its southern pipeline run off, and that continued this quarter.

• Northern lots under contract, land it has agreed to buy but not yet paid for: 13,396, up 24% from a year ago
• Southern lots under contract: 12,113, down 21%
• Northern orders: up 1% from a year ago
• Average price of a northern home in backlog: $577,000, up 2%

This matters because last quarter the company reported a higher gross margin in the north than in the south, so every lot it adds there replaces a weaker southern one. But Northern brings in only 40% of orders, so a stronger north cannot offset a weaker south on its own, and new lots take years to become homes.

What to watch: the Northern lot count in the land position table next quarter. A further rise while Southern lots fall would mean the builder is moving its growth to the Midwest for good.

🟢 𝗢𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗦𝗹𝗶𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗱 𝟮% 𝗔𝗳𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗤𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵
New contracts are the orders a builder signs in a quarter, and they lead revenue by a few months. M/I Homes had grown orders for three straight quarters, with a record spring. This quarter it signed 1,861, 2% fewer than a year ago, against a weak base: last year's third quarter was itself down 6%.

• Orders in the first nine months: 6,598, up 5% from a year ago
• Cancellation rate: 12%, up from 8% last quarter and level with a year ago
• Sales per community per month: about 2.6 by our math, down from 3.4 last quarter
• Average community count: 240, up from 234 a year ago

So the homebuilder sold from more communities but sold less in each, which fits the "weaker demand" chief executive Robert Schottenstein described. One quarter does not settle it, but the record spring no longer looks like the start of a trend.

What to watch: fourth-quarter orders against 1,921 a year ago, reported in late January. A second decline would mean the spring recovery has run its course.

🟢 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝗘𝗾𝘂𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗔𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 $𝟱𝟬 𝗠𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗕𝘂𝘆𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸
M/I Homes buys back its own shares at the same pace whatever the quarter brings. It spent another $50 million in the third quarter, as it has every quarter for more than two years, and chief executive Robert Schottenstein described its financial condition as "excellent".

• Shareholders' equity: record $3.25 billion, up 3% from a year ago
• Book value per share: $129.94, up 8%
• Diluted share count: 25.9 million, down 5% from a year ago
• Borrowings on the $900 million credit line: none; homebuilding debt is 18% of capital, unchanged

The buyback matters because it softens the fall in profit per share, and the builder does it without borrowing. One caution: cash fell to $621 million from $734 million a year ago. Operations used cash in the quarter because it kept buying land while deliveries fell, so it now carries net debt of 2% of capital, against a net cash position a year ago.

What to watch: the buyback amount in the fourth-quarter release. A move above $50 million would mean the board is spending the cash pile rather than holding it for land.

🐻 𝗕𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲

🔴🔴 𝗘𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝗛𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗦𝗮𝗹𝗲 𝗘𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗮 𝗬𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗔𝗴𝗼
Chief executive Robert Schottenstein said the company "produced fairly solid results". The margin numbers say otherwise. Gross margin, the share of revenue left after the cost of land and building, fell to 20.9%. Before a $4.7 million write-down of land and homes it was 21.3%. A year ago the same measure stood at 24.5%.

Cost of sales, the line for land and construction, took 78.7% of revenue, up from 75.5% a year ago. Prices went the other way, with the average closing price down 4%. So M/I Homes paid more to build each home and sold it for less, and the margin took both hits at once.

Operating income fell 38% on revenue down 5%, because overhead did not shrink with sales. The margin before write-downs now sits below every quarter of 2025, even the fourth, when the builder took $40 million of write-downs and still reported 22.6% before them. Write-downs have now appeared in five of the last six quarters.

What to watch: the gross margin before write-downs in the fourth quarter, reported in late January. Another fall would mean the money spent lowering buyers' mortgage rates, plus land costs, is still rising faster than prices, and the margin has not found a bottom.

🔴 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗻 𝗕𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗜𝘀 𝗦𝗵𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻 𝗘𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗠𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲
The Southern region, M/I Homes' operations in Florida, Texas, the Carolinas and Tennessee, brings in about 60% of its orders. Management has named Tampa, Sarasota and Austin as weak markets in earlier quarters, and this quarter the whole region moved backwards while the north held level.

• Southern orders: 1,115, down 4% from a year ago
• Southern deliveries: 1,292, down 5%
• Southern backlog value: $508 million, down 16%
• Average price of a southern home in backlog: $501,000, down 8%

The price figure is the one to worry about, because a falling backlog price means the builder is accepting less, or selling smaller homes, to keep selling at all. Southern backlog value has been below the year before in every quarter of the past year, and the gap widened again after narrowing in the spring.

What to watch: Southern backlog value against $514 million at the end of last year. A further double-digit fall would mean the weakness is spreading beyond the three markets management has named.

🔴 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗞𝗲𝗲𝗽𝘀 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝗦𝗮𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗦𝗵𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗸
General and administrative expense, the cost of head office, division staff and systems, rose 8% to $76.6 million while revenue fell. Selling expense, the cost of sales staff and model homes, was level in dollars. Together they took 13.1% of revenue, against 11.9% a year ago.

This matters because overhead is the one cost the company controls. It has climbed from 11.6% of revenue at the end of last year to 13.1% now, as the builder opened communities and kept staff for a recovery that has not arrived. By our math each point of overhead costs about $11 million a quarter in pre-tax profit.

What to watch: general and administrative expense in dollars in the fourth quarter. A figure above this quarter's on lower revenue would mean the cost base is set for growth the market is not delivering.

🔴 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗖𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁 𝗧𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗡𝗲𝗲𝗱𝘀 𝗮 𝗕𝗶𝗴 𝗙𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗤𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿
M/I Homes gives no revenue or profit outlook, but it does set one target each year: the average number of communities it sells from. Three months ago the company said the 2026 average would be about 5% above 2025, which by our math means about 240. Communities matter because orders equal communities times the sales pace in each.

The third-quarter average was 240, and the nine-month average 236. To reach the full-year target the fourth quarter therefore has to average about 254, by our math. The builder ended September with 246 communities, so it would need to open many more than it closes in the next three months. The release does not repeat the target.

What to watch: the average community count for the fourth quarter and the full year, in the January release. A full-year average near 236 would mean the target slipped by a year, and that the 2027 order base is smaller than planned.

🔴 𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗸𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗤𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗗𝗶𝗱𝗻'𝘁 𝗔𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿
Five standing concerns got no new numbers in the press release, because the figures that would test them live in the quarterly filing or on the earnings call, neither of which is in these materials. Each one could move the case on its own.

• Unsold homes under construction: the count and dollar value will show whether the builder is carrying a large stock of speculative homes into a weaker market.
• Mortgage rate buydowns and incentives as a share of housing revenue: a rise above last quarter's 6.2% would say the margin fall is self-inflicted.
• Florida warranty claims: $3.4 million was still accrued at mid-year for attic ventilation problems in two communities; the warranty note will show whether that figure has grown.
• Mortgage warehouse lines: $252 million of financial services borrowings were due to expire on 20 October; the debt note will show whether the lender renewed them.
• The margin gap between speculative and built-to-order homes: management has declined to give it in every recent quarter.

👓 𝗢𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗲𝘀

𝗦𝗰𝗵𝗼𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗶𝗻 𝗦𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁 𝗚𝗼𝘁 𝗛𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗤𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿
"Our third quarter results reflect increasingly difficult market conditions, including higher mortgage interest rates, weaker demand and growing economic uncertainty," chief executive Robert Schottenstein said. Deliveries fell 2% even though the builder sold from more communities than a year ago. Three months ago Schottenstein rated housing conditions as above average. He still cites "the long-term fundamentals of the housing industry", but offers no view on the fourth quarter.

— • — • —

💲 𝗢𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗞𝗣𝗜𝘀

𝗕𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗹𝗼𝗴 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): $𝟭.𝟭𝟬 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝟮,𝟬𝟰𝟲 𝗵𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀  ⇒ stable
Backlog, the homes customers have signed for but not yet received, is worth 9% less than a year ago, with 7% fewer homes. The gap to last year had narrowed for four straight quarters, then widened slightly this quarter. The average price in backlog slipped to $539,000 from $553,000.

𝗜𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): $𝟯.𝟲𝟬 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻  ⇘ decelerating
Inventory, the land and homes on the balance sheet, grew 5.5% from a year ago while revenue fell. Land and lot purchases rose 17% to $135 million. Development spending fell 15%. The builder is still buying land faster than it sells homes, which is why operations used cash this quarter, and inventory growth has slowed from 9% a year ago.

𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗽𝗿𝗲-𝘁𝗮𝘅 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): $𝟭𝟯.𝟰 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻  ⇘ decelerating
The mortgage and title arm earned 19% less than a year ago, on revenue down 5.5%. Its profit has been level or lower than the year before in each of the last three quarters as fewer homes closed. A year ago it was growing while homebuilding shrank, so it no longer cushions the group.

— • — • —

❓ 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿?
The full-year community count target needs a fourth-quarter average near 254 by our math, against 246 communities at the end of September. The release neither repeats the target nor says how many openings are scheduled.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀?
Last quarter mortgage buydowns and incentives took 6.2% of housing revenue, up from 4.2% a year earlier. The gross margin fell again; the split between buydown cost, lot cost and mix decides whether the fall is temporary.

𝗗𝗶𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗢𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗯𝗲𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗴𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀?
About $252 million of financial services borrowings were due to expire on 20 October. At mid-year the company said it expected an extension but could give no assurance. The release, dated the next day, does not mention the outcome.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝗹𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗱𝗮 𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘁𝘆 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝘄?
At mid-year $3.4 million remained accrued for attic ventilation problems in two Florida communities, after $5.5 million of charges in the first half. Such claims tend to grow after the first estimate.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘁𝗵-𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀?
The company gives no revenue, delivery or margin outlook. With backlog worth 9% less than a year ago and the sales pace slowing, readers have no company figure to set against the fourth quarter.

Democratic Senators Move to Block U.S.-Saudi Nuclear Deal https://t.co/req5OH24DG 

Should Iran Have a Nuclear Bomb—and Why?

(The choice should be obvious. Offer Iran economic incentives, demand intrusive inspections and enforce clear limits. Preventing a nuclear-armed Iran is a legitimate objective; another war is not the only way to achieve it.)

Nobody is threatening Iran with a nuclear bomb. So why does Tehran insist on pursuing nuclear capabilities that could eventually produce one? The answer appears to be less about survival than prestige, regional influence and strategic equality.

Iran’s implied argument is straightforward: Pakistan has the bomb, Israel is widely believed to possess nuclear weapons, and Saudi Arabia has pursued nuclear cooperation with the United States. Why, then, should Iran be denied the same status?
The argument may be strategically understandable, but it is hardly a compelling justification. Yet Iran’s leadership appears determined to pursue its nuclear ambitions, whatever the cost.

Can America stop it by force?
 A full-scale invasion aimed at seizing Iran’s highly enriched uranium and destroying its nuclear infrastructure would be extraordinarily costly. It could require a massive ground force, inflict thousands of casualties and cost hundreds of billions of dollars. Even then, there would be no guarantee that Iran’s nuclear ambitions would disappear. Washington has little appetite for another prolonged war.

Negotiation, backed by economic incentives, offers a far more sensible alternative.
America should revisit the 2015 nuclear agreement negotiated under Secretary of State John Kerry, strengthen its inspection provisions and seek verifiable limits on Iran’s nuclear programme. In return, Iran should receive meaningful economic relief. The objective must be clear: prevent weaponisation through enforceable safeguards rather than launch another potentially disastrous war.

Pakistan’s record also deserves attention. Its nuclear proliferation network, associated with A.Q. Khan, demonstrated how dangerous the spread of nuclear technology can be. International controls must remain rigorous to prevent any recurrence. Economic desperation, however, is not proof that Pakistan will sell nuclear technology again; the danger must be assessed through evidence and effective monitoring.

India, meanwhile, has strengthened its nuclear deterrent through its nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarines. A credible second-strike capability reduces an adversary’s confidence that their first nuclear attack could escape devastating retaliation. It is an important component of strategic stability in South Asia.

But Iran’s circumstances differ. Pakistan’s principal strategic rivalry is with India, while Iran’s confrontation centres largely on Israel and its relationship with America. Neither rivalry makes acquiring a nuclear bomb inevitable or necessary.

Iran’s pursuit of nuclear weapons could trigger a regional arms race, invite further attacks and deepen its economic isolation. The prestige Tehran seeks could become a strategic liability.

Washington must therefore choose between two imperfect paths: a costly, dangerous military campaign or a difficult diplomatic settlement.

text:
🇺🇳 #UNSG10 | Will Lana Nusseibeh enter the race before the next straw poll — or will the Security Council hold another round before diplomatic manoeuvring produces a new candidate?

The race for UN Secretary-General has reached the point where arithmetic gives way to architecture. With António Guterres’s term ending on December 31 and the straw polls having narrowed the field without producing a candidate acceptable to all five permanent members, the question is no longer who has the most support. It is who can survive the veto test.

The sixth straw poll, held on October 16, was the first to use colour-coded ballots. Rebeca Grynspan topped the field with nine “encourage” votes, but also drew five “discourage” votes, two of them from permanent members. Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Rafael Grossi each drew “discourage” votes from two permanent members as well.

Every one of the seven candidates received at least two “discourage” votes from among the five permanent members. Macky Sall, Olara Otunnu and María Fernanda Espinosa each received three; Ivonne A-Baki received five. Straw polls are informal and a “discourage” vote is not a formal veto, but the colour coding made the underlying problem hard to ignore. A field in which every candidate carries a red mark does not close the race. It reopens it.

Timing matters. A late entry can force Council members to reconsider their options while the search for a candidate acceptable to all five remains unresolved. Late candidacies are not necessarily signs of weakness; they can reflect a recognition that the existing field has failed to settle the only question that matters: who gets through the Council without a veto?

Lana Nusseibeh fits that logic. She served as the UAE’s Permanent Representative to the UN from 2013 to 2024, more than a decade inside the Council’s negotiations, rivalries and compromises, and she brings the networks of a country that has expanded its influence through engagement with competing powers rather than exclusive alignment. Reports that Washington is looking beyond the declared candidates, while Grynspan is still described as the front-runner, suggest the field is less settled than the roster implies.

Yet experience is an entry ticket, not a mandate. A Nusseibeh candidacy would face three structural challenges.

The first is regional rotation, which has pointed towards Latin America this cycle; a Gulf candidate would have to overcome the argument that the region’s turn belongs elsewhere. The second is alignment. The UAE’s multi-vector diplomacy, spanning Washington, Beijing, Moscow and its relationship with Israel, could be an asset in negotiation and a liability in a vote, because what reassures one capital raises questions in another. She would need to show that her reach translates into independence rather than being read through the UAE’s strategic interests. The third is the veto, which measures neither qualifications nor popularity. It asks only whether one permanent member is prepared to block the outcome, and that single objection can outweigh broad support elsewhere.

Her candidacy would also speak to a pressure the UN can no longer ignore: no woman has ever served as Secretary-General. That demand carries weight among member states and in the General Assembly, even if gender alone cannot overcome a permanent member’s opposition.

The decisive question is whether she could emerge as a genuine consensus candidate rather than another name in a crowded field. Consensus in the Council does not mean universal enthusiasm. It means no permanent member is willing to block, which is considerably harder than assembling a list of supporters. The next straw poll may offer an early signal, and the identity of those casting “discourage” votes will matter more than the headline tally.

In Security Council politics, the winner is rarely the candidate with the most friends. It is the one who gives none of the five a reason to pull the veto trigger.

text:
On October 20, 2026, in Mumbai, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio proposed that Indian refiners—particularly Reliance Industries—process more Venezuelan crude and explore oil production there.

India must examine the terms carefully. Buying crude, rebuilding Venezuela’s oil industry and reducing Russian supplies are three separate decisions, with very different costs and risks.

Before committing, New Delhi needs answers to seven questions.

1️⃣ WHAT MORE DOES WASHINGTON WANT?

India is already diversifying.

• Venezuelan crude imports jumped from $255 million in FY2026 to nearly $3.6 billion in April–August 2026.
• U.S. crude purchases rose from $405 million in July to $790 million in August.
• Russian purchases fell about 25%, from $7.3 billion to $5.4 billion, reducing Russia’s share from 51% to 45%.
With this shift already underway, what additional commitments does Washington seek—and what would India gain?

2️⃣ WHY THE FOCUS ON RELIANCE?

Reliance accounted for 74.3% of India’s $3,585.6 million Venezuelan crude imports in April–August:

• SEZ Jamnagar: $1,695.3 million—47.3%.
• Sikka: $968.2 million—27%.

The remainder came through Indian Oil’s Paradip facility, $421.3 million; Mundra storage terminals operated by HPCL and others, $405.8 million; and Nayara’s Vadinar facility, $95 million.

Reliance is already the dominant buyer. Any further commitment must make commercial sense for the company.

3️⃣ DOES CHEAPER CRUDE MEAN CHEAPER FUEL?

During April–August, India paid an average $612 per tonne for Venezuelan crude, compared with $821 for Saudi crude.

But the discount is only the starting point.

Venezuela’s mostly extra-heavy crude requires specialised diluents, upgrading and transport infrastructure. Lower yields and higher handling and refining costs can absorb part of the price advantage.

India has the capability: Reliance’s Jamnagar complex, Nayara’s Vadinar refinery and suitable IOC and HPCL facilities can process heavy crude.

The test is the final refining margin, supply reliability and delivered cost.

4️⃣ IS INDIA BEING ASKED TO BUY OIL—OR FINANCE RECONSTRUCTION?

Venezuela produces roughly 1.1–1.2 million barrels a day and exports about 650,000–750,000 barrels.

Restoring production above its historical peak of 3 million barrels a day could take 7–10 years and $75 billion to more than $100 billion.

That means rebuilding upgraders, restoring power and repairing export facilities.

India must establish whether Rubio’s proposal offers reliable crude supplies or seeks Indian capital to rehabilitate Venezuela’s damaged oil industry. The investment burden, ownership terms, payment security and expected returns must be explicit.

5️⃣ WHO BEARS THE COST IF U.S. POLICY REVERSES AGAIN?

India has already experienced this risk.

U.S. sanctions disrupted ONGC Videsh’s Venezuelan investments. Restrictions on Venezuelan state oil firm PDVSA, culminating in the 2019 oil embargo, also pushed Indian refiners to stop purchases.

Hundreds of millions of dollars in Indian dividend earnings were stranded, production from equity investments was effectively frozen and expansion plans were abandoned.

Washington once discouraged Venezuelan oil purchases. It now encourages them. What protects Indian investments if it changes direction again?

6️⃣ WHY MUST INDIA REDUCE RUSSIAN PURCHASES WHILE THE U.S. BUYS RUSSIAN DIESEL?

On October 9, Washington agreed to buy Russian diesel to improve domestic availability.

The arrangement provided sanctions relief until April 7, 2027, potentially generating dollar earnings for Russian producers, including Rosneft and Lukoil.

Washington must explain why its energy needs justify Russian purchases while India faces pressure to reduce its own.

India’s sourcing decisions must serve its energy security and commercial interests.

7️⃣ HOW MUCH MORE CAN RELIANCE COMMIT?

On March 11, 2026, President Trump announced a $300 billion refinery project involving Reliance at Brownsville, Texas.

Any request for Reliance to invest in Venezuelan oilfields must be assessed alongside its existing commitments, financing capacity and execution risks.

India should seek clear terms on pricing, supply continuity, investment obligations, commercial returns, sanctions protection and how long Washington’s support will last.

Buy Venezuelan crude where the economics work. Assess oilfield investment on its own merits. Decide Russian sourcing according to India’s needs.

An American invitation is no guarantee that Indian capital—or India’s energy security—will be protected.

European leaders may soon hold direct talks with Vladimir Putin and offer two paths to peace in Ukraine, according to a Financial Times column by Gideon Rachman. 

The first would freeze the war on the current front line in exchange for a guarantee that Ukraine never joins NATO. 

The second would see Ukraine give up the rest of the Donbas and then join the alliance. 

Rachman writes that European capitals, frustrated with President Trump’s approach and now primarily funding Ukraine after US aid cuts, reject leaving talks solely to Washington, with channels already open. 

Both options could face Ukrainian resistance, though President Zelenskyy might accept either amid war fatigue. 

Europeans doubt Putin would accept either; he may prefer a Trump-Xi summit excluding them.

text:
A man walked into a Texas prison in 1979 at twenty-five and walked out in 2010 at fifty-six.

On the day Cornelius Dupree was released, he had served longer than any other DNA exoneree in Texas history.

Four months before that, he had been offered parole. He turned it down.

Dallas, 1979. A woman was robbed and raped. Dupree, 19 at the time of the offence and 25 at conviction, was picked up with a friend while walking to a party. They were in the area. That was the connection.

Eyewitness identification. No physical evidence that held up. Seventy-five years.

He filed for parole repeatedly over thirty years. He was offered it more than once.

And here is the part that matters.

Parole in Texas required him to register as a sex offender and to acknowledge the offence.  Taking it meant saying he did it.

He refused. Every time. He stayed in prison rather than say he had raped a woman he had never met.

In 2010, with DNA testing finally available and the Dallas County Conviction Integrity Unit reviewing old cases, the evidence was tested. It excluded him.

He was released in July 2010 and formally exonerated in January 2011, after thirty years and change.

Four months before the DNA came back, he had been offered parole again, and turned it down again.

Four months.

He married shortly after he came out. He has spoken about the ordinary things — a mobile phone, a supermarket, choosing what to eat.

Thirty years, and every single year he could have walked out early by agreeing to be what they said he was.

How many lives have been stolen by wrongful convictions? , confront the We confront these stories that demand accountability.

1. Swift and DTCC are financial market infrastructures that are member-owned, operated, governed, co-ops for themselves. It is neutral infrastructure amongst their users. 

2. "Mitsubishi Corporation first Japanese corporate to advance intragroup cash management with Kinexys by J.P. Morgan"

https://t.co/y2s1PsKqzP
This was just announced a few months ago.

3. The premise that "someone is building on someone else's chain" is the actual antiquated mental model of what the tech is and how multi-chain development actually looks now.

Blockchains are the databases. Protocols like Chainlink are the TCP/IP equivalent that connect all of these isolated databases (whether public or permissioned) both to each other and to other legacy financial networks. Your private database can talk to my public database.

With Chainlink Runtime Environment, you can natively build workflows and applications that are not only natively multi-chain, but they are also cross-system in that they are composable with non-chain financial networks like Swift, DTCC, Fednow, Fedwire, FIX, ACH, credit card networks, etc. On top of that, you can add compliance tools, end to end privacy (even on the non private public chains), etc.

So, no one is confined to building on a single chain, regardless of whose chain it is or how much liquidity it has. You can deploy these cross-chain + cross-system workflows across as many chains as you want. 

If the chain offers any utility in being there, you can add onto your list of total chains you are deployed to. 
"Build once, run everywhere"

See the attached demo video from last week's Swift SIBOS conference of 24/7 collateral management application that is natively cross-chain and cross-system across Ethereum and DTCC's permissioned chain.

text:
I fear @TheStalwart is falling into the trap a lot of crypto pros have over the years, which is to swing from one extreme view to the other based on "what's exciting in crypto today."

The problem with the "blockchain, not Bitcoin" narrative is not that it violates some naive maxi view of Bitcoin being the only viable application of blockchain tech, it's that it ignores the reality that the only safe and useful blockchain (for any application) is one secured by a protocol-issued & censorship-resistant native coin.

If you read the Bitcoin white paper, it's clear that Satoshi didn't create the components we collectively call blockchain to enable a digital hard currency. He was trying to invent a peer-to-peer payment system, and realized the only way to secure it was to give it a native coin.

(The paper is surprisingly non-ideological and talks a lot more about the flaws of intermediated payment & settlement than it does inflation or fiat money).

The first application of P2P and censorship-resistant settlement was Bitcoin. Then came Ethereum which abstracted the service to any asset (tokens) and made them programmable (smart contracts).

But you still need ETH (or SOL or HYPE or whichever native coin) to make P2P settlement of stablecoins, tokenized securities, perps, and any other asset, along with their smart contracts, secure while decentralized.

The  "blockchain, not Bitcoin" approach originally decided to do away with the coin, which also meant it had to do away with permissionless consensus, and as a consequence, the pure P2P settlement and censorship resistance. 

This was Corda, Fabric, Quorom, DAML etc etc. Billions of dollars got plowed into them, lots of hype was generated, but it all failed. 

Why? First, permissioned networks have none of the end-user protections of a decentralized system. Their use of consensus and cryptography is mostly performative. The gatekeeper that rules who is allowed to validate is all powerful: it can shut down the network, censor specific users, or reverse settlement. It can be forced by a government to do this. It can also be hacked.

Second, even if such a network succeeds, it becomes a monopoly, and the gatekeeper now has total control over pricing and access, which it will monetize, because that's what happened with card networks, exchanges, and clearinghouses. 

They all began with the same egalitarian goals of permissioned networks. Many were none profits or mutually owned at the start. Today, they are more valuable than the companies that founded them.

The latest wave of enterprise networks pretending to be blockchains (Canton, Tempo, Ark, likely many more to come) are just rerunning the same playbook. Some have a coin, but its existence is more about monetization and signaling than utility. It has nothing to do with consensus (since that's permissioned) so it doesn't enable P2P activity. Access is controlled by the whitelisted validators, who are controlled by the gatekeeper.

The other problem with such a coin is that it has no supply guarantees. Bitcoin's 21m hard cap only works because it's set by the protocol and nobody has the power to unilaterally change that (possibly to a fault - see quantum threat). In a permissioned network the gatekeeper can order the supply increased tomorrow and it'll go up, guaranateed.

The purveyors of these networks, some of whom own billions of $$ of its dubious coin, act like their systems offer tokenization and smart contracts, too. 

But they don't. They are just databases with a button, so they can offer asset and code - same as any other clearinghouse with a ledger and APIs. Every enterprise network is just an unregulated clearinghouse, with all the counterparty risk and vendor lock-in of any clearinghouse, but without regulatory protection.

Going back to Joe's original point, what makes stablecoins, tokenized assets, and non-custodial perps on real blockchains interesting is the way they can flow freely, from anyone to anyone else, sans interferences. 

This isn't about decentralization ideology, it's about diminished counterparty risk, guaranteed settlement, and knowing that should your solution succeed, you won't get a knock on the door from the gatekeeper saying "nice business you got there on top of my network, I'm afraid it's going to cost you $100m a year to keep running it. You know, because maintenance costs."

I'm sure that will happen because it has already happened on every privately owned social media platform, payment system, and clearinghouse.

But if you issue stablecoins on Ethereum, or build a useful application on Solana, or build a perps market on top of (a future) Hyperliquid (when it's more decentralized) then you'll never get that knock, because nobody has the power to give it.

This is only possible on a permissionless system empowered by a native coin - Blockchain, and Bitcoin.

text:
Filipinos ‘most willing’ to adopt AI-backed services in Asia Pacific 
By Joann Villanueva

MANILA – Filipinos’ tech-savviness and strong use of social media likely played in the strong momentum for artificial intelligence (AI) utilization in the country compared to other countries in Asia Pacific.

This was noted by Mao Gen Foo, vice president for Asia of Genesys, a global player on agentic orchestration for customer experience (CX), during a briefing on Wednesday in the company’s office in Quezon City,

Results of the 2026 State of Customer Experience (CX) Report, a survey conducted by an independent research firm to around 5,811 consumers and 1,560 consumer experience and business leaders in over 20 countries in Asia Pacific from March to April 2026, showed that 64 percent of the respondents from the Philippines are more positive on AI-powered services compared to two years ago.

This level is higher than 56 percent across Asia Pacific, and 60 percent globally.

The report, released in the country on Wednesday, also showed that 35 percent of the Filipino respondents have good experience on the use of AI-powered services, thus, the shift toward this service. 

It said Filipinos now have higher expectations for CX because of AI, and this was seen as the reason for their loyalty to brands and their buying intentions. 

Also, CX leaders are also planning to employ AI-backed tools to bolster the performance of their human agents, supervisors and other CX employees, the same report said. 

Foo cited as possible drivers of this bullishness to Filipinos love for technology, strong usage of mobile phones and good experience on AI-backed services.

“Talking to many customers as I move around the different regions, I think the Filipinos actually are very welcoming to technology. I mean, if you look at social media adoption, mobile phone adoption, Filipinos are among one of the highest across the region. So I would say that Filipinos are actually very digital savvy, very willing to adopt something new relative to some markets where maybe they are more fixed in their ways, are more rigid, are more structured and organized,” he said. 

Kulachart Ngernpermpoon, at the same briefing, said the size of the Philippines’ population also likely contributed to the large number of AI-welcoming Filipinos. 

He said the country’s diverse population, language, and geographic background were main factors on this shift. 

He said talks with one of their clients, a telecommunications firm, in the past showed that “transformation starts from personalization.” 

He said initially the telco firm only offered top-up services, but later on provided better and faster service, and encouraged migration from pre-paid to post-paid services.

“Before, you only sell a mobile plan. Now, you're seeing them sell the content. In the very near future, you will also see them selling the AI. So, that, again, coming to the scalability, matched with the size of the population, matched with geographic (factor) the needs for AI becomes much more stronger among the CX leader in the Philippines,” he added. (PNA) 

======

Filipinos are now more willing to embrace artificial intelligence-related services compared to other individuals from Asia Pacific, results of a survey released in the Philippines on Wednesday (Oct. 21, 2026) showed. I watched a guy with 0 internships and a 6.9 CGPA crack a ₹18 LPA backend role in 1 interview round.

Meanwhile, our batch topper with 600+ LeetCode problems got rejected in Round 1 of the exact same company.

We asked the interviewer afterwards what actually happened inside that 45-minute call:

> The 600-LeetCode guy memorized optimal C++ solutions, but froze when asked how an API handles 10,000 concurrent requests
> The 6.9 CGPA guy had built and deployed a live payment-queue system that crashed 4 times in production
> Instead of reciting textbook definitions, he shared his screen, opened his logs, and walked through how he fixed the database bottleneck
> For 35 minutes, it stopped being an interview and turned into two engineers debugging architecture

DSA gets you past the automated filter.
Showing a messy system you built and fixed with your own hands gets you the offer letter.

India: where colleges train you for the MCQ test, and the industry hires you for what you broke and fixed at 2 AM.

What is one question in a tech interview that caught you completely off guard? 👇

text:
Consumer apprehension grows as US retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools | Dee-Ann Durbin & Anne D'Innocenzio, AP News

U.S. consumers aren’t just frustrated with high prices. They’re angry and confused about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting those prices.

Digital price tags are rapidly replacing paper ones in grocery aisles. Artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like “dynamic pricing” and “surveillance pricing” are stirring anxiety on social media, where users wonder if different people are getting different prices for the same product.

Americans have grown accustomed to changing prices when booking flights, hotel rooms and rides, but the prospect of everyday spending shaped by algorithms they don’t understand and personal data they may not realize they’re sharing has touched a nerve.

“There are major tensions happening right now between who’s really going to have the power with some of these algorithms and usage of bots and AI: the companies or the shopper,” said Katie Thomas, who leads an internal consumer behavior think tank at the management consulting firm Kearney.

Companies using the technology say some concerns stem from misconceptions about how their pricing tools work. Walmart CEO John Furner said in a blog post last month that digital price tags save workers’ time and keep prices up to date. He said the labels aren’t used to raise prices based on the weather, time of day or individual shopper.

“We price the product, not the person,” Furner wrote.

But companies aren’t always transparent about the customer data they collect and how it’s used, which has made consumers suspicious and led to speculation. For example, social media posts falsely imply that electronic shelf labels Walmart plans to put in all its U.S. stores scan shoppers’ faces or cellphones to set individualized prices, Thomas said.

Lawmakers and regulators are taking action. Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

The Federal Trade Commission has proposed an enforcement policy warning businesses that failing to disclose their use of personal data to set individualized prices could violate consumer protection law.

Here are some of the pricing practices and technologies drawing scrutiny.

Dynamic pricing can raise and lower prices

What it is: Dynamic pricing means adjusting prices in response to changing market conditions, including supply and demand. An airline that adjusts ticket prices as departures approach is using dynamic pricing. Uber’s practice of lifting fares when demand outstrips the supply of available drivers, such as during rush hour, is a type of dynamic pricing known as surge pricing.

Why it matters: Frequent price changes extend well beyond food. Decodo, a web data company, tracked price changes in 2025 across products ranging from electronics to clothing and home improvement supplies. About half the U.S. changes it recorded were decreases, contrary to consumers’ assumptions that dynamic pricing only raises prices, said Gabriele Vitke, a senior product marketing manager.

Digital price labels are coming to more US stores

What they are: Digital displays that let stores update shelf prices electronically instead of replacing paper tags.

Why it matters: Digital price labels, long used in Europe and Asia, are drawing more attention as they spread to major U.S. retailers like Walmart and Whole Foods. Consumer advocates have argued that digital labels could eventually be used for surge pricing or personalized pricing. Labor unions also have opposed the technology.

The electronic shelf labels make frequent changes easier but don’t necessarily lead to higher prices during periods of strong demand. Retailers typically update electronic shelf prices on a regular schedule, often weekly, because shoppers value consistency, said Asa Farquhar of Relex Solutions, a retail technology company. Researchers who tracked prices at an unnamed grocery chain found “virtually no surge pricing” after the labels were introduced.

“Changing prices throughout the day, the way airlines or rideshare apps do, is exceedingly rare in grocery and general merchandise today,” Farquhar said.

Personalized pricing, also called surveillance pricing, draws on customer data

What it is: Personalized pricing means offering customers different prices and discounts based on their locations, incomes, web-browsing habits and other information about individuals or groups of shoppers. Some advocacy groups and regulators use the term “surveillance pricing” for the same practice.

Why it matters: It’s unclear how widely businesses use personal information to customize prices. An FTC staff report released in January 2025 found that intermediaries offering tools that can tailor prices and promotions worked with at least 250 clients, including grocery and clothing retailers.

Lawmakers in Maryland, New Jersey and Connecticut recently enacted restrictions on using shoppers’ personal data to determine what they pay. The Maryland and New Jersey laws focus on groceries, with exceptions for certain loyalty discounts and other promotional offers. Connecticut’s legislation covers a broader range of retail purchases.

California prosecutors sued Target in 2022, alleging that the retailer’s app displayed lower prices before shoppers entered stores and raised them once they were inside.

Target agreed to a $5 million settlement and a ban on using so-called geofencing technology to increase prices.

Target said the app functionality at issue was used to “provide guests with accurate pricing, which can vary across stores and channels.” The retailer said it didn’t personalize prices based on a guest’s data or behavior and remains “committed to clear, transparent pricing.”

Different prices do not necessarily mean personal data was used. Last year, an investigation by Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative and More Perfect Union found that shoppers on Instacart were shown different prices for identical products at the same stores. Instacart subsequently ended what it described as tests that randomly assigned shoppers to groups rather than setting prices based on their personal information.

Algorithmic pricing gets an assist from AI

What it is: Algorithmic pricing uses software to recommend or automatically set prices. Companies have used such systems for decades. AI can help the software identify patterns in sales, competitors’ prices and other information to predict demand and estimate how different prices would affect sales and profits. These tools can support both dynamic and personalized pricing.

Why it matters: It’s unclear how widely retailers use AI to help set prices, but research suggests businesses across industries are adopting it.

Simon-Kucher, a global consulting company, surveyed more than 2,200 business leaders in 28 countries and 39 industries last year, and 41% said they used AI software to gather market intelligence, including competitors’ prices. Another 28% said they used it for “real-time price optimization.” Price optimization means choosing prices that advance business goals, such as increasing profits, attracting shoppers or clearing unsold goods.

The National Retail Federation, which represents big and small stores, said algorithmic pricing is a new method of doing what retailers have always done: monitor and adjust prices depending on supply, demand, seasonality, competitors’ prices and other factors.

Some lawsuits have alleged companies used pricing algorithms to undermine competition.

A 2023 anti-monopoly lawsuit the FTC brought against Amazon challenged, among other practices, an algorithmic tool codenamed Project Nessie. The agency alleged Amazon used the tool to identify products whose prices it could raise with competitors likely to follow, generating more than $1 billion in excess profits.

A trial is scheduled for next year. Amazon said the FTC allegations “grossly mischaracterize” the pricing tool.

Project Nessie was intended to stop retail price-matching practices from creating unsustainably low prices, the e-commerce giant said. Amazon said it tested the tool for a few years but it didn’t work as intended and was scrapped before the federal agency’s lawsuit.

A recent consumer lawsuit against McDonald’s alleged that its pricing system use nonpublic sales data from competing locations to coordinate prices. The Chicago-based burger giant said the lawsuit was “filled with inaccuracies” and that the company makes the tool available to U.S. franchisees to help them set prices at their individual restaurants.
