14:05 SWITZERLAND 🇨🇭 | 07:05 CME / CHICAGO 🇺🇸
NQ / NASDAQ — FIRST REPORT / PRE-OPEN REGIME RADAR

MAIN CONCLUSION: NQ begins Wednesday with a constructive recovery attempt after last week's aggressive AI and semiconductor repricing. Nasdaq futures are outperforming the broader market, supported by stronger corporate earnings and renewed interest in AI infrastructure. But the deeper structural problem has not disappeared. Oil remains above $110, Treasury yields are still restrictive, and investors continue questioning the financing economics of the AI expansion. Today's key distinction is between an earnings-driven rebound and a genuine improvement in the broader market regime.

KEY CONFIRMATION / RISK: The critical test is whether semiconductor participation can extend beyond individual earnings winners. A sustained NQ advance accompanied by improving SOX breadth and stable Treasury yields would suggest the recovery is gaining credibility. A rally concentrated in a handful of AI names, while oil and yields remain elevated, would leave the market vulnerable to another reversal.

YESTERDAY DID NOT RESOLVE THE STRUCTURAL QUESTION

Tuesday delivered a mixed equity session.

The Dow advanced more than 1%, whilst the Nasdaq remained broadly flat.

That divergence matters.

Investors were willing to take equity risk, but leadership was not concentrated in the technology companies that normally drive NQ.

After last week's severe semiconductor sell-off, the market is still trying to determine whether the correction represented temporary positioning stress or a more durable reassessment of AI valuations.

Wednesday offers another opportunity to answer that question.

NASDAQ FUTURES ARE LEADING THE REBOUND

Nasdaq futures were reported approximately 0.75% higher during the European morning, substantially outperforming S&P 500 futures.

The recovery has been supported by AI-linked shares in Asia, Europe and the United States.

Japan's Nikkei advanced.

South Korea's Kospi recorded a particularly strong session.

US semiconductor names also attracted renewed pre-market demand.

This is constructive.

But the important question is not whether NQ can bounce.

It is whether the rebound can survive the US cash-session opening and attract broader institutional participation.

SUPERMICRO IS REOPENING THE AI EARNINGS ARGUMENT

Super Micro Computer delivered a stronger-than-expected outlook, supporting renewed confidence in AI infrastructure demand.

Its shares surged in pre-market trading.

Dell and HPE also benefited from improved sentiment.

This matters because investors have spent much of the recent correction questioning whether the enormous capital expenditure associated with AI infrastructure can generate acceptable investment returns.

Stronger revenue and margin expectations provide evidence that demand remains real.

But demand alone does not resolve the financing question.

The market must distinguish:

AI INFRASTRUCTURE DEMAND

from

AI INFRASTRUCTURE INVESTMENT RETURNS.

Both matter, but they are not the same thing.

THE AI TRADE IS ATTEMPTING TO REPAIR ITS INTERNAL DAMAGE

Monday's recovery followed an exceptionally difficult period for semiconductors.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had previously suffered eight consecutive declining sessions.

That degree of weakness can produce a substantial technical rebound.

However, the first recovery move after an extended sell-off is not automatically a new bullish trend.

The important distinction is between:

SHORT-COVERING + POSITION REBALANCING

and

SUSTAINED INSTITUTIONAL ACCUMULATION.

The latter requires confirmation through market breadth, volume, price acceptance and follow-through.

This is why SOX remains one of the most important references for NQ.

THE 10Y IS HELPING — BUT NOT ENOUGH TO REMOVE THE RISK

The US 10-year Treasury yield has been reported around 5.11%.

That represents some relief from the more extreme stress levels experienced recently.

But it remains a restrictive yield environment for long-duration growth assets.

For NQ, the transmission mechanism remains straightforward:

10Y ↑ → DISCOUNT RATE ↑ → GROWTH VALUATIONS UNDER PRESSURE.

The reverse can support a recovery.

However, the reason yields move is crucial.

Falling yields caused by improving inflation expectations are generally constructive.

Falling yields caused by deteriorating growth expectations are much more ambiguous.

Today's equity recovery therefore needs bond-market confirmation rather than simply a lower headline yield.

OIL IS STILL THE MOST IMPORTANT MACRO HEADWIND

Brent remains above $110 per barrel amid geopolitical uncertainty.

That is not a benign background condition.

Persistently expensive energy can reinforce inflation expectations, complicate the Federal Reserve's policy choices and increase operating costs across the economy.

The chain is:

OIL ↑ → INFLATION RISK ↑ → FED FLEXIBILITY ↓ → YIELD PRESSURE ↑ → NQ VALUATION RISK ↑.

The danger is not necessarily an immediate rise in yields.

The danger is that elevated energy prices prevent yields from declining sufficiently to support the next stage of the AI recovery.

This makes oil an important confirmation variable throughout today's session.

THE FEDERAL RESERVE REMAINS A MAJOR CONSTRAINT

The next FOMC decision is scheduled for 28 October.

The Federal Reserve is currently in its pre-meeting communications blackout period.

Following the recent inflation surprises, investors cannot assume that policy easing will arrive quickly enough to offset financial tightening.

Today's recovery is therefore occurring against a less accommodating monetary backdrop than the one investors enjoyed during earlier stages of the AI expansion.

Strong earnings can support equities.

But they must now compete with a much higher cost of capital.

TODAY IS MORE ABOUT EARNINGS THAN MAJOR MACRO RELEASES

Wednesday does not feature a major scheduled US inflation or employment release comparable to last week's CPI and PPI.

The important scheduled events include:

16:30 SWITZERLAND | 09:30 CME / CHICAGO
EIA Crude Oil Inventories.

19:00 SWITZERLAND | 12:00 CME / CHICAGO
US Treasury 20-Year Bond Auction.

The EIA report matters because energy prices remain one of the principal inflation risks.
The Treasury auction matters because demand for longer-duration US government debt may provide another signal about investor confidence in the rates market.
Corporate earnings remain equally important, with particular attention on Tesla, Meta and semiconductor-related companies.

THE FIRST MAJOR TEST IS THE CASH OPEN
15:30 SWITZERLAND | 08:30 CME / CHICAGO | 09:30 NEW YORK.
The cash-session opening will reveal whether pre-market optimism is supported by broader institutional demand.

A convincing opening would require more than positive index futures.

Watch for:

NQ ↑ + SOX ↑ + BROADENING TECH PARTICIPATION.

A weaker configuration would be:

NQ ↑ + NARROW LEADERSHIP + SOX UNDERPERFORMANCE.
The second combination can produce impressive index candles without establishing a durable bullish regime.
THE MOST IMPORTANT INTERMARKET SEQUENCE

Today's monitoring hierarchy remains:

2Y → 10Y → DXY → SOX → NQ.

But oil deserves an additional place in the analysis because of its inflation implications.

The 2Y reflects the immediate monetary-policy interpretation.

The 10Y reflects broader discount-rate and inflation expectations.

DXY indicates whether dollar-driven financial conditions are becoming more restrictive.

SOX reveals whether semiconductor investors are confirming the recovery.

NQ provides the final index-level expression of these forces.

A rising NQ without broader confirmation should be treated more cautiously than an advance supported by all five variables.

THE BEST BULLISH OUTCOME

The strongest bullish configuration would involve:

10Y STABLE OR LOWER + DXY STABLE OR LOWER + SOX LEADERSHIP + NQ ABOVE OPENING STRUCTURE.

This would suggest investors are again willing to accept technology valuations despite the elevated cost of capital.

The cash opening should attract buyers rather than become an opportunity to distribute positions accumulated overnight.

A successful retest of the opening range, followed by expanding participation, would strengthen the recovery argument.

THE MOST DANGEROUS BEARISH OUTCOME

The principal bearish risk is a failed earnings-driven breakout.

NQ opens higher.

Initial buying fades.

Semiconductor leadership weakens.

Oil remains elevated.

Treasury yields stop declining or begin rising.

The market then loses the macro and sector confirmation needed to sustain the advance.

The warning sequence would be:

SOX WEAKNESS → NQ LOSS OF OPENING SUPPORT → LOWER HIGH → SELLER CONTROL.

This would suggest that the recovery was driven more by short covering and selective earnings enthusiasm than by a durable change in positioning.

BULLISH SCENARIO — ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE: 55%

The bullish case has a modest advantage because earnings have provided a credible catalyst for renewed AI buying.

The semiconductor complex begins to stabilise.

Treasury yields avoid renewed acceleration.

NQ holds its opening structure and attracts additional buyers.

The most important confirmation would be continued sector participation after the initial cash-session volatility.

BEARISH SCENARIO — ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE: 45%

The bearish case remains substantial because the macroeconomic constraints have not disappeared.

Oil is still expensive.

Treasury yields remain restrictive.

The AI financing debate is unresolved.

A failed opening advance, accompanied by semiconductor underperformance, could rapidly shift the session back towards selling pressure.

These probabilities are discretionary scenario estimates, not statistically calibrated forecasts.

ANALYTICAL EDGE

BULLISH: 55%
BEARISH: 45%

EDGE: MODESTLY BULLISH — CONDITIONAL ON CASH-SESSION CONFIRMATION AND SEMICONDUCTOR PARTICIPATION.

The balance has improved compared with last week's sell-off.

But the evidence does not yet justify treating the recovery as a complete structural reversal.

CURRENT REGIME

CURRENT REGIME: AI EARNINGS RECOVERY / SEMICONDUCTOR REPAIR ATTEMPT / RESTRICTIVE TREASURY YIELDS / ELEVATED OIL / PRE-FOMC UNCERTAINTY.

The positive development is renewed confidence in AI-related corporate revenues.

The unresolved problem is the financial cost of sustaining that growth.

Both forces are active simultaneously.
FINAL ANALYTICAL VIEW

Wednesday's market is trying to demonstrate that the AI trade can recover without waiting for a major improvement in the macroeconomic environment.

Strong earnings provide support.

But strong earnings do not automatically neutralise oil above $110, restrictive Treasury yields or financing concerns.

The decisive information will come from how technology behaves once the US cash market opens.

Watch SOX.
Watch 10Y.
Watch oil.
Watch the opening-range reaction.
Then trust NQ.

The central question is no longer whether AI demand exists.

It is whether renewed earnings confidence is powerful enough to overcome the cost of financing the AI expansion.

That is today's real test.

Notre Dame Fully Funded Scholarship USA 🇺🇸2027/28!! Full Breakdown 

Today, I decided to talk about a top opportunity in the US alot of people dont realise. 

You see The Notre Dame doesn't just admit PhD students, it pays them to do the work. Most people who tell me they want a PhD in the US assume the hard part is finding the money. 

At a university like Notre Dame, the money is the part that is already settled, and the real question is whether your application is strong enough to be chosen.

Here is what the funding looks like. Almost every doctoral student at Notre Dame receives a full tuition scholarship, and for 2026/27 that tuition is $69k.

About 94% of PhD students also hold a fellowship or assistantship that pays a 12-month stipend. 

Right now that stipend can be as high as $44k depending on the program.

The university also covers the full health insurance premium for eligible students, and their legal dependents are included, which matters a great deal if you are planning to travel with your family.

Then there are the select fellowships. Each year roughly 60 to 70 of about 470 incoming graduate students receive one, with stipends up to $50k. You don't apply for them separately. 

Your department reads your admission file and decides whether to nominate you. 

When I explain this to clients, the reaction is almost always the same: they realise their statement of intent was never just an admission essay, because it was quietly their fellowship application as well.

People also ask me what a US PhD gives you beyond the scholarship itself. 

The first thing is that you finish without tuition debt.

The second is that the US lets eligible graduates work for 12 months after their degree through OPT, and STEM graduates can extend that by another 24 months. 

The third benefit is harder to measure and, in my experience, the most valuable. 

Five years inside a serious research community gives you publications, conference experience and faculty relationships that open doors to academic and industry roles across the world.

On the practical side, you need a bachelor's degree from an accredited university, and many programs will take you without a master's. 

The application fee is $75, and the Graduate School offers fee waivers if you request one early.

If Notre Dame is on your list, or you're not sure whether your profile is ready for a US PhD, send me a DM.

text:
The 1710 Tavern stands in Tappahannock, Virginia, along the Rappahannock River, and holds a strong claim as the oldest tavern in the state. Its core structure dates to the early eighteenth century, when the town, then known as Hobbs Hole, thrived as a tobacco port. The building began as a private residence, with the right side of what is now the dining room raised in 1710 and the left side added two years later. A bar area followed sometime between 1718 and 1758, and by at least 1732 the property had become an ordinary-a licensed colonial tavern and inn that offered food, drink, and lodging to travelers, sailors, and merchants.

In its early decades the tavern sat near the waterfront, oriented toward the river rather than any road, and served as a practical stop for those arriving by ship or horseback. Guests could settle accounts in cash or with tobacco, the region's chief commodity. Overnight visitors occupied small upstairs rooms and were sometimes locked in at night to deter theft. The establishment also became a gathering place during the years leading to the American Revolution. Local leaders and the Sons of Liberty met there to organize resistance to the Stamp Act, and the building witnessed some of the political ferment that later produced the Leedstown Resolves and Essex Resolutions. George Washington is recorded as having visited the Tappahannock area in 1760, placing him in the same orbit as this busy ordinary.

Over the centuries the building passed through many hands and uses. It operated as a tavern at various intervals, later served as a private residence-including a long period as the home of a pharmacist-and eventually fell into disrepair. For years it stood empty, its plumbing removed and its fabric damaged by time and neglect. In the early 2020s the property was acquired by owners who undertook a careful restoration, reinforcing the original stone foundation, repairing hand-hewn beams, and preserving original floors, windows, ceilings, and fireplaces. Additional historic materials were incorporated, such as flooring salvaged from an old hardware store and a bar crafted from three-hundred-year-old walnut.

The restored tavern reopened in 2023 as a restaurant and bar that continues the long tradition of hospitality on the site. Diners now sit in rooms that retain the proportions and materials of the colonial era while enjoying modern service.
Although the building spent stretches of its history as a private home rather than a continuously operating tavern, its early construction date, documented use as an ordinary by the 1730s, and survival as one of the oldest commercial structures in the Northern Neck distinguish it among Virginia's historic inns. Today it remains a living landmark where the architecture and atmosphere of early eighteenth-century life can still be experienced firsthand.

Lecture: 
Mortality, Theodicy, 
and Comforting Beliefs in Later Life

Interdisciplinary Perspectives 
from Psychiatry and Social Anthropology

Students in 
psychiatry and 
social anthropology, 
consider the following vignette 
as a window into 
how individuals 
negotiate death,
 belief, 
and meaning 
when professional proximity 
to human suffering 
meets personal confrontation 
with loss.

In 2016, at age 69, 
while working as a contract psychiatrist 
at Atascadero State Hospital 
(a forensic psychiatric facility in California), 
the individual 
began receiving frequent messages 
about the deaths of friends and relatives. 

Raised Seventh-day Adventist, 
he had become an atheist 
in adolescence 
precisely because 
he could not reconcile 
the coexistence of good and evil 
within religious frameworks
—the classic problem of theodicy. 

In later years 
he adopted a selective afterlife belief
 that discarded any “dark side” 
(hell, punishment, residual evil) 
and retained only 
the possibility of continued existence 
in a form that offered comfort. 

As he put it: 
it felt good, 
so why not? 

This stance 
formed the personal background 
to a Facebook memory post
 from 21 October 2016: 
“Rest in peace, Aunt Gladys,” 
followed by a cluster 
of condolence replies 
from relatives and acquaintances.

The questions this raises
—implicit in the narrative 
and explicit for our disciplines
—are these: 

How do people 
revise metaphysical commitments 
when confronted 
with cumulative mortality? 

What psychological 
and social functions d
oes a “comforting” afterlife serve 
when traditional religious accounts 
of evil have already been rejected? 

And how 
do modern platforms 
mediate collective mourning?

Psychiatric Perspectives
From a clinical standpoint, 
the vignette 
illustrates adaptive meaning-making i
n late middle age and early later life, 
a period 
when awareness 
of personal finitude intensifies 
(Erikson’s integrity versus despair, 
or more contemporary models of d
eath anxiety and terror management). 

Frequent notifications 
of peers’ deaths 
while working 
inside a forensic psychiatric institution
—where severe mental illness, 
violence, 
and institutional containment 
are daily realities
—can amplify existential confrontation. 

The earlier rejection 
of Adventist cosmology 
on theodicy grounds 
is consistent 
with many developmental trajectories: 
adolescence 
is a common window 
for critical evaluation 
of inherited religious systems 
when empirical 
or moral contradictions 
become salient.

The later adoption 
of a stripped-down afterlife 
is best understood 
as pragmatic cognitive reframing 
rather than doctrinal conversion. 

It preserves 
the psychological benefits 
documented in research 
on belief and well-being
—reduced death anxiety, 
continued bonds 
with the deceased, 
and a sense of continuity
—while jettisoning 
elements 
(eternal punishment, residual evil) 
that had previously been rejected. 

In psychiatric terms 
this resembles 
a self-generated cognitive-behavioral 
or acceptance-and-commitment strategy: 
the belief is retained 
to the extent 
that it decreases suffering 
and increases behavioral flexibility 
in the face of loss. 

Clinicians 
working with older adults, 
especially those in high-mortality environments 
(hospitals, 
forensic settings, 
long-term care), 
routinely encounter 
similar individualized 
spiritual or philosophical constructions. 

The task 
is not to adjudicate their truth value 
but to assess 
whether they support 
adaptive functioning, 
social connection, 
and the processing of grief 
without inducing new forms of distress.

Social Anthropological Perspectives

Anthropologically, 
the sequence tracks 
common patterns 
in the cultural construction 
of the afterlife 
and in the management of theodicy. 

Seventh-day Adventism 
supplies a particular eschatology 
(soul sleep, 
investigative judgment, 
eventual annihilation of the wicked 
rather than eternal torment 
in many formulations). 

Rejection of that system
 on moral grounds, 
followed by selective reappropriation 
of continuity
 without retributive elements, 
is an instance of what 
anthropologists 
have long observed: 
individuals and groups 
edit cosmological packages 
according to local moral economies 
and lived experience. 

Comfort becomes a selection criterion.

The Facebook post itself 
is a contemporary mourning ritual. 

The “On this day” memory 
resurrects a past announcement 
of death and reactivates 
a network of condolence. 

Replies range from formulaic sympathy 
(“Sorry for your loss”) 
to shared reminiscence 
(“I remember Grandma’s sister… she was very kind”) 
to religious affirmation (“Amen”). 

This digital gathering 
performs the classic anthropological functions 
of funeral rites
—public acknowledgment of loss, 
reinforcement of kinship 
and community ties, 
and the social distribution of grief
—while operating 
asynchronously 
and at low cost. 

It also illustrates 
how secular 
or post-religious individuals 
can still participate in, 
and benefit from, 
collective practices 
that affirm continuity 
(“Rest in peace”).

The explicit rationale 
“it felt good, why not?”
 is an emic statement 
of pragmatic epistemology. 

Across cultures, afterlife beliefs are frequently evaluated not solely by doctrinal consistency but by their capacity to sustain social relations and emotional equilibrium in the face of death. Discarding the “dark side” removes a source of moral and emotional dissonance while retaining the relational benefit of imagining the deceased as still accessible in some benign form.

Intersections and Implications for Students

The psychiatrist’s professional setting 
(forensic hospital) 
and personal biography intersect. 

Daily exposure 
to severe psychopathology 
and institutional constraint 
may heighten sensitivity t
o questions of agency, 
suffering, 
and finality; 
the personal solution 
of a non-punitive afterlife c
an be read 
as one way of containing that exposure. 

For psychiatry students, 
the vignette underscores 
the clinical relevance 
of existential and spiritual assessment, 
the legitimacy of patient-generated meaning 
systems 
that do not match institutional 
or cultural norms, 
and the risk of pathologizing adaptive belief. 

For anthropology students, 
it supplies a micro-ethnography of belief revision, 
the digital mediation of kinship obligations
 around death,
 and the enduring human preference 
for cosmologies that minimize 
unnecessary suffering.

Discussion prompts:

When does a comforting belief become clinically significant (protective versus avoidant)?

How do digital platforms alter the temporality and social distribution of mourning compared with earlier ritual forms?
In what ways do professional roles (psychiatrist, anthropologist) shape or constrain the beliefs practitioners themselves hold about death?

Poem in the style of “(Don’t Fear) The Reaper”
(Blue Öyster Cult)

Seasons don’t fear the reaper
Nor do the wind, the sun or the rain
We can be like they are

Come on, Aunt Gladys, don’t fear the reaper
Baby take my hand, don’t fear the reaper
We’ll be able to fly, don’t fear the reaper
Baby I’m your man

Raised in the light of the Sabbath day
Questions of good and of evil stayed
I walked away when the dark side stayed
Could not reconcile what the books all said

Later the years brought the messages down
Friends and the kin in the hospital town
Sixty-nine years and the names came around
Rest in peace, and the comfort was found

No more the fire, no more the claim
Only the quiet, only the name
It felt good, so why not the same
An afterlife stripped of the dark and the blame

Come on, Aunt Gladys, don’t fear the reaper
Baby take my hand, don’t fear the reaper
We’ll be able to fly, don’t fear the reaper
Baby I’m your man

Valentine is done
Here but now they’re gone
Romeo and Juliet
Are together in eternity
We can be like they are
Don’t fear the reaper

(The lecture and poem are offered as teaching materials; they interpret the supplied personal narrative without claiming clinical authority over any living individual.)

text:
HOTEL CARCOSA

MID-NOVEMBER RELEASE

#sunshinenoir 

CHAPTER ONE

HOTEL CARCOSA, HOTEL BAR

California sunshine. Another day. It was hot and dry. Hell of a season. I’d often hear people say that dry heat is better than humidity and I wanted to punch those stupid people in the face. Maybe you can tell. I don’t like heat. I know. I know. “Then what are you doing in Southern California?” And my response would be, “Mind your goddamn business.” It wasn’t all bad, though. I was at a hotel in Santa Barbara nestled in hills that overlooked the ocean. The highway was nearby below, and further out, the Pacific Ocean. The ocean wasn’t far away, one could walk. But I felt like I had been rode hard and hung out to dry. It probably had something to do with the beatings I’d received during the course of my investigation and the fifth of scotch I drank last night. I don’t often drink a fifth of scotch, but sometimes I do.

My attempts to awaken early were thwarted by bright light, anxiety, and a headache. I wrangled myself up sometime before noon and cursed myself for not waking up early. I was hungry. I took a late breakfast—Mexican style—of refried beans, tortillas, rice, fried eggs, and black coffee. The meal made me sleepy so I drew the blinds and went back to sleep.

I awoke a few hours later. I was starting to feel better. The hotel had a small bar. I walked over there through the heat. It was quiet. And then she walked in and ruined a perfectly good time of me wallowing in my own loneliness and misery. I was officially awake. She was everything bad wrapped in everything good. She was tall and comely and had curves in all the right places. She was pushing buttons I didn’t know I had. She was Asian or half-Asian—I don’t know, but whatever it was it was killing me. Brown eyes and shiny, silky, black, hair. She was tall for an Asian and tall for a woman. That’s intimidating. I didn’t need that right now. It was heaven to see, but hell not to act on. I tried not to pay attention to her. Let it go and press on with being a lonely sap.

She saddled up beside me in that sequin dress. I couldn’t resist. “You’re a bit overdressed.”

“My night out was cancelled,” she said flatly without looking my way.

Her English was good; it betrayed her exotic look. She was probably raised in California. She seemed like she was accustomed to the good life. She had that air about her. Hands were clean and manicured. With looks like hers it wouldn’t be difficult to find a financier to keep her living in luxury. Hell, she might even have more than one. But I’d seen this kind of dame around before. The luxury life is too easy. They start drinking—maybe over the counter or street drugs—and it all spirals down and goes out of control. Then it turns into a tragic story. Medicated until dead. It’s a Southern California thing, a Hollywood thing. I couldn’t understand it. People with money and still not happy. I guess it’s mental illness. If it is, it’s rampant in Southern California.

“That’s a real shame. Maybe you could do something else,” I offered.

“Maybe. Maybe you could pay for my drink.”

“Yeah, sure.” I was deep in the hole so what was another drink?

The bartender set down the martini glass and she was off. “See you around, slugger,” she said.

“See you around.”

Oh, I see. One of those types. She liked to play hard to get. I didn’t like her much at all, but I found her irresistible. I had a feeling I’d be seeing her again.

Principal Secretary for Irrigation @EphantusKim , this morning led a delegation from the State Department for Irrigation on a working visit to Hyderabad, Telangana, and Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh, India, following an invitation by United Port Services Private Limited to explore its agricultural investment model and opportunities to transform 35,000 acres of the Bura Irrigation Scheme into a large-scale rice production hub.

The visit is providing the Kenyan delegation with an opportunity to learn how private-sector investment, modern agricultural technologies and large-scale irrigation infrastructure can be integrated to increase agricultural productivity, strengthen food security and reduce dependence on food imports.

The delegation visited the Polavaram Irrigation Project, one of India's major multipurpose water infrastructure investments. The project has a reported gross reservoir storage capacity of approximately 5.51 billion cubic metres (BCM) and is designed to bring an additional 720,000 acres under irrigation while stabilising water supplies for a further 2.35 million acres across the Godavari and Krishna delta regions, supporting a combined agricultural area of approximately 3.07 million acres.

The project also incorporates a 960-megawatt hydroelectric power plant and facilitates the transfer of water from the Godavari River to the Krishna basin, demonstrating how integrated investments in water storage, irrigation and hydropower can support agricultural productivity, water security and broader economic development.

India's experience offers important lessons for Kenya as the country pursues strategic investments in irrigation and agricultural modernisation to meet growing food demand. With a population of more than 1.4 billion, projected to reach approximately 1.7 billion by 2067, India has continued to invest in irrigation infrastructure and agricultural systems capable of supporting large-scale food production.
The proposed transformation of the Bura Irrigation Scheme presents an opportunity for Kenya to apply relevant lessons from this experience. The planned development of 35,000 acres has the potential to produce approximately 1.05 million bags of rice per production cycle, based on an estimated yield of 30 bags per acre. At 75 kilogrammes per bag, this translates to approximately 78,750 metric tonnes of rice per production cycle.

Such an investment would significantly contribute to increasing domestic rice production, reducing the country's food import bill, creating employment and improving farmers' incomes while stimulating economic activity across the agricultural value chain.
With reliable water supply, modern irrigation infrastructure, appropriate agricultural technologies, efficient production systems and strong market linkages, Bura has the potential to emerge as a major rice production hub and contribute significantly to Kenya's food security agenda.

The initiative is also aligned with the Government's implementation of the National Irrigation Sector Investment Plan (NISIP) 2025–2035, which targets the expansion of irrigation by one million acres over ten years. Under the plan, partnerships with the private sector remain critical in mobilising the capital, technology, expertise and management systems required to accelerate irrigation development and enhance the productivity of existing schemes.

A NEW TEAM. A NEW SCORING OPPORTUNITY.

Tyler Herro’s scoring ceiling is the focus here. We’re backing his ability to turn shot volume, perimeter efficiency, and an expanded offensive role into a performance of at least 23 points.

Herro averaged 19.9 points per game across 34 appearances in the previous season. That baseline is below our current line, so this isn’t a pick that can be justified by looking at his scoring average alone. The case depends on his role in Milwaukee, his ability to generate efficient attempts, and the upside he’s shown when his shot is falling.

THE CASE FOR THE OVER

1. THE CEILING IS ALREADY VISIBLE

In Milwaukee’s preseason finale against Indiana, Herro scored 25 points in 24 minutes, shooting 10-for-16 from the field and 5-for-7 from three-point range.

That performance shows the scoring ceiling required to clear this number. It also illustrates the importance of his perimeter shooting: a strong night from beyond the arc can move a player toward 23 points without requiring an unusually high number of free throws.

One preseason performance doesn’t prove that the same output will repeat in the regular season. It does, however, provide a concrete example of how quickly Herro can reach this range when his efficiency and volume align.

2. ROLE AND SHOT VOLUME

The key question is how Milwaukee uses Herro throughout the regular season. His ability to score off the dribble, shoot off movement, and convert catch-and-shoot opportunities gives the offense multiple ways to generate points from him.

For this bet to work, the minutes and attempts need to support that versatility. We want Herro involved early, taking enough shots to give himself a realistic path to 23—not relying on an extreme shooting percentage from limited volume.

text:
Podcast Summary | Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard: Malcolm Gladwell #4

Overview
Malcolm Gladwell’s central argument is that America is not a high-crime society so much as a high-violence one, and that the country keeps having the wrong conversation about guns. Crime and violence, he argues, have different causes, different perpetrators, and different remedies. The U.S. shares culture, food, and television with Canada and the U.K., yet its homicide rate is roughly three times Canada’s and four times the U.K.’s. What separates America is not crime in general but lethal violence, concentrated in identifiable people and places, and masked by everything from emergency medicine to the emotional pull of mass shootings. The conversation moves from Gladwell’s Mennonite upbringing in rural Ontario to assault weapons bans he calls largely cosmetic, to the Second Amendment’s origins in slave patrols, to trauma care and police staffing, to Baltimore’s recent steep decline in gun violence. The throughline is that the problem is smaller and more solvable than the national paralysis suggests, and that honest conversation, not pageantry, is the prerequisite for change.

Key Themes
- Crime and violence are separate problems with separate fixes; America overindexes on lethal violence rather than on crime overall.
- Assault weapons bans regulate cosmetic add-ons on a modular platform, making them pageantry that avoids the broader gun-violence problem.
- The Second Amendment is argued to have been written to protect state militias understood as slave patrols, a history the courts have not honestly acknowledged.
- Falling homicide rates can reflect better trauma care and proximity to hospitals, not necessarily less violence, creating a moral hazard.
- Most American lethal violence is expressive rather than instrumental, yet the legal system is built almost entirely to deter instrumental violence.
- American cities are dramatically underpoliced relative to Western Europe, and police violence is framed as a symptom of too few officers rather than too many.
- Violence is highly concentrated: small, identifiable at-risk populations can be reached directly through outreach and de-escalation rather than arrest or shows of force.
- Gun politics on both sides is driven by fear, and fear escalates disagreement rather than resolving it.
- Change is framed as achievable through grassroots, state, and city action rather than waiting on federal legislation.

Detailed Summary
Gladwell grew up in a Mennonite pacifist community in rural Ontario with no television, reading Time magazine cover to cover weekly and becoming obsessed with America. His hometown had one police officer known to his family; he had never seen a gun. He recalls eavesdropping on his mother’s friend from Jamaica describing racism and violence in 1970s Atlanta, which sounded foreign and mysterious. After getting his driver’s license, he and a friend took a four-day road trip to America.

That distance from violence became a lens. He notes he has written about crime and violence in almost every book, and that his views have evolved; part of what drove this book was uncovering things about crime he had never considered despite thinking about it for 30 years. He says he avoids self-censorship on controversial topics, arguing it is acceptable to say controversial things if intentions are clear, honest, and in good faith. What upsets people, he argues, is feeling played, manipulated, or condescended to. He says he has warm feelings toward people who profoundly disagree with him when he perceives their intentions as pure.

The book opens with a test ranking Chicago, New York, Toronto, Paris, and London by homicides, then by robberies, to scramble assumptions. The claim is that cars are far more likely to be stolen or broken into in Montreal than New York City, and homes more likely broken into in Paris or London than Chicago. The Canada–US contrast anchors the argument: despite shared TV, food, and culture, the US has roughly three times Canada’s homicide rate and four times the UK’s.

A 24-year-old woman interviewed for the project describes hearing what she thought were fireworks at a family restaurant chain in a rural college town, standing to look out the window, and being shot; about 20 men in the parking lot fired roughly 60 rounds. The emotional pull of such scenes is discussed as distinct from the statistical scale of gun deaths, including the difficulty of reconciling them with one’s sense of society.

On assault weapons, the argument is that bans are largely cosmetic. They target modular add-ons and appearance rather than the underlying firearm, and the bills include long exemption lists, with short main language and appendices of dozens of pages listing exempt guns. The AR is characterized as a modular platform, compared to Lego, so parts can be swapped and bought online. The public misunderstands assault rifles as machine guns, the speakers argue; they fire one bullet per trigger pull and are not inherently more lethal than handguns. Handguns are claimed to be the most lethal weapon in mass shootings and responsible for most deaths in those incidents, while assault weapons are more visible and less concealable. Mass shootings are portrayed as a small share of total gun deaths, with a claimed figure of 1,342 deaths in mass shootings over 57 years versus two million killed by guns in general, making the assault-rifle focus pageantry that gives gun-rights advocates a free pass.

The Second Amendment chapter is called the most fascinating. The argument is that the amendment was written to protect state militias understood as slave patrols, responding to Virginia’s fears that the federal government would take them away. Virginia’s ratification was pivotal; its convention in Richmond debated militias, with full transcripts, and Madison was asked to write an amendment ensuring slave patrols could continue. In parts of Virginia and South Carolina, slave-to-white ratios could be as high as 20 to 1. The Stono Rebellion, involving roughly 100 people who went door to door killing people, exemplifies slavery’s roots in white anxiety and fear of rebellion. The amendment’s grammar is used to show the second part supports the first, tying the right to bear arms to militia needs, and Madison frequently used that grammatical device. The Revolutionary-era militia was widely seen as ineffective, undercutting the belief that the amendment was a response to fighting the British.

Carl Bogus is cited for a book on the Second Amendment written about 25 years ago; the speaker calls it genius and asks why it did not change understanding of the amendment. The court is criticized for not acknowledging these origins; the author asks for honest acknowledgment rather than a specific verdict.

Homicide rates reflect medical capability and proximity to trauma care, not just underlying violence. Surviving certain gunshot wounds requires attention within about 20 minutes; beyond roughly an hour, survival is unlikely. The same shooting can be a homicide in a rural area like the Hudson Valley but an aggravated assault near a trauma center like USC Medical Center in downtown LA, where a victim may arrive in 10 minutes. Poor people typically live farther from trauma centers, contributing to elevated homicide rates. Trauma surgeon Eddie Cornwell estimates he has treated roughly 3,000 career gunshot wounds, starting at USC in South Central during the ’80s gang era, then Baltimore, then Howard University. Medical advances over roughly 30 years mean the U.S. would have had 45,000–70,000 gun deaths over the past five years instead of the usual 15,000–20,000. Cornwell assessed past presidents who were shot: Lincoln would still have died; most others would likely have survived with modern care; Reagan would probably have died if shot before 1940. The U.S. has developed a paradoxical expertise in treating gunshot wounds that masks the true scale of gun violence, a moral hazard problem. For every one homicide death, roughly three other people are shot.

America’s lethal violence is overwhelmingly expressive, arising from fights, feuds, crimes of passion, and impulse, rather than instrumental violence planned for gain. Yet the legal system is built almost entirely to deter instrumental violence, which is only about 18% of total homicides. An assistant watched two seasons of Law and Order and logged every homicide; nearly all were instrumental, as was every homicide in Agatha Christie’s Hercule Poirot books. Expressive examples include jealous rage, a fight at Taco Bell, and tit-for-tat retaliation among relatives. Mass shootings are characterized as instrumental but too small in number to change the 18% figure.

Western European cities generally have about twice as many police officers per capita as American cities. Berlin and LA are both about 3.9 million people, wealthy and educated; the LAPD employs 8,000 officers versus Berlin’s 18,000, or 26,400 including trainees, technical and civilian staff. The U.S. and Europe spend roughly the same share of GDP on public safety, but the U.S. spends far more on prisons and less on police, while Europe does the opposite. Understaffed officers stay in their cars racing between emergencies and project force because they are overwhelmed and alone, which the speakers argue produces more aggressive, militarized behavior and higher rates of police violence. They claim the countries with the most police per capita have the best-behaved police, while the U.S. shares high police-killing rates with countries like Pakistan, Iran, Brazil, and South Africa. Dan Oats, a progressive police chief formerly in Aurora, Colorado, said with double the officers he could do real community engagement, school liaison to spot troubled kids early, and reach bar fights in five minutes instead of 10–15. About half of calls are described as mental health-related, with officers untrained for that. LAPD is described as chronically underpoliced with one of the worst reputations for police violence, policing a vast city like an occupying army; New York is cited as one of the few cities with a reasonably adequate number of officers.

Prevention should focus on teaching conflict resolution and interrupting retaliation rather than only punishment or shows of force. Baltimore’s weekly multi-agency meetings involve about 25 people reviewing the week’s shootings and identifying who knows the victim or shooter’s circle; teams with pastors and crisis counselors visit family and social circles to de-escalate before violence spreads. After “Joey” is shot, the team asks who knows Joey and visits his brother to prevent retaliation. Chicago’s Interruptors use similar outreach: trusted people, not police, knock on doors and offer help like breakfast to interrupt the cycle. David Kennedy’s key insight is that kids carrying guns are often scared and traumatized, not predators; treating them as predators leads only to locking them up. A Chicago program teaching conflict resolution to teenage boys in a year-long class showed dramatic decreases in violence later. Marvin Wolfgang followed all 10,000 boys born in Philadelphia in 1945 until about age 25; roughly 675 accounted for basically all the violence. A West Side Chicago study found that in an area of 50,000 people, about 400 were at risk at any given time of being shot or shooting someone, small enough to identify and help directly without arrests, gun policy, or the National Guard.

The Bruen Supreme Court decision overturned a 100-year-old New York handgun licensing law without mentioning suicide, despite evidence the law affected suicide rates rather than homicide rates. New York’s law, enacted after a prominent writer was murdered in downtown Manhattan by a crazed fan, did not significantly affect homicide rates since most homicides involve illegal guns smuggled from out of state, but it did affect suicide rates. New York State’s suicide rate has historically been half the national average; suicide deaths in the U.S. outnumber homicide deaths. Suicide is described as often spontaneous, with most attempters regretting it if given a second chance, and accessible handguns increase lethality. A parallel is drawn to England’s poisonous oven gas: suicides dropped sharply when the gas was removed or an odor added. The historical foundation gun-rights advocates cite, the Sir John Knight case, is described as fabricated or badly misunderstood; Knight, a 17th-century English knight, racist and slave owner, did not bring guns into a church, and English historians reportedly say the case has been completely misunderstood. The proposed approach is to rearrange priorities between prisons and police and pursue direct homicide intervention through grassroots, state, and city action rather than waiting on federal legislation. The book is framed as optimistic because the problem is solvable.

In poor communities with few resources or status pathways, respect can be the only thing a person has, raising the stakes of perceived disrespect. Gun politics on both sides is framed as driven by fear: liberals fear the other with a gun, conservatives fear needing a gun for protection, and confrontation worsens disagreement because scared people escalate into fight-or-flight. The host strongly endorses the book, calling it a top-10 all-time favorite and urging the audience to read or listen immediately. The book is titled The American Way of Killing: An Invention of an Epidemic and is described as out now. Drew Holk wrote a song called “Troubles,” used at the start of the audiobook, inspired by hearing about a school mass shooting after dropping his kids off; it captures fatigue and a wish for the violence to end, matching the book’s tone. A mass shooting in Scotland, noted as one of the country’s only ones, occurred while Andy Murray was in the classroom; he has never talked about it.

Two years ago, on Oct 21, 2024, Santander launched the digital bank Openbank in the U.S. as a division of Santander Bank, N.A.

Santander is a Spanish multinational financial company with banks in several countries in Europe and the Americas. Under its Openbank brand, Santander operates digital banks in several of these countries. Many of these Openbanks are further along in product offerings than the U.S. Openbank. For example, in September, Santander announced the launch of a cryptocurrency trading service for Openbank customers in Germany.

The U.S. Openbank has been offering a high-yield savings account since its 2024 launch. Last year on Openbank’s one-year anniversary, Santander announced that Openbank had reached $6 billion in deposits. Also last year, Santander announced the opening of a physical location in Miami, FL. According to Santander, this was the third Openbank-branded physical location in the world.

Santander Bank N.A. has recently acquired another digital bank. In August, Santander completed its acquisition of Webster which operates the digital bank BrioDirect. It’s not yet known if BrioDirect will be merged into Openbank. Coincidentally, both BrioDirect and Openbank currently offer only one product, a high-yield savings account. In Santander’s Openbank one-year anniversary press release, it did state that “Openbank will continue to expand its product offerings, including plans to launch Certificates of Deposit (CDs) and introduce new daily-use transaction products.”

text:
Every time a hurricane threatens Florida, two things come to my mind:

My daughter and her husband’s family in Tampa, my friends, mastermind members and anyone in my online family who might be in a storm’s path. I’m always hoping each of you comes through with as little disruption as possible. Safe and healthy, no matter which hurricane shows up next.

And my winter home, sitting squarely in the bullseye whenever a storm decides to make landfall at full force.

My conclusion, before and after every storm:

**People first. Stuff second.**

Whether it's a natural disaster or daily life, keeping this focus is paramount.

And that doesn’t just apply to Florida disasters. 

Let it guide your business, too:

👉 People over profit

👉 Connection over commodities

👉 Family over frenzy

👉 Mastery over material

👉 Community over chaos

And maybe most importantly:

👉 **Serving over selling**

**Dan Sullivan** (the top coach for entrepreneurs in the world) and **Joe Polish** (the top connector for marketers in the world) introduced *“the five ways we get paid”* years ago…and it’s a prescription I keep coming back to.

What struck me then, and still does now, is how every part of their framework puts people first.

Not tactics. 

Not transactions. 

**People**.

The more you lean into that idea, the more every relationship, every opportunity, and every form of “payment” grows from genuine connection rather than strategy alone.

**The 5 Ways We Get Paid:**

**1. Utilize**

*How do people utilize you?*

*How do you utilize others?*

Are you “collecting” contacts… or actually contributing in a way that creates real connection and lets both you and your contacts tap into your unique talents — starting with a 100–0 mindset?

Teaching and sharing what you know with no expectation of a return is the best way for folks to utilize you.

The advanced course on utilization also includes the notion that your mentors choose you… you don’t choose your mentors.

What do you have to offer to people you want to learn from… again with a 100-0 mindset?

That is the best way for them to utilize you at the deepest level… and if you’re lucky, they will become a mentor to you as a bonus.

**2. Enhance**

*How do you enhance other people in your world?*

*How are you enhanced with every relationship?*

Here’s what it looks like when you put enhancement into action:

👉 Outwork everyone. Not to show anyone up, but to lead through action. When you “show, don’t tell,” your effort becomes a form of generosity. Others rise because you set the pace.

👉 While you’re working that hard, stay endlessly curious. Be interested, not interesting. Curiosity used to lift others, not to spotlight yourself, is a powerful enhancer.

👉 Never aim to be the smartest person in the room. If you are, you’re in the wrong room. Stay a student as much as a teacher, learning to enhance others while sharing what you know for their benefit.

👉 Enhance others by saving lives. Literally if that’s your profession, or more broadly as a caretaker in any form. Caretakers show up in many roles, including marketers who take responsibility for the results they create. Taking care of your audience pays out in countless ways. However you show up, keep asking, *“How can I contribute to lifesaving?”.* That’s the highest level of enhancement you can offer.

**3. Appreciate**

*How often do you slow down long enough to truly appreciate the people in your world?*

*And are you showing that appreciation in ways they can actually feel?*

*And when you are appreciated by others are you truly taking it in fully?*

You’re probably sick of hearing this one from me…but simply put, be grateful for those in your life and look for random acts of kindness and specific “utilization” and “enhancements” to show up as gifts to represent your appreciation.

Things like [*“Christmas cards in July”*](https://t.co/YRBh7A6fvd) and [*“Fishing without bait”.*](https://t.co/nzEp8vbyv8)

Also: Treating your list as family which includes *“eating with intention”* (e.g. hosting intentional dinners, creating a warm culture inside the webinars and Zoom calls you host, treating everyone like they belong).

These are all examples of supreme appreciation.

By now you all know how to appreciate others in many ways unique to your way of giving and you don’t need suggestions from me. 🙂

**4. Refer**

*How often do you refer someone simply because they’re good and not because there’s something in it for you?*

Be the first to refer others (assuming they are solid at what they do, and they are referable).

And don’t be a “toll booth” expecting to be reimbursed for everyone you refer or recommend to others.

I know it’s tempting to try to cash in on setting up deals and partnerships… or to take a finder’s fee for an introduction; but if you are playing a long game, your time will come.

Resist the temptation to monetize everything.

Why should you refer first?

Because when others utilize you… and you enhance and appreciate others… it should lead to referrals both ways… and getting paid is a natural outcome… without even asking.

**5. Reward**

*How do you think long-term enough to let the real rewards show up on their own?*

*How do you build relationships so steadily that asking for anything later feels completely natural?*

You get paid over time through ***utilization***, ***enhancement***, ***appreciation***, and ***referrals***.

And it always flows both ways. It may feel like magic, but it’s really patience and consistency. Follow the formula and the rewards are plentiful.

You won’t feel like you’re making an “ask from nowhere”. You’ll know when the moment is right to ask for utilization, enhancement, appreciation, or a reference—it will feel natural.

Getting there comes from credibility and transparency as you practice the four ways to get paid before any money changes hands.

A couple of speed bumps on your way to this exalted state:

👉 Recognize “givers, takers and matchers” (in the words of Adam Grant).

👉 Stay humble even when you think you’ve made it.

👉 And the “interest” is compounded when you are building “relationship capital”—rather than a “network’. Never look at it as a year-to-year project, or a one-shot, resulting in starting over each year from scratch. Build on each year from the previous year.

The criterion for anything I bring to you:

You will want to utilize it, while enhancing your life and business… always under the umbrella of “I appreciate you.”

I’ll also refer many of you under the right circumstances. Especially those in my inner circle.

And yes, making money matters… but it’s the fifth way we get paid if you choose to follow the approach in this post… offered for your consideration.

I’ll close with a quick exchange from our 7th **Breakthrough Advertising Bootcamp**.

During a hot seat, one participant told me she’d been part of my online family for 10 years, reading my weekly blog posts. She joined the Bootcamp to finally engage directly.

She’d applied what I’ve shared over the years (i.e. utilization), that I enhanced her business and personal life, that she appreciates me (because I regularly tell her and everyone else that I appreciate them)… and she has recommended me (i.e. referred me) to many others.

Has she ever joined my mastermind? No.

But she’s bought books… and now completed a Bootcamp.

Is a 10-year sales cycle worth it? 

Would it still be worth it if she never bought *anything*?

That depends on what you’re serving. And how you define getting paid.

In this case, I got paid in a big way. 🙂

And if you’ve been quietly reading my work for years, well, just know… I see you, too. 

And I appreciate you more than you might realize.

9/ There has since been an important development.

On September 29, 2026, a three-judge panel of the Eleventh Circuit declined to suspend the district court’s sanctions pending appeal.

The judges noted that the appellants had offered no evidence explaining their litigation conduct or demonstrating that the lawsuit and settlement were not collusive.

They concluded that the challengers had not made the strong showing necessary to overturn the district court’s findings at this interim stage.

This was a stay decision, not a final appellate judgment. The distinction matters.

So how accurately did Senator Whitehouse describe the Florida slush fund case?

Substantially accurately.

His central allegations are supported by explicit judicial findings. His account includes some political rhetoric and an inference about DOJ’s motives, but relatively little substantive distortion.

The underlying issue is far more consequential than the terminology.

A federal judge found that the president and officials within his own administration used litigation between supposedly opposing parties to give legitimacy to an extraordinary financial and legal arrangement.

The subsequent appellate ruling left the sanctions in place.

That is not merely a partisan accusation.

It is a documented judicial finding, subject to further appellate review.

And it raises a question that deserves scrutiny regardless of which party controls the White House:

What happens to the rule of law when the officials responsible for defending the public interest are also negotiating with the president whose interests they are supposed to scrutinize?

Pakistan's cybercrime agency has arrested a man accused of running a counterfeit operation that caused $126 million in losses to the US Postal service.

Faheem Akram is accused of having sold fake stamps via a fraudulent website in the US since 2023. He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida last month for selling more than five million counterfeit shipping labels to thousands of US customers over the years. US authorities have now shut down the website.

Earlier this month, the US Postal Inspection Service offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest. According to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, the 33-year-old from Khanewal, Pakistan, operated LabelsBank dot com. 

US prosecutors alleged that he sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate regardless of a package's weight, size or destination. The counterfeit labels, usually sold at $2 each, allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.

An investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals purchased more than 5.1 million  counterfeit shipping labels, the office said in a press release. Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud.

If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts, and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, the office said.

Mid-Week Ag Roundup Wednesday, October 21, 2026

Combines continue making significant headway across the Corn Belt following favorable harvest weather, with the latest USDA Crop Progress report pegging national corn harvest at 44 percent and soybean harvest advancing past the halfway mark to 64 percent. Meanwhile, grain futures continue to feel pressure from seasonal harvest supply and higher yield projections, while country cash cattle trade holds a steady tone heading into late October.

Grain and Livestock News Brief
Monday's USDA Crop Progress update showed national corn harvest advancing 11 percentage points to reach 44 percent complete, trailing slightly behind the five year average pace of 52 percent, with 95 percent of the crop fully mature. 

Soybean harvest reached 64 percent complete nationwide against the 65 percent five year average, with 96 percent of acres dropping leaves. The remaining corn crop condition held steady at 56 percent good to excellent. Grain futures traded under light pressure mid-week as hedge selling from peak harvest deliveries weighed on active contracts, with December corn holding near $4.56 per bushel. 

In Nebraska, harvest activity is moving into its final stretch for soybeans while corn combines make rapid progress across central and eastern counties. Feeder and live cattle futures continue to trade in a firm range supported by historically tight calf supplies, though packers are attempting to regulate slaughter paces to manage operating margins. Country cash cattle trade remains quiet early in the week, with feedyard owners holding out for steady bids against packer leverage.

Key Market Overview

Daily cattle slaughter continues running disciplined around 112,000 to 115,000 head daily as packers balance margins against tight cash supplies. Hog slaughter remains steady near 475,000 head daily, with wholesale pork cutout values showing stable autumn demand. USDA weekly export inspection data showed steady demand for U.S. corn and soybeans, helping cushion futures against seasonal harvest delivery pressure. 

Wheat export inspections remain seasonal but face strong competition from foreign origin. High replacement cow costs and strong beef-on-dairy calf values continue to keep the national dairy herd expanded. Fall milk production across northern sheds is holding steady, keeping Class III futures trading in a tight range. 

Negotiated live cash cattle trade remains quiet with asking prices firm near $228 to $230 in Nebraska, while dressed bids sit around $345 to $350 delivered. Feedlot offerings stay exceptionally tight. Spot corn basis across Nebraska country elevators reflects peak harvest delivery pressure, averaging -40 cents to -20 cents under December futures. 

Regional ethanol plants and processors offer narrower basis at -5 cents to +10 cents to secure spot pipeline needs. Country elevator spot soybean basis averages -45 cents to -25 cents under November futures, while crush facilities in eastern Nebraska maintain strong basis premiums at +15 cents to +25 cents over to draw harvest deliveries.

Harvest and Field Development Progress
The USDA Crop Progress report confirms fall fieldwork is in full swing across the central U.S.. National corn progress reached 95 percent mature and 44 percent harvested, with the remaining crop rated 56 percent good-to-excellent. National soybean progress stands at 96 percent dropping leaves and 64 percent harvested. Winter wheat planting crossed 63 percent complete nationally. In Nebraska, corn and soybean harvest is moving ahead rapidly as dry fall weather allows field work to continue with minimal weather delays. While recent localized rainfall provided temporary moisture relief, subsoil levels and pasture ratings remain heavily depleted across the region.

Cattle Inventory and Supply Outlook
Structural supply tightness across the livestock complex continues to underpin long term cash market fundamentals. In the latest WASDE report, the corn season average farm price was projected near $4.10 per bushel, with soybeans projected near $10.80 per bushel. Record low late summer placements guarantee a tightening pipeline of market ready fed cattle into late autumn and winter. The smallest July beef cow herd on record at 28.5 million head keeps feeder cattle supplies constrained nationwide.

Markets and Outlook

Harvest pace, producer grain holding strategies, and late week cash cattle development will dictate market direction through the weekend. Market participants will be watching weather patterns across the Midwest that could impact harvest wrap up and field prep. Local elevator and processor basis bids will be monitored closely as commercial facilities manage peak harvest receipts. Late week negotiated cash cattle trade in the Northern and Southern Plains will provide direction for the livestock complex.

Producers across the Western Corn Belt should track local cash basis opportunities and processor bids to manage harvest logistics.

Futures trading involves significant risk. Information provided is for educational purposes only.

1SG 🫡 AWP DAILY ORDER — October 21, 2026
Promise #294 • SUPPLIED BY GRACE, READY TO SERVE

1 — THE ORDER

Today’s 365Promises summary: “I will meet all your needs so you can overflow with good works.” 

“And God is able to make all grace abound toward you … may have an abundance for every good work.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:8, NKJV (excerpts) 

Battle Line: I receive Christ’s grace and put His love into action.

2 — THE TRAINING

Warrior Doctrine — God’s provision equips you for generosity.

Paul is encouraging believers to support others in need. The purpose is practical care and thanksgiving to God—not a promise that giving will make you wealthy. Read 2 Corinthians 9:6–12 in that setting. 

Begin with dependence. Bring your actual need before the Father: patience, wisdom, courage, or practical help. You can serve while acknowledging your own limitations.

Then notice what is already in your hands. Time to listen. Experience to share. A meal. An encouraging word. Resources that can meet a need. Ask what would genuinely help, and give willingly within your responsibilities.

1SG, today’s mission can happen in an ordinary encounter. Give someone your attention. Listen without rushing to fix everything. Offer useful kindness without needing recognition or control over the result.

Armor Fit

Belt of Truth: Let Scripture define provision and generosity.
Breastplate of Righteousness: Serve honestly, without seeking credit.
Boots of Peace: Approach others with patient attention.
Shield of Faith: Trust God while taking the next wise step.
Helmet of Salvation: Remember that you belong to Christ by grace.
Sword of the Spirit: Read today’s passage slowly.

Cross-reference study, NKJV: 2 Corinthians 8:12–15; Ephesians 2:8–10; 1 Peter 4:10–11.

3 — THE EXECUTION

Commander’s Orders

Read 2 Corinthians 9:6–12.
Pray: “Father, I need Your help with _____.”
Identify one resource you can wisely share.
Ask one person what would help, then complete one practical act of care.

Tonight’s review: Where did I depend on God? What did I share? Whom did I serve?

Prayer of Deployment

Father, thank You for receiving me through Jesus Christ. Supply the grace I need today. Give me attentive ears, willing hands, and wisdom to offer useful help. Teach me humility to receive help as well. Lord Jesus, my Commander, lead my words and actions so that others encounter Your love. Amen.

text:
Podcast Summary | Matt and Shane's Secret Podcast: Ep 642 - Popstar Halftime (feat. SWIM)

Overview

A loose, joke-dense conversation that keeps circling back to the same uncomfortable question: what people will do when nobody official is watching. Workplace affairs, AI-faked jobs, true-crime cannibal plots, rage-bait prank channels, and halftime-show conspiracy theories all get the same treatment, with the hosts testing where the line between fantasy and action actually sits. The strongest through-lines are the collapse of professional and social boundaries, the way money and attention reward increasingly mean behavior, and the hosts' habit of treating dark material as comedy while still disagreeing about what crosses a line. Cultural touchstones like The Office and Sex and the City get reread as artifacts of changing relationship norms, while the Super Bowl halftime show becomes a lens for how pop spectacle, politics, and manufactured outrage now overlap.

Key Themes

- Workplace life is treated as inherently prone to affairs and awkward triangles, which the hosts half-jokingly link to pushes for remote work and to the idea that office dynamics just relocate online.
- AI is framed less as a tool than as a way for office workers to completely fake productivity, producing long bullet-pointed emails that then get summarized by other AI.
- True-crime fascination runs alongside genuine legal ambiguity, especially in cases where elaborate violent fantasies were never acted on and the courtroom had to decide what intent means.
- Armie Hammer serves as the cautionary example: disturbing messages and biting talk ruined a career even without proof anyone was eaten, raising questions about where fantasy ends and harm begins.
- Rage-bait and public prank content is described as mean, possibly staged, and clearly lucrative, with the hosts predicting most viral content will eventually look like this.
- Parents filming children's tantrums for content draw open contempt, framed around consent and humiliation rather than comedy.
- The Super Bowl halftime show is read as a long shift from local marching-band spectacle to global pop event, with the Bad Bunny and TPUSA shows treated as a paired culture-war artifact.
- The Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce relationship is defended as real, and the outrage over her being shown during games is called misplaced.
- Drinking stories anchor the back half, with blackouts and "wild card" behavior treated as nostalgia and warning at once.

Detailed Summary

The episode opens in familiar territory: travel sports, hotel bars, and the social ecosystem that forms around youth hockey and baseball families. One host describes how light an NHL stick feels, and the group trades memories of street hockey, full pads, and nets, plus a story about telling a father he wanted to be a hockey player instead of a football player and being discouraged. From there the conversation slides into adult misbehavior, including a story about a young electrician foreman kissing an older coworker's wife at a bar and the company drama that followed. Jokes about "work husbands" and "emotional bulls" lead into a real disagreement about whether emotional cheating matters as much as physical cheating.

That thread runs straight into The Office. The Jim, Pam, and Roy triangle gets summarized, with Roy framed as a hardworking delivery man and one host arguing the show normalized or even celebrated cuckolding. Another host resists that reading. One says he fell off the show around season two or three, and a later documentary-crew storyline gets mentioned. Sex and the City comes up as a cultural marker of shifting relationship norms, including the two movies and a lesbian storyline, with mixed reactions across the group.

The workplace theme turns into a joke about office life being a breeding ground for affairs, and then a joke about that being the real reason work is being pushed to work-from-home. Remote work doesn't solve it: flirtation just moves into Zoom private messages, and people dress up at home for no practical reason. AI enters as the next layer, letting office workers completely fake their jobs by generating long, bullet-pointed emails. One host says he now uses ChatGPT to summarize AI-written emails and respond to them. Email itself gets dismissed as inferior to texting, with a stated refusal to read long messages.

The conversation takes a dark turn into true crime. The Wheel of Fortune announcer is discussed, reportedly fired after someone behind him on a plane photographed his screen showing a CSAM chat group, while he wore a Wheel of Fortune windbreaker. One host questions whether merely chatting in such a group is illegal and says he doesn't know if the announcer went to jail. The Girl Meat Hunter documentary gets a strong recommendation, with one host saying he wants to rewatch it. The case involves a New York City cop who allegedly used a screen name along those lines and made detailed plans with another self-described cannibal to lure and kill an ex-girlfriend or ex-wife, discussing a trip and the perfect crime. Investigators were reportedly triggered by plans involving his family. In court he allegedly claimed the exchanges were fantasy and that the two men were masturbating and sending stories. The hosts note he used a police database, say he likely lost his job and may have faced probation, and repeat that he did not actually eat anyone.

Armie Hammer follows as the famous girl eater case. The hosts say he was biting and saying he was going to eat people, without actually eating anyone, and that his career was ruined anyway. That leads into a discussion of right-wing filmmaking, including a claim that a Daily Wire film was shut down over unionization and that Shapiro refused to deal with it. Paul Schrader's alleged project Three Guns at Dawn is described as using AI black guys because no Black actors would take roles about corrupt Black brothers. Danny Trejo is mentioned as someone allegedly sandbagged into a Ben Shapiro film.

A wedding story about being asked to wear a dress during ultimate frisbee becomes a bit about refusing and standing on business. Billy allegedly played ultimate frisbee with a roughly 60-year-old man in a dress. A photo is described of one host and Billy recreating a Tom Brady picture with a baby, shirts off and a cowboy hat. Billy is said to have a baby and a new puppy on the way, and one host jokes that Billy said postpartum issues are just vitamins.

The baby and puppy talk sharpens into a broader point about first-time parents underestimating difficulty. One host researched postpartum issues and concluded it's just vitamins, while another says he used to think having a kid would be like having a dog and found it much harder. The comedy scene gets similar treatment: a crabs-in-a-bucket dynamic, comics making reaction videos and trashing each other, and claims that the Austin comedy scene is dead. Eminem and Kid Rock are said to be collaborating on a Christian rap and rock project, framed as the country healing and a new arc for Eminem. Christian rap and rock are argued to be commercially massive, with mentions of large play counts and award shows, and P.O.D. gets debated as to whether the Christianity was subliminal, with Boom, Southtown, and How You Like Me Now referenced. Creed is called Christian rock, then joked into agnostic rock.

A priest killed when a large wall-sized cross fell on him during a Eucharist service draws dark humor and then realization that it was fatal. The hosts strongly criticize the idea of livestreaming a firing squad execution, calling it one of the dumbest ideas they've heard, though some say they don't object to firing squads in principle. The planned execution discussed is of the Fort Hood shooter, described as having killed 13 people and wounded 30, a soldier who decided in his mind he was a double agent, was wounded, and is now a paraplegic. The last U.S. execution by firing squad cited is World War II. A woman on death row is discussed who survived two lethal injections, the first leaving her snoring and the second putting her in a coma before she was resuscitated. Her crime involved torturing and murdering a classmate with a boyfriend, including carving pentagrams. One host claims a contact in a criminal justice program interviewed her and described her as wild.

Sponsorships inside rage-bait content become their own thread. Gambling-style apps like Stake are said to fund much of the trolling content the hosts watch. A genre of prank videos built around screaming a sponsor name in public places gets described, with stunts like covering a car in tin foil at a car wash or shouting the name in Walmart, Target, and furniture stores. One host initially assumed the sponsorships were a parody of product placement and is told they're real. The pranks escalate into fake conflicts in stores with planted accomplices, provocative lines to strangers, explicit audio in fast-food places, a man in a neck brace provoking people, interviewers dropping their shorts, and a bum spinner prank using Meta glasses on passed-out people. One prankster is said to be banned from many Walmarts and Targets and to have moved to a new state. The hosts say they couldn't handle being targeted and would spaz if pranked, acknowledge the content is demonic and mean but still funny, and debate authenticity, with some videos relying on real bystanders and hidden cameras. One argues this is the future of the internet. Disneybounding gets contrasted as harmless dress-up and TikTok dancing at Disney parks.

Parents filming children's tantrums for content draw open contempt, especially when the child cannot consent. The hosts note that bad kid content has precedents in older talk-show culture, like Jerry Springer, rather than being entirely new. Conspiratorial jokes about intelligence agencies, private military companies, and the Illuminati run through the conversation, including Blackwater being founded in 1996 by Eric Prince and Al Clark from North Carolina and a mention of Hessian mercenaries fought by Washington's forces.

The halftime show discussion ties the episode together. The hosts trace the Super Bowl halftime show from local-style performances like marching bands and color guards, through Carol Channing as the first celebrity performer singing When the Saints Go Marching In, to New Kids on the Block in 1991 as a pop transition, and on to Michael Jackson and Prince as earlier mega-performers. Bad Bunny's performance is praised, with one host saying he listened to his music for several days afterward. The TPUSA alternative halftime show is treated as a weak counterpoint, reportedly drawing 400 live-stream viewers, with a country-style song about drinking beer and a violin solo singled out. The hosts joke the two shows were meant to be watched as a pair and tied together.

Jay-Z is discussed as a possible halftime performer, with speculation about guests and whether Kanye West would be excluded, and a note that Jay-Z picks his own guests. The outrage over Taylor Swift being shown during games is called misplaced, since she's the most famous person at the game. A conspiracy theory that Swift and Travis Kelce's relationship is a stunt allegedly arranged by CAA is mentioned and dismissed; the hosts believe it's real.

Drinking stories dominate the close. One host describes blacking out after about three beers and turning into a wild card, and another discusses escalating blackouts as he aged. A story is told of a man arrested for stealing a flamingo from a zoo and bringing it to a Vegas hotel, who said in court he'd had 30 to 40 beers. One host says he was a Buffalo Bills bandwagon fan and later a Braves bandwagon fan, switching around the time the Braves played the Phillies, with Greg Maddux and Dave Justice mentioned. The hosts joke about a brother podcast modeled on the Kelce brothers' show. One claims he never fully quit drinking and once tried to get drunk with his wife but couldn't, while another suggests he's suppressed fire and offers to take him out drinking, joking about livestreaming it. References to the Irish bug and a joking plan to livestream a future drinking outing close the loop on the episode's running theme: what people do when a camera is pointed at them.
