text:
Podcast Summary | Call Her Daddy: Sophia Bush: Brooke Davis, Breakups & Beginning Again

Overview
Sophia Bush turns a conversation about her memoir into a candid account of how early fame, on-set sexualization, and an engineered culture of silence shaped her sense of self, her friendships, and her relationships. The throughline is self-trust: learning to hear her own instincts over louder voices, whether a showrunner rewriting a young cast, a partner she wanted to believe, or a public narrative she had no tools to answer. Her relationship with Ashlyn Harris becomes the proof of concept that choosing yourself, however painful and public, can lead to a life that finally feels like her own.

Key Themes
- Memoir writing is less an act of authorship than a forced excavation: it pulls you into places you did not plan to go, and pride coexists with the urge to take it all back.
- One Tree Hill's Brooke Davis was pitched as comic relief, but producers sexualized her far beyond that, and the resulting public perception followed Bush into real life with no channel to answer it.
- A showrunner deliberately kept the young women apart, telling each what the others supposedly said; the injury was not only what happened but the years of friendship lost to manufactured distance.
- The collective response to #MeToo, including an anonymized statement built by interviewing each woman, was an exercise in doing justice to victims without turning their pain into entertainment.
- Toxic relationships thrive on self-doubt and external blame; Bush describes holding onto the fairy-tale phase and dismissing intuition as ordinary nerves.
- Dissociation and overwork were professionally rewarded but left her a shell personally, and it took until roughly age 40 to admit she often was not fine.
- Her relationship with Ashlyn Harris emerged through long acquaintance, jealousy, and uncanny alignment, framed as an invisible string rather than a sudden rupture.
- Public backlash during the divorce was brutal, but refusing to retaliate and protecting children and privacy helped the relationship survive the noise.
- A private backyard wedding became the most embodied choice of her life, the opposite of a public spectacle, and a marker of asking for more rather than settling.

Detailed Summary
Bush describes writing her memoir as a process that drags you and takes you to unplanned places, a baptism by fire. Her feelings about the finished book swing between pride and the wish to withdraw it entirely. One chapter, titled after the best-of-times, worst-of-times line, centers on One Tree Hill.

Her path to acting was never planned. She wanted to be a heart surgeon and did not intend to act until a required school play changed her trajectory. She attended USC, first in the acting program and then the journalism school; her parents did not want her to become an actor. She booked a big ABC pilot with Jeff Nordling playing her father, but the pilot was not picked up. The same production company had made a pilot called Ravens, which she had read; she had been considered for the Peyton role and felt she was wrong for it. She was then asked to read for the new girl character introduced after the pilot, despite having no cheerleading experience, and she referenced having seen Bring It On many times. She was 21 when she moved to North Carolina, having completed three years at USC, and was philanthropy chair of her sorority. An Annenberg advisor encouraged her to take the screen-test opportunity, telling her she could always return to school. It became nine seasons, roughly a decade.

She entered One Tree Hill without having been part of the pilot and without knowing the cast or their prior relationships, feeling like a fish out of water who was quickly taken under others' wings. She frames the early cast experience as summer camp, young people carrying adult-level responsibility while figuring it out together. She credits both parents, including her father, a photographer who worked in advertising in a crew or cameraman role, for her work ethic. The show keeps finding new audiences; as she puts it, we get older but the show stays the same age.

Brooke was pitched as comic relief and a pot-stirrer, jokingly the HBIC, because the other characters were dealing with dark storylines: narcissistic abuse, absent fathers, economic struggles, a dead mother. The audition included four scenes, one the leopard-bra-in-the-car moment, which made her uncomfortable; it was explained as an introductory stunt to signal the audience could not ignore the character. She describes Brooke as a hype woman who tells her best friend she is hot and desired, something she identified with personally.

A mandate by the fourth episode called for more Brooke, and she says the way their boss communicated this created a weird dynamic among a cast competing for screen time. No adult on set explained that these were common things that happen to young people on TV, or offered someone to talk to. In the hot-tub episode, wardrobe gave her bathing suit bottoms and a nude strapless bra; she objected that it would look topless on screen and was told it came from producers in LA. She describes a screaming match on her flip phone with her boss, telling him to keep writing those scenes because she would start coming to set every day in a turtleneck. She recounts her boss, old enough to be her father, saying on the phone that she was the one with the chest everyone wanted to see. She reflects that she was naive and did not know it was dangerous to defend herself so loudly. She cites the media culture of the era, the way Britney Spears and her body were picked apart, as context. She praises a Brooke line: know that not even your fantasy of me is interested in you. The show's resurgence means she now meets mothers her age whose 12-year-olds watch it; she jokes she apologizes for her character's first-season behavior and says Brooke grows up and has a really good heart.

Portraying Brooke affected how people saw her hugely. A random man filming her in public once called her a piece of meat, a TV prostitute. There was no social media and no op-eds, no way to communicate for herself; about five years in she was on the campaign trail. She describes being reduced and not taken seriously, with people shocked at her education, writing ability, and intellect, as a recurring experience of women being reduced to serving male desire.

The showrunner deliberately tried to prevent the women from befriending each other, fearing the talking circle would blow everything open; he weaponized his power to make the women see each other as threats rather than him as the problem. The cast built an informal support network: group chats, warnings to new hires that if he invites you to dinner, call us, and showing up in pairs or groups at dinners so no woman had to be alone with him.

The 2017 #MeToo moment prompted a collective reckoning, and the cast faced the impossible task of doing justice to victims while protecting privacy. A writer who worked on the show, a woman she adores, broke the story with a thread about her experiences without naming the showrunner or the show, but people could identify them. Cast members learned everyone's stories; Daphne called saying her agents were being contacted even though she did not experience it with him. Daphne suggested a collective statement to anonymize who things happened to while being clear about what happened.

Sophia, described as obsessed with the law and having taken a constitutional law class for fun, handled the legal and interview process and said it became an outlet to process her own worst experiences. Her own experience was on the lower end of the sliding scale, which she describes as up to about a four, while other women experienced him at a ten. Eighteen women signed their letter; 25 women from his then-current show signed a response letter. She cites that one in four women has been harassed or assaulted by age 22, and notes she worked on a Shonda Rhimes show and never had to do this to get something out of Grey's Anatomy.

The response letter from 25 women served as a collective statement and evidence for believe women, rejecting the idea that actresses fabricated claims for career gain. Collective action restored connection and a sense of balancing the scales, though it did not fix the system. A central tension: women are told they are mistaken or crazy when they sense wrongdoing, and men deny knowing any man who commits such acts, which she calls the math not mathing. Siloing women from one another is a tactic; a boss told women on set things other women supposedly said, creating distance and preventing them from talking. As a young person in a pressurized situation, she trusted everyone else in the room more than herself, and her lesson is to choose yourself. She describes an adult boss making choices for two essentially young people, rewriting them together and requiring intimate scenes and skin-to-skin wardrobe, and says experiences she reported were never rectified or taken seriously. She describes moving 18 weights from the shitty scale to the good side through the collective experience. A man on Twitter responded to the claim that having sex with a blacked-out woman is assault by saying that basically means every guy has raped someone; the response was that he was so close to getting it.

In her memoir she writes about her relationship with Chad Michael Murray; her editor told her Google exists when she wanted to omit it. She frames it as involving kids who are now adults and parents, no harm, no foul. Hilarie Burton warned her not to date him, based on a prior bad work experience on another show. She attributed years of distance from Hilarie to not listening to that advice, then later learned the boss had been telling each woman things the others supposedly said. A coworker said she was most angry about years missed being friends with the other women because she believed what he said.

A recurring dynamic in toxic relationships is that distance and self-doubt are often engineered by the other person so you will not speak up, and both parties can tell entirely separate stories about why there is distance. She describes holding onto the fairy tale early phase and wanting to believe a partner over others' warnings, reasoning that she would not lie, so why would he. She identifies a pattern of blaming external circumstances, such as her mother's illness and chemo, for unhappiness rather than naming the relationship problems, driven by good girl syndrome and pressure to be grateful. Distinguishing pre-wedding nerves from genuine intuition has no roadmap; marriage is hard is not the same as suffering, and trust your gut is hard to separate from ordinary anxiety. Dissociation and overwork were rewarded professionally, the I can do anything you need posture, but made her a shell of a human personally; it took until about age 40 to admit she often was not fine. She reframes gratitude so it is not experienced as punishment and says she wants to live differently rather than look fine and be miserable.

A groomsman dropped out of the wedding; when she called to ask why he did not show, he asked why she had not called him that morning. He was willing to be honest, and she wishes more men were. She physically manifested stress with a rash head to toe that she initially dismissed as an allergic reaction. She describes working 110-hour weeks and 17-hour set days followed by forced calls and red-eyes. In 2003, she says women had no tools and were expected to just be happy. She wrote about friendships with women the world might assume she would never speak to, some of the people her ex cheated with, and now cherishes them, saying in a lineup she would take any of them.

She describes realizing her marriage to her second ex-husband, Grant, was likely a mistake; they were better as friends and maybe should not have married. She had Esther Perelled herself by over-relying on the idea that one person cannot replace a village. She had closed off tender parts of herself before 2020, and after left had not worked, she decided to make a right, mistaking a shared passionate project with Grant for the importance of the relationship itself. She met former US soccer star Ashlyn Harris on Instagram in 2015 and in person at a 2019 artist and activist luncheon, years before her own divorce and before dating Grant.

She describes the shame of performing a happy public marriage while privately knowing it was over, noting many women around her were going through similar experiences at the same time. She realized her feelings for Harris through jealousy when friends sent Harris's dating profiles, then through moments of saying the same thing at the same time, framing it as the invisible string, every odd edge fitting like the last puzzle pieces. She was so unnerved that she paced her house for about two weeks; a friend filmed her, and she says she broke her own brain.

She was in London alone during divorce fallout, barely coping, doing a brand-partnership panel to raise money to elect women and invest in women's sports, then returning to eight West End shows that week. Her friends surprised her at a dinner where Harris was present with about 10 other friends. She had posted about being happy on her anniversary after already telling her best friend she could not stay in the marriage, fearing the internet would come for her. She describes not sleeping in the same bed, living on separate floors, and parents knowing she was miserable. She told Harris at a friend's company presentation event, timed as a layover before leaving the country so she could cry into her mother's arms for nine days if rejected. She mumbled so much that Harris asked if she was asking her on a date, and she said yes. Before their first date she tried on 900 tops.

The relationship began with a surprisingly intense first date after years of casual acquaintance, which she describes as alignment and oxygen for the first time. Both had already filed for divorce and lived separately from their exes before the first date; she says there was no overlap and acknowledges wishing she could have handled timing differently. The public backlash, including tabloid home wrecker framing, speculation, and scrutiny of queerness, was extremely painful and became like a sport; she emphasizes refusing to retaliate or expose private information, especially with children involved. Strike season provided quiet and helped the relationship survive the media storm, and long familiarity with each other's past heartbreak and divorce experiences helped them stay solid.

After recovery from public commodification, they chose a private backyard wedding over a big public event; she describes it as the most in her body she has ever been. The proposal was made by her, not her partner; she says she was never supposed to be asked. The wedding was planned quickly for the coming weekend, with food prepped and put on the smoker, married in the backyard, followed by dinner. She contrasts this with a previous big Vogue wedding, saying it was beautiful but they were not compatible. She describes gratitude as once feeling toxic and now being overwhelming.

The host highlights a pattern: ignoring a gut feeling, settling for asking too little, filling one's cup elsewhere, then reaching a point of being back in the body after dissociation. The guest frames the idea that it is too late, you are too old, or who are you to want more as patriarchy. She describes loving the life inside my four walls and not needing to always be moving or cramming every day with work as profound. Despite ongoing work, the reps of growth have only made things better, and the host stresses that the answer to can I even get better is always yes, as a message for women. She says she had never had something that was mine. After a significant personal event, she and her partner told friends and family in person, flying home to see her dad for his birthday and telling her parents, taking all the time they wanted to tell every favorite person face to face before anyone could find out on the internet. She describes nearly slipping in conversation and now being able to say that is my wife. The conversation closes with mutual appreciation, thanks for sharing stories and advice on her own terms, and a warm sign-off.

⭐️Founded: 2003 (Headquartered in Bengaluru, India) 
⭐️IPO Details: The Initial Public Offering (IPO) valued the issue at ₹852.18 crores via a 100% Offer for Sale (OFS) with a price band set between ₹665 and ₹700 per share.
⭐️Market Capitalization: Approximately ₹4,009.75 crores at the upper price band.
⭐️Listing & Status: The bidding window ran from October 15 to October 19, 2026, seeing strong overall market demand (subscribed over 132x–135x). The share allotment was finalized on October 21, 2026, with a tentative listing date on the NSE and BSE scheduled for October 23, 2026. 

2͟.͟ C͟o͟m͟p͟a͟n͟y͟ P͟r͟o͟f͟i͟l͟e͟ &͟ F͟u͟n͟d͟a͟m͟e͟n͟t͟a͟l͟s͟

Tonbo Imaging designs, develops, and manufactures advanced electro-optics (EO), infrared (IR), and thermal imaging systems, alongside complex target acquisition and missile guidance architectures. 
🎖️Asset-Light & IP-Driven Model: The company leverages a vertically integrated design methodology covering optics, electronics, and computer vision software. Its edge lies in proprietary intellectual property (IP), allowing it to build ruggedized, mission-critical systems efficiently. 
🎖️Global Footprint: As of mid-2026, Tonbo has successfully deployed over 28,000 systems across 24 countries, servicing domestic and international defense agencies, border security forces, and aerospace contractors.
🎖️The "ITAR-Free" Advantage: A core fundamental differentiator is that its primary EO/IR product suites are not subject to US International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR). This structural advantage gives Tonbo immense flexibility to export to global markets without restrictive US regulatory bottlenecks.

3͟.͟ B͟u͟s͟i͟n͟e͟s͟s͟ V͟e͟r͟t͟i͟c͟a͟l͟s͟ &͟ P͟r͟o͟d͟u͟c͟t͟ P͟o͟r͟t͟f͟o͟l͟i͟o͟

Tonbo’s technological ecosystem targets modern network-centric warfare and situational awareness needs. Its major product lines include:
⭐️Thermal Imaging & Night Vision: Lightweight, uncooled and cooled thermal sights for individual soldiers and crew-served weapons.
⭐️Surveillance & Targeting Systems: Long-range observation systems, situational awareness packages for armored vehicles, and ruggedized gimbals (e.g., the Avenger AVG-30HD EO/IR Gimbal tailored for naval vessels).
⭐️Missile Guidance & Advanced Defense Electronics: Sub-systems that enable precise tracking, automated threat detection, and computerized ballistic calculation in high-clutter environments.

4͟.͟ K͟e͟y͟ D͟e͟f͟e͟n͟s͟e͟ C͟o͟n͟t͟r͟a͟c͟t͟s͟ &͟ R͟e͟c͟e͟n͟t͟ D͟e͟v͟e͟l͟o͟p͟m͟e͟n͟t͟s͟ 

Tonbo acts as a critical tech supplier under India's defense indigenization mandate (Atmanirbhar Bharat), while maintaining a healthy export profile:
🎖️Indian Navy ADITI 3.0 Contract: Secured a landmark contract to integrate High Power Microwave (HPM) systems for next-generation maritime defense.
🎖️Naval Expansion: Continuous rollout of indigenous tracking systems like the Avenger AVG-30HD for naval fleets, augmenting tracking capabilities on high seas. 
🎖️Global Collaborations: Backed historically by institutional investors like Celesta Capital, Artiman Ventures, Exim Bank, and domestic players like HBL Power Systems, driving its penetration into international defense supply chains.

⭐️Revenue & Profitability Trends: For the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026, the company experienced a temporary contraction in financials, with revenue dipping roughly 22% and profit after tax (PAT) softening compared to FY25 (FY26 PAT was reported around ₹362.6 million / ₹36.26 crores depending on consolidated restatements). Note: Defense supply chains are frequently lumpy, characterized by revenue recognition tied to project milestones and major batch deliveries. 
⭐️Valuation Metrics: Based on FY earnings and post-issue tracking, the stock commands a high growth-oriented valuation multiple (P/E roughly in the upper 70x range based on annualized periods), mirroring investor enthusiasm for niche Indian defense tech plays.
⭐️IPO Proceeds: Because the IPO is structured entirely as an Offer for Sale (OFS), the company itself will not receive primary capital proceeds; all cash raised goes directly to exiting pre-IPO shareholders and institutional investors.

6͟.͟ C͟o͟m͟p͟e͟t͟i͟t͟i͟v͟e͟ L͟a͟n͟d͟s͟c͟a͟p͟e͟ &͟ P͟e͟e͟r͟s͟

🎖️Global Giants: International competition comes from legacy defense contractors and imaging powerhouses like Teledyne FLIR, Safran, and L3Harris.
🎖️Domestic Peers: In the Indian context, companies operating adjacent to defense electronics and optics include Data Patterns, Optimized Electrotech, and Astra Microwave, though Tonbo holds a distinct edge specifically centered on AI-driven thermal optics and computer vision architecture.

7͟.͟ B͟u͟s͟i͟n͟e͟s͟s͟ L͟o͟n͟g͟e͟v͟i͟t͟y͟ &͟ F͟u͟t͟u͟r͟e͟ P͟o͟t͟e͟n͟t͟i͟a͟l͟

⭐️Secular Tailwinds: Global military budgets are pivoting heavily toward automated surveillance, unmanned systems, night-fighting capabilities, and electronic warfare. Tonbo's hardware-software integration positions it right at the center of this shift.
⭐️Scalability via Software: Because a major portion of Tonbo's moat is driven by proprietary edge-computing and computer vision algorithms, software updates and modular upgrades provide strong recurring revenue potential and high operating leverage over time.
⭐️Risks to Monitor: Defense contracting inherently carries execution risks, reliance on government policy cycles, lumpiness in order book conversion, and geopolitical trade dynamics affecting export licenses.

text:
The Biggest Issue With the 2026-27 Bulls: Defensive Geometry - See Red Fred Bulls Historian/Podcast Host/Prophet

The Chicago Bulls are in a rebuild, and the single biggest problem on the floor right now is their defensive geometry. The three players with the greatest All-Star potential (Caleb/Matas/Giddey) are all best suited defensively to guard the same position (PF).  That creates a “defensive” logjam that will shape everything else this season.  

Today, Matas Buzelis and Caleb Wilson’s greatest defensive asset is blocking shots/providing some rim protection. You’d prefer to keep both of them closer to the basket than asking one of them to chase quicker 3’s  out on the perimeter, but both will be thrust into that role for much of the season.  Josh Giddey is likely optimized defensively guarding 4’s as well. He may also end up as one of the team’s top 3 rebounders, which further ties him to the frontcourt. Leonard Miller looked awesome in the preseason, & he’d be your 4th player best suited to play the 4 defensively. If you believe in Noa Essengue, he becomes the 5th player optimized at power forward. That’s 5 players whose defensive home is the PF position. This is not a sustainable setup.

The center position offers no relief while Claxton/Collins remain injured. There is currently no one on the floor to clean up the mess that will inevitably occur in the paint. On the perimeter, the Bulls have only 1 player (Okoro) who is considered above average in perimeter defensive versatility (He can guard every PG-SG-SF in the league & many PF’s) Tre Jones is fantastic, but his size will always limit his effectiveness against bigger/more physical wings.

The results are predictable. This team is going to have many defensive disasters this year, nightd where the geometry simply does not work…where the paint is soft…where quick perimeter players create advantages the roster is not built to answer. Hard decisions will have to be made over the next 3 years to address the logjam at PF.   Some of these players will need to develop into more versatile defenders. Others will need to be moved. The current configuration cannot stay intact if the goal is long-term competitiveness.

All that said, that problem doesn’t need to be fixed today.  The focus for this season should be around one thing:  Determine what players can play with Caleb Wilson, and cut/move/maximize the return for:  1. everyone who cannot compliment CW.  2. Players than can compliment him but are not on his timeline (Powell/Collins).  

Regardless, it’s rare to see a player so gifted athletically with the skills/motor/attitude of Caleb Wilson.  He alone will be worth the CHSN subscription cost. 

Enjoy the season.  Go Bulls.

text:
After the US Civil War, thousands of Southerners moved to Brazil, and a Brazilian city still carries their name.

Brazil's emperor, Dom Pedro II, wanted them to grow cotton, so he offered them land.

Life in the tropics was hard, and many families gave up and went back home.

The ones who stayed settled in the São Paulo countryside, around a town called Santa Bárbara d'Oeste.

Slavery was still legal in Brazil until 1888, and some of the settlers bought enslaved people after they arrived.

The settlers brought plows pulled by animals, at a time when many local farmers still worked the soil with hoes.

In 1871, they started the first Baptist church in Brazil.

They were Protestants, and the local Catholic cemetery would not bury them.

So in 1867, one settler buried his wife on his own farm, and the other families buried their dead beside her.

Their descendants still care for that field today.

In 1900, the train station near their farms was renamed Villa Americana, after the American families living nearby.

That stop grew into Americana, a Brazilian city of more than 230,000 people today.

Over the generations, the families learned Portuguese, married Brazilians and became Brazilian.

When Jimmy Carter visited in 1972, he was surprised to hear descendants speaking English with a South Georgia accent.

For decades, the descendants held a yearly party with Confederate flags and hoop skirts.

In 2022, the city of Santa Bárbara d'Oeste banned racist symbols, including the Confederate flag, from its events.

Brazil kept the families, the plows and the churches, and voted the flag out of its public events.

text:
Muscovy ducks are omnivorous, opportunistic feeders with a highly varied diet. Because they are excellent foragers, they eat a mix of plant material and small animals found in and around wetlands, fields, and parks.

Core Components of Their Diet

Insects and Invertebrates: They eat a massive amount of mosquitoes, flies, beetles, dragonflies, ants, and spiders. They are especially valued around homes and farms because they act as natural pest control.
Small Aquatic Life: They forage in shallow waters for small fish, minnows, tadpoles, frogs, crustaceans (like crayfish), and aquatic snails.
Plant Matter: Their diet includes the roots, stems, seeds, and leaves of aquatic plants, grasses, sedges, and agricultural grain crops.
Terrestrial Pests: They will actively hunt and consume slugs, snails, and earthworms from lawns and gardens.

What to Feed Domestic or Park Ducks

If you are feeding domestic Muscovy ducks or looking for healthy options for park ducks, you should avoid bread, which lacks nutrition and causes health problems like "angel wing." Instead, offer:
Commercial duck pellets or waterfowl starter crumble
Cracks or whole corn, wheat, oats, or barley
Chopped leafy greens (such as kale, romaine lettuce, or cabbage)
Frozen peas or sweet corn (thawed)

text:
Got on a call with a guy who hasn't sent a single ad to a store in 3 years.

His words: "it's a waste of ad spend."
When we talked, he was doing $30–50K a day.

He's 32 and calls himself a dinosaur. He started in CPA marketing in 2016 selling Teespring t-shirts, learned on the Stack That Money forum, then built a brand in Sweden, where his parents had moved with one goal: put food on the table.

Then 2020 hit him. Right before the US election, Facebook locked him out for six wholemonths. No agency accounts, no backup profiles, no connections. The brand started bleeding money in what he called a negative spiral.

So he walked away from it, took one month off, and came back with 5 new offers.

Every one of them runs the same way: ad, then an advertorial or a long sales page, then an
order form. Never a product page.

He builds the advertorials in Webflow.
How he builds them:

3 weeks of research before he writes a word, and 3 advertorial angles per offer

He writes the headline last
He never launches an advertorial without an image ad
Klarna one-click upsells, which he calls his edge
And the one that broke my brain. If 40–50% of readers click through from his advertorial, he's not happy. He says it's not filtering enough. His sweet spot is 25–35%.

Most people would kill for a 50% click-through. He wants the page to scare off everyone
who was never going to buy.

Early on, a $600-a-day profit made him comfortable. Two months later, in his words, it just
died.

And while he writes copy, he keeps a printed photo of his customer next to him. Her name is Susan.

Why this works:
A product page shows the product to someone who didn't wake up wanting it. An advertorial sells the problem first, then the mechanism, then the product. 

By the time someone hits the order form, they've already decided.

That's also why he wants a lower click-through. A click from someone who isn't sold yet turns into an abandoned checkout. 30% of people who already decided beats 50% of people who are just curious.

How to steal it this week:

1. Pull the 10 longest-running advertorials in your niche. Anything live for 90+ days is printing, or the brand would have killed it. I use GetHookd for this.
2. Write down the order of each one: hook, story, problem, mechanism, product, offer. You'll see the same skeleton over and over.
3. Pick 3 angles and write one advertorial per angle. Headline last.
4. Launch each one with an image ad, and track click-through to the order form. His target is 25–35%.

Your product page is not a landing page.

text:
My attempt to make Dexpot faster included making it more polite. The server responded by getting slower in one of the workloads.

I’m building Dexpot as an open-source hobby, aiming for the fastest Pythonic API framework on both ordinary and free-threaded Python, while keeping handlers simple synchronous functions.

Ordinary Python has a lock called the GIL that normally lets only one thread execute Python code at a time. Free-threaded Python removes that restriction. Multiple workers can actually run Python together, which also gives me more creative ways to discover scheduling problems.

Here’s what happened.

Think of the server’s workers as waiters. A worker handles a request, sometimes waits for something, then sends the response. The operating system decides when each worker gets a turn.

In our mixed-workload test on macOS, a simulated 1 ms I/O wait, standing in for waiting on a network or disk operation, could take roughly 9 ms. The worker used very little CPU during that interval. It was waiting to resume.

My first fairness experiment made workers offer someone else a turn after every completed response. It helped CPU-heavy work, but made the mixed workload worse. I had taught the waiters to finish an order and immediately hold a meeting about whose turn it was next.

Switching to a CPU-time budget reduced unnecessary handoffs, but still didn’t clear the mixed-workload latency limit.

The correction needed both pieces:

1. Change the macOS scheduling setting only for Dexpot’s own free-threaded connection workers, helping them resume promptly. Restore each worker’s previous setting when it exits. Leave the main thread and the machine’s power settings alone.

2. Let a worker accumulate roughly 1 ms of actual CPU work before offering others a turn, after finishing its current response. Time spent waiting doesn’t spend that budget, and we don’t interrupt a handler halfway through its work.

At 10,000 requests/second and 16 connections, the final macOS version had about 3 ms p99 latency, compared with 31–36 ms for the earlier fast control. “p99” means 99% of measured requests finished within that time. Our unchanged limit was 20 ms.

Then we checked Ubuntu ARM64 in Docker. Those macOS mechanisms stayed disabled. Throughput was roughly unchanged, and mixed-load p99 was about 4.6 ms for both versions. These are local, workload-specific results, not a claim that every server on every machine behaves this way.

We also found that our HTTP tests left servers alive after the tests finished. Those servers could encounter temporary fake functions installed by later tests. We fixed that cleanup, then Windows caught our assumption that terminating a process should return the same exit code everywhere.

I started out chasing faster responses and ended up reviewing worker breaks, wake-up calls, and whether the restaurant actually closes.

The ambition is still the fastest simple Python API framework. The current achievement includes knowing when to let a waiter sit down.

If this is your kind of open-source rabbit hole, I’d love some company:

text:
17 client problems before morning coffee?

You wake up and BOOM...

One guy wants Facebook ads.

Another wants email stuff.

A third wants you to build him a funnel, write his book, and maybe walk his dog too.

I see it all the time.

Wanna know the fix? It's dumb simple…

If you want to scale, you need to pick ONE thing, and do it really, really well.

I know you don't want to hear this… but more offers = more headaches.

(I used to launch companies after natural disasters, trust me, I know)

Every time you add a new offer, you're not adding more money.

You're adding a whole new business.

New offer means…

- new systems
- new team
- new training
- new problems
- new fires to put out at 11pm on a Tuesday

Agency owners think having 5 offers makes them look big and fancy.

But nobody goes to a buffet and says "wow, this is the best crab leg I've ever had."

Your clients feel the same way when your offer is all over the place.

If you're running 3 business models inside 1 brand…

No wonder you feel stuck.

You need to pick the ONE offer you love.

The one where your clients get amazing results, but feels super easy to deliver.

Go all in on that.

"But how do I get more of these clients?"

Great question.

There's lots you can do, I talk about them a bunch.

But know this:

It's a problem you need to solve if you want to scale, and a lot funner than being a buffet of services.

Belgium: Despite limited progress, the "Arizona" coalition—the five-party government—is looking to raise 5 billion euros through the sale of the Belgian state’s stake in BNP Paribas.

The idea is gaining traction within the government. According to Bloomberg, some members of the Belgian administration are in favor of selling the 5.7% stake held by the state in BNP Paribas.

Sources familiar with the matter indicate that such a sale is not expected to happen immediately and is not linked to the currently tense budget negotiations. Nevertheless, there is a clear desire within the government to divest this holding, once other planned divestments have been completed.

The Belgian stake is valued at approximately 5.4 billion euros (6.1 billion dollars), based on BNP Paribas’s current market capitalization of nearly 95 billion euros.

The government is well on track to sell a 20% stake in Belfius Bank SA by the end of the year and is currently in the process of receiving firm offers.

Discussions have also explored potential options for the insurer Ethias SA, including the spin-off of its IT subsidiary, Keyes, and a possible tie-up with Belfius. Any sale of the state’s stake in BNP Paribas would likely take place only after the country’s ongoing divestment processes have been finalized, according to a source familiar with the matter who requested anonymity.

Spokespersons for the ministers from the five parties that make up the Belgian government, as well as representatives for BNP Paribas, declined to comment. Belgium became the largest shareholder in BNP Paribas following a 2008 agreement, in which the French bank took control of Fortis—at the time Belgium’s largest financial services company—as part of a state-led rescue operation.

Quote by 김여정, Department Director of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea, on October 08, 2026.

◾

In my commentary on 김여정’s press statement dated October 8, 2026, I want to start first and foremost with this very sentence that I have selected as a quote, because the diplomatic catastrophe on the part of the ROK authorities is exposed by 김여정 with this sentence in an exceptionally succinct manner.

Two words stand out particularly sharply from this sentence by 김여정: “vulnerable class” (koreanisch 취약계층). Due to the completely differing ideological leanings of the two states spanning the whole of Korea (조선), “취약계층” carries two entirely distinct meanings.

In the DPRK, “취약계층” means “vulnerable class.”

In the ROK, “취약계층” means “vulnerable stratum.”

In the Democratic People's Republic of Korea as a socialist state, the word “stratum” for the purpose of a capitalist-sociological categorization of segments of a population into a “lower stratum, middle stratum, upper stratum” can have no right to exist within the official state and ideological vocabulary for its own working people as the working class. In socialism, there are fundamentally no superimposed strata consisting of a lower, middle, and upper stratum, but rather the social and material equality of all working people, comprising workers, intellectuals, and lastly, farmers, as symbolized by the party emblem of the Workers’ Party of Korea, which consists of the hammer, the writing brush, and the sickle. In the DPRK, the characters “계층” are instead assigned to the word “class.” Due to the Marxist-Leninist class consciousness in the DPRK, the word “class” exists within the vocabulary of the DPRK, not the word “stratum.”

The Western academic left uses the word “stratum” revisionistically because it has adapted to bourgeois-capitalist sociology and, through this adaptation, has largely abandoned Marxist-Leninist class theory. The DPRK, however, has not, because it has not replaced its vocabulary. Therefore, contrary to self-proclaimed “friends of the DPRK,” the DPRK also knows that communism is a borderless and stateless society. Globally organized, alleged “friends of the DPRK” contradict me on this and claim that I am clinging to an “outdated definition of communism” or, more precisely, to its “simplified banalization by Western leftists.” Insane, this chaos among the leftists in the West.

The careless emphasis on “계층” is what makes the undiplomatic insult against 김여정 and against the DPRK by the ROK authorities so severe, and it wonderfully demonstrates that the Republic of Korea cannot be a partner for reconciliation in the DPRK. The ROK is a capitalist state that is incapable of considering the socialist thinking of the DPRK in its alleged “diplomatic efforts.” I have deliberately referred strictly to the Republic of Korea in my phrasing in order to avoid a generalization. It can happen that a government comes to power in a capitalist state that would be capable of considering the class consciousness of a socialist state in its diplomatic endeavors to avoid unintended insults and diplomatic blunders against a socialist state. The Republic of Korea, however, fails in this completely.

Although I myself originate from a capitalist state, I am capable of empathizing with the class consciousness of 김여정 and the DPRK, and I duly consider 김여정’s class consciousness within my writings. Were I to carelessly emphasize the term “취약계층” regarding the DPRK, I would insult 김여정, because I am fully aware that within the socialist context of the DPRK, “취약계층” means “vulnerable class.” Because the Republic of Korea, bound by its anti-socialist, capitalist stratum-consciousness, fails to consider that only a single class exists within the DPRK and that 김여정 is consequently socially and materially equal to all working people, the ROK authorities insinuate an internal domestic division between rich and poor by emphasizing a “vulnerable class.” It is understandable that 김여정 perceives this as an insulting provocation against herself and her state.

These alleged “offers of assistance” made in the supposedly “good faith” of the Lee Jae-myung cabinet are in reality a poisoned, subversive attempt to deny the social and material equality in the North and to depict a bourgeois division. Definitely a grave insult against the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, which is rightfully condemned in the harshest terms by 김여정.

Furthermore, the legitimacy of the government of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea under the leadership of the Chairman of the State Affairs Commission, 김정은, is being called into question. This is because the ROK authorities act as if they are the guardian of the people of the DPRK. However, this also beautifully shows that the ROK authorities want to prepare the international community for a world without 김여정 and Marshal 김정은, so that there will be no one left in the world to condemn a renewed self-inflicted military confrontation by the ROK army into the territory of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

But I must disappoint the ROK authorities. I am 3 weeks younger than the General Secretary of the Workers’ Party of Korea, 김정은, and I have no intention of dying prematurely. Therefore, as long as I live, 김여정 and Marshal 김정은 will always have someone who does not deny or silence them!

◾

With this commentary text on her press statement, I also intend to supplement the Department Director of the Central Committee of the Workers’ Party of Korea, 김여정, on the material depth level. I explain what the ROK authorities additionally intend with these alleged “offers of assistance” in supposedly “good will.” Namely, the Republic of Korea is pursuing a long-term military strategy. The strategic war aims of the ROK against the DPRK include the establishment of medical bridgeheads for the medical supply of the ROK army inside the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

How do I come up with the term “medical bridgehead”? I explain.
As everyone should actually know, the DPRK, the USA, and the ROK are still at war. A classic bridgehead in a war is a fortified and armed facility in enemy territory built with concrete, barbed wire, and sandbags to deploy one’s own troops in enemy territory.
An example: In World War II, the Ludendorff Bridge across the Rhine at Remagen was a bridgehead for the deployment of US troops. Germany was enemy territory for US troops.

Madurai Sambavam was released in 2009. It was a good film, and I genuinely enjoyed watching it. But seeing a song from the film being used as a situation song during the funeral of #SullanMadhan, a rowdy who was murdered in real life, made me realise just how deeply rowdy culture has taken root in the minds of today's youngsters.

#Madurai, along with neighbouring districts such as #Sivaganga, #Theni and #Dindigul, has so much more to offer beyond caste divisions and violence. What I cannot accept is how certain filmmakers, in the name of cinema, have reduced our hometowns to places associated with caste pride, rowdyism and sickle wielding gangs. They portray people from our region as if violence is our identity.

Madurai is home to the Nayakkar Mahal, Meenakshi Amman Temple, Pazhamudhircholai, Rajaji Park, Park Murugan Temple, Alagar Kovil, Gandhi Memorial Museum, Samanar Hills, Vandiyur Mariamman Theppakulam, Race Course Ground near Outpost, Puthu Mandapam area, Thiruparankundram, Koodal Azhagar Perumal Temple, Vishaal de Mall, Paravai Market, Pasumalai, Narasingam Perumal Temple, Yanaimalai and Airport Road. These are just some of the many places that define the beauty, history and culture of our city. Yet, filmmakers repeatedly choose to portray sickles and knives as the central identity of Madurai. That is what I find unacceptable. The same goes for Theni, which has so many beautiful places and stories worth telling.

Sivaganga has its magnificent Chettinad mansions, Pillayarpatti Temple, Thirukoshtiyur Sowmiya Narayana Perumal Temple and its Theppotsavam, Nattarasankottai Kannathal Temple, Vettangudi Bird Sanctuary and Kalaiyarkovil. These places, their traditions and their people deserve to be represented with the same passion that filmmakers show when portraying violence.

This is a time when filmmakers need to act with greater social responsibility. Youngsters are fascinated by cinema, carrying machetes and sickles, glorifying caste pride and making reels that celebrate violence. The film industry must take the first step towards changing this culture. A state government can take the necessary law and order measures to prevent crime. But preventing the glorification of violence and protecting the next generation is also a responsibility of the society around us. And cinema is one of the most influential parts of that society. It is an industry that reaches millions of people effortlessly, with four films releasing every week and around 20 to 22 films every month.

I am not saying filmmakers should stop making films based on real incidents. I am saying that they must also show the consequences of violence in a way that leaves a lasting impression on young minds. When villains are glorified as heroes, when knives and sickles are portrayed as the only way to protect ourselves, and when youngsters are encouraged to believe that even our gods are symbols of wielding weapons, we must ask ourselves what message we are sending them.

Young men get caught up in this glorification, take up weapons and end up killing one another. Their lives are destroyed, and their families are left devastated, struggling to survive the consequences. Cinema has the power to influence society. It is time the industry recognised that power and used it responsibly. @CMOTamilnadu @TVKVijayHQ @tnpoliceoffl @siaaprnews @VishalKOfficial

🇮🇱 Inside Israel Intel: The Daily Strategic Brief
October 21, 2026 | 9:02 a.m. EDT

Iran’s demands, the widening cost of regional insecurity, and Israel’s unfinished security tasks

🧭The strategic picture
The central question this morning is whether military and economic pressure is producing durable security gains. Tehran is demanding relief while insisting on retaining its enriched material. Netanyahu has publicly defined success as bringing down Iran’s regime. Washington continues to welcome mediation while insisting Iran must never acquire nuclear weapons. Those positions leave major questions about an acceptable settlement unresolved. 

Meanwhile, shipping incidents and Britain’s expanded support for Saudi Arabia show how broadly regional insecurity is being felt. America’s diesel shortage adds another consequence: pressure to ease restrictions on Russian fuel.

My assessment is that endurance increasingly matters alongside military capability. Israel and its partners need arrangements that prevent enemies from rebuilding, while sustaining the economic and political capacity to enforce them. That connects the Iran negotiations, the dispute over Hezbollah disarmament, and continuing operations against Hamas. Israel is also entering the final week before its election, with soldiers beginning to vote today. 

📰What you need to know

🇮🇷1. Iran wants relief first. The unresolved question is what it would surrender afterward.

📌The facts
On October 20, Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei told Pakistan’s army chief that Iran would retain all its enriched nuclear material. Iranian leaders also demanded sanctions and blockade relief before renewed negotiations. These are Tehran’s stated conditions, not a verified account of its stockpile’s condition or accessibility.

At Tel Hai University that day, Netanyahu called eliminating Iran’s regime Israel’s primary objective and said he had discussed it with President Trump. That establishes Netanyahu’s position, not American endorsement. Today, Secretary of State Marco Rubio welcomed mediation by Qatar and Pakistan while reiterating that an agreement must prevent Iran acquiring nuclear weapons. The Times of Israel

🔎My assessment

Tehran is trying to make economic concessions the entrance fee for negotiations while protecting a central bargaining asset. Granting substantial relief before enforceable nuclear restrictions would reduce American leverage precisely when it is needed most.

The allied question is equally important. Preventing a nuclear weapon, dismantling proxies and missile programs, and bringing down a regime require different commitments, resources and definitions of success. Israel needs clarity about what Washington will enforce and what Israel must be prepared to do itself.

Continued mediation means a negotiated outcome remains possible. The evidence that would change my assessment is a verifiable change in Iran’s nuclear position, with inspection and enforcement arrangements. Another meeting, by itself, would tell us little.

🚢2. Regional insecurity is imposing military costs and changing America’s economic choices.

📌The facts
UK Maritime Trade Operations reported two tanker incidents: one near Iraq’s Al Faw at 2:30 p.m. EDT on October 20, and another near Oman’s Bukha at 9:45 p.m. EDT. A fire on the latter vessel was extinguished; both crews were reported safe. Neither notice identified the attacker, but it is safe to assume Iran is behind both.

Britain announced additional Saudi support on October 20, including defensive Typhoon missions. Its expanded refueling assistance also supports Saudi operations against Houthi military targets. Separately, Turkey, Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia signed a defense cooperation accord today covering production, training and research, not mutual defense. These measures operate on different timelines: immediate protection and longer-term capacity.

The American connection is concrete. Russia’s deputy prime minister said today that a 40,000-ton diesel cargo would depart for the United States on October 22; departure has not been verified. An October 9 Treasury license authorized specified Russian-diesel transactions through April 7, 2027. The vulnerability predates these latest shipping incidents: September US East Coast distillate inventories were 32 percent below their seasonal five-year average, according to the Energy Information Administration. Reuters

🔎My assessment

Disruption creates leverage when governments must absorb higher defense costs and pressure on household and industrial energy supplies. 

The Russian fuel arrangement exposes a strategic tradeoff. Washington has a legitimate interest in relieving shortages, but reopening commercial opportunities for Moscow can weaken economic pressure on another adversary. Its value should be judged by additional supply actually delivered and inventories restored. Let us also not forget that Iran and Russia are strategic allies and relief for Russia may eventually end up aiding the Iranians as well.

🛡️3. Lebanon and Gaza remain unfinished security problems as Israel begins voting.

📌The facts
Israeli, Lebanese and American military representatives began talks in Tampa on October 20. Hezbollah disarmament and Israeli operations remain disputed. That day, the IDF released footage it said showed Hezbollah removing weapons from a site the Lebanese Army had reported addressing. 

The Lebanese Army offered a specific competing chronology: it said work had stopped under Israeli threats, with the monitoring mechanism informed that weapons remained, and that clearance was completed October 16. It dated the truck-strike footage to July 3. 

In Gaza, Israel announced today that an October 18 strike killed Hamas operative Musa Hamouda, whom the IDF and Shin Bet linked to an attack that killed four soldiers and to renewed operational activity. 

🔎My assessment

The Lebanon dispute goes directly to what would make an agreement safe for northern Israel: demonstrable removal of Hezbollah’s military capacity and a mechanism that detects its return.

The monitoring records matter. If they substantiate Lebanon’s chronology, the allegation concerning this site needs reassessment. If they establish premature clearance claims, further withdrawal requires stronger safeguards as this would be a return to the historical issues behind UNIFIL lead disarmament. Israel’s security interest is served only by an accurate operational picture. Frankly the same can be said for Lebanon in terms of being freed from Hezbollah.

Gaza presents a related challenge. Removing experienced operatives disrupts attacks, but eliminations do not establish that Hamas has lost its ability to recruit, command or rebuild. Those are the measures of lasting progress and have yet to be seen through.

✡️4. Antisemitism policy must recognize the Jewish connection to Israel.

📌The facts
An October 20 preview of Sir David Bell’s review of antisemitism in English schools reported 27 recommendations, including encouraging the IHRA definition and improving teaching about contemporary Judaism. The full recommendations and government response could not be verified by this edition’s cutoff, so a definitive assessment remains premature. 

An American case illustrates the issue. An October 15 complaint against Maryland’s Montgomery County Public Schools, publicized October 19 and followed by a district response October 20, alleges that an Orthodox Jewish student faced threats and exclusion as a “Zionist,” including after announcing plans to study in Israel. The complaint acknowledges protective measures but says they failed to restore full participation. 

🔎My assessment

My test is explicit: does the policy recognize that Zionism is core to Judaism, and that uniquely vilifying it is classic antisemitism?

Israel and Zion are embedded in Jewish religion, history and peoplehood. Zionism expresses Jewish national self-determination. That connection cannot be treated as something Jews must renounce to be accepted in school or public life. Canada’s IHRA handbook provides useful substantive guidance on Jewish identity and discriminatory denial of Jewish self-determination. 

Training and complaint procedures matter, but their content determines their value. If a school recognizes antisemitism only when it uses familiar Nazi imagery, while overlooking discriminatory exclusion expressed through “Zionist,” it leaves a central vulnerability unaddressed. Bell’s published recommendations should be judged against that standard.

👀What to watch: the next 24–72 hours

🇮🇷Iran: Any concrete change on enriched material, inspections or the sequencing of relief. That would distinguish bargaining movement from repeated positions. This is very unlikely prior to elections.

🇱🇧Lebanon: A Tampa outcome specifying verification, access and consequences for violations. Those details determine whether withdrawals can produce durable security.

🚢Shipping and fuel: Verified additional attacks, changes in vessel movements, and confirmation of the proposed Russian cargo’s departure. Actual flows will test the economic response.

🗳️Israel: Documented threats to polling or changes to election security arrangements. Elevated readiness alone does not establish an imminent attack.

✡️Jewish safety: Bell’s full recommendations and government response, specifically their treatment of Zionism, Jewish identity and discriminatory exclusion.

If you appreciate this report, please share and comment. Your engagement makes it possible for me to continue providing this kind of information. Thanks and stay safe!

@grob verification 

Yes, the claim is verified. It comes from a real interview with the then-Qatari Ambassador to Germany, Sheikh Abdulla bin Mohammed bin Saud Al Thani (Abdulla bin Mohammed bin Saud Al Thani), published by The Jerusalem Post in mid-February 2024.0
When and where he said it
•The interview was conducted by Jerusalem Post Editor-in-Chief Zvika Klein in Berlin, around 14 February 2024, during the “Joint Perspectives” conference co-hosted by The Jerusalem Post and the German paper WELT.
•Articles reporting it appeared on 15–16 February 2024 (one by Tovah Lazaroff, one by Zvika Klein himself).45
Original quotes (from the JPost reporting)
Thani said of Gadi Eisenkot (then a minister and former IDF Chief of Staff):
“friend. I know him. I know his family. I visited him in his office, and we had lunch together, and he gave me a nice tour, by the way.”
After Gal Eisenkot (age 25) was killed in Gaza in December 2023, Thani said he contacted Eisenkot to offer condolences and that he was saddened by the news. He added:
“I always have a link with him. This is a friendship and I will keep it.”45
They first met as students at the US Army War College in Pennsylvania. Thani has visited Israel multiple times (including in earlier professional roles).46
Context on the “aquarium”
The Hebrew post’s reference to the “aquarium” (האקווריום) is the common Israeli nickname for the IDF General Staff building / Chief of Staff’s office area in the Kirya in Tel Aviv. The visit and lunch/tour therefore took place while Eisenkot was Chief of Staff (2015–2019).
The circulating Hebrew text is a close, accurate paraphrase of what the ambassador said in that February 2024 interview. The original source is the Jerusalem Post reporting of the public interview in Berlin, not a later or different statement.

text:
$DAVE business model is insane.

Dave offers cash advances from $25 to $500, typically approved within 5 minutes with no credit check. The average advance is $213.

Instead of charging interest or late fees, they use a simple fee structure: 5% of the advance, with a $5 minimum and $15 maximum. Dave's average revenue per ExtraCash advance is $13.70.

Dave funds a big chunk of ExtraCash through its partner bank, Coastal Community Bank $CCB. It pays Coastal the federal funds rate plus a margin to use their balance sheet for up to 60 days. After that, Dave has to buy the advance back at full value. That’s fine, though, because most advances are repaid on the customer's next payday, usually within 10–14 days.

Now here's where it gets crazy…

Assuming a funding cost of about 6.5% (the fed funds rate plus Coastal's margin), lending $213 for 12 days costs Dave only about $0.45.

$213 × 6.5% × (12/365) = $0.45

Dave's average fee: $13.70

Coastal's funding cost: –$0.45

Spread before credit losses and processing: $13.25

Even after losses and processing costs, Dave keeps about 72% gross margins.

Millions of people use it for gas, groceries, bills, and rent. To them, $13 to access a couple hundred dollars doesn't seem like much, right?

But annualize that over a year instead of 12 days, and it works out to an APR of about 195%.

Crazy that nobody on FinX is talking about this stock.

text:
Tabletalk Devotions with R.C. Sproul
Duration: 365 days
Running for the Hills
Matthew 24:15–22 “Let the one who is on the housetop not go down to take what is in his house, and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak” (vv. 17–18).

In addition to wars, false messiahs, and the preaching of the Gospel to the Roman empire, Jesus also said martyrdom, famines, earthquakes, and apostasy would precede the destruction of the temple (Matt. 24:4–14). And as our Savior predicted, all these things occurred prior to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. Earthquakes shook Laodicea and Pompeii in 60–61 and 62, respectively. Agabus, an early Christian prophet, predicted a famine (Acts 11:27–30) that did take place in the years 45–47. The book of Hebrews offers warnings to the early Christian community, imploring God’s people not to let their love grow cold and apostatize (3:7–4:13; 6:4–8; 10:26–31; 12:25–29). Finally, many Christians were martyred for their faith in the decades leading up to Jerusalem’s destruction. Acts records the deaths of Stephen (7:54–60) and James, the brother of John (12:1–2). James the Just, brother of Jesus and author of the New Testament epistle of James was stoned to death in the year 62. Reliable church tradition says Nero crucified Peter upside down and beheaded Paul in the mid-60s.

Tomorrow we will study the “abomination of desolation” (Matt. 24:15), the Roman desecration of the temple during the siege of Jerusalem, in more detail. Today we will focus on Jesus’ instructions to His disciples regarding what to do when this sacrilege appears. The abomination will signify that the end is near for Jerusalem and portends great destruction and loss of life. Believers, therefore, must flee in haste, not pausing to rescue their possessions or grab their cloaks before leaving the city (vv. 15–18). Jesus laments the pregnant and nursing women who will have to flee, for their children will hamper their ability to escape quickly (v. 19). He also tells the disciples to pray that they will not have to travel during times that will slow down those fleeing to the hills: the cold, rainy, Palestinian winter or the Sabbath, when provisions are not obtainable (v. 20).

Ancient history confirms that the remaining Jewish Christians in Jerusalem did indeed flee the city before it fell. This fact shows that the earliest believers knew that Matthew 24:1–35 applied directly to their situation, and therefore supports our view that these verses apply primarily to Jerusalem’s destruction.

Coram deo: Living before the face of God
Jesus words in today’s passage indicate that it is not necessarily wrong for believers to flee when calamity comes or when men rise to persecute the church. Certainly, if we are caught we must be willing to die for Jesus; however, there is nothing commendable about looking for martyrdom specifically. Pray today for the suffering church around the world to have wisdom to know when to stay and when to flee persecution.

text:
@Dear Elon Musk and the SpaceX Team,

My name is Karol Dynarski, and I am writing to you from Poland with a dream that goes beyond any single person, country, or generation: the survival and future of humanity.

Since childhood, I have lived with a congenital disability and congenital hypothyroidism. These challenges are part of my life, but they have never taken away my ambition to think about the future and what humanity might achieve if we work together.

I believe that one of the greatest challenges facing our species is ensuring that humanity has a future, even if one day life on Earth faces dangers that threaten our survival. We should do everything we reasonably can to protect our home planet, while also exploring whether humanity could one day live sustainably beyond Earth.

That is why the idea of Mars fascinates me. I think about the possibility of protecting its atmosphere, studying its interior, investigating artificial magnetic shielding, and discovering what might someday make the planet more suitable for human life. I understand that these are enormous scientific and engineering challenges, and that many ideas would require years of research before we could know whether they are feasible.

I am not claiming to have all the answers or a complete scientific plan. I am writing because I want to learn, develop my ideas, and encourage people to think boldly but responsibly about humanity’s long-term future.

To me, space exploration is about more than rockets, technology, or reaching another planet. It is about giving future generations more possibilities, protecting life, and improving humanity’s chances of surviving challenges that we may not yet fully understand.

I also believe that no person, company, or nation can secure humanity’s future alone. We need cooperation across borders, the sharing of knowledge, and a willingness to work toward goals greater than our individual interests. If humanity can unite around a common purpose, we may achieve things that seem impossible today.

My disability has given my own life its share of challenges, but it has not taken away my desire to contribute something meaningful. I hope that people will continue to judge ideas by their value and recognize that people from many different backgrounds can contribute to humanity’s future.

I hope that one day, when people look back at the history of humanity’s journey into space, they will remember that ordinary people from all over the world also dreamed of protecting our species and giving future generations a second chance.

I am Karol Dynarski, from Poland, and I want to be one of those people who believe that humanity’s future is worth working for through knowledge, cooperation, scientific curiosity, and peaceful determination.

I would be grateful if my message could reach you, Elon, or someone at SpaceX who shares an interest in humanity’s long-term future. If there is any advice you could offer about how someone like me could begin learning more about planetary science, space exploration, and the challenges of making humanity a multiplanetary species, I would greatly appreciate it.

I would also like to ask you an important question, Elon. Am I communicating with the real Elon Musk through an authentic and officially verified channel? Is this your genuine account, protected by an official security code or verification system? I ask because I have encountered people online who impersonate you, and I want to make sure that I am speaking to the real person and not a fake account. Authenticity and trust are very important to me.

Thank you for your time and for the work being done to advance space exploration.

With respect and hope,

Karol Dynarski
Poland

4. Fear of Another "Budapest Memorandum"

Ultimately, Ukraine’s deepest dissatisfaction is structural. The 2024 bilateral agreement remains a political executive agreement rather than a legally binding, Senate-ratified treaty. Without automated enforcement tools or an ironclad commitment modeled directly after NATO's Article 5, Ukrainian leaders fear the current assurances will suffer the same fate as the 1994 Budapest Memorandum—offering plenty of political paperwork but no actual military intervention when borders are violated. 

https://t.co/EgYcYiIWpU

One of the problem also is, the Ukraine seeing US is like the friendship

I have hit on the exact core of the emotional and diplomatic friction. From Ukraine's perspective, the deepest problem is that Kyiv views the relationship through the lens of a values-based friendship and mutual sacrifice, while Washington treats it as a cold, transactional business deal.

This fundamental mismatch in how both nations view the partnership creates several distinct points of frustration:

1. "Friendship" vs. "Transaction"

Ukraine approaches the United States as an existential ally. Ukrainian officials frequently emphasize that their people are shedding blood to defend the democratic values of the entire Western world. Because of this shared sacrifice, Kyiv expects the loyalty, consistency, and emotional solidarity that comes with a true friendship.

https://t.co/aRx2YQGTGf

In sharp contrast, the current U.S. administration views foreign policy strictly as a business transaction. President Trump evaluates the relationship based on immediate American economic indicators (like global diesel prices) rather than historical or moral obligations. 

https://t.co/SFIWZ1Wona

2. The Asymmetry of Trust

To Ukraine, a friend does not cut deals behind your back. President Zelenskyy expressed profound personal pain and a sense of betrayal after learning that the U.S. bypassed Ukraine to negotiate the "Diesel Deal" and temporary sanctions relief directly with Vladimir Putin. From Kyiv's viewpoint, the U.S. acts like a fair-weather friend—willing to offer support when convenient, but quick to look the other way or make side deals with the enemy when domestic energy prices spike. 

https://t.co/pkIg0zNO6Q?

3. The "Gratitude" Complaint

Because the U.S. views the relationship transactionally, it often behaves like a demanding creditor rather than a partner. Trump has frequently publicly chided Zelenskyy, demanding more "gratitude" for the billions in U.S. military aid provided since 2022. 

https://t.co/9Vv0XhTTKH

For Ukrainians, this is deeply insulting. They feel they are already paying the ultimate price in human lives, making the American demand for political "thank yous" feel incredibly hollow and insensitive to their daily reality. 

https://t.co/aRx2YQGTGf

4. Treaties vs. Handshakes

In a true alliance (like NATO), an attack on one is an attack on all. Ukraine wants a legally binding, ironclad friendship backed by the U.S. Senate. However, the U.S. has carefully kept Ukraine at arm's length by utilizing Executive Agreements instead of formal treaties. By keeping the relationship informal, the U.S. retains the power to walk away or adjust its support based entirely on domestic political winds—leaving Ukraine feeling utilized but never truly protected.

That mismatch in expectations is exactly why the relationship has hit such a rocky patch. When one side feels they are sacrificing lives for a shared democratic cause, and the other side is looking at it through an economic ledger or a campaign promise, frustration is inevitable.

text:
You're losing ad dollars in ZIP codes your inventory can't reach

It's early Saturday afternoon, October 10, 2026, and I'm looking at one of my own listings from sixteen cities at once.

From my desk in Atlanta it looks fine. In stock, fulfilled by Amazon, Prime. I have checked it that way for as long as I have sold it, from my own ZIP code, the way every seller does. I look at the badge. I never look at whose name is next to it.

So I run the same lookup from Seattle, Boston, Denver, Dallas, Chicago, New York and ten more cities, and lay the results out in a table.

Seattle: Prime, two-day delivery. Boston: Prime, two-day delivery.

Denver: a different seller holds the Buy Box. No Prime badge. Delivery four to five days out.

Dallas: the same different seller. No Prime.

Chicago. Houston. Phoenix. Washington. New York. Los Angeles. Row after row, the same non-Prime seller sits in the Buy Box.

And then the part I did not expect. My own name is not in a single row. I have units of this product in Amazon's warehouses, and I am not winning the Buy Box anywhere on the map.

THE BUY BOX FOLLOWS THE INVENTORY

Nothing about that listing changed between cities. Same product, same page, same offers. What changed was where the shopper was standing.

Amazon picks the Featured Offer based on criteria it lists as "competitive pricing, delivery speed, and performance." Delivery speed depends on how far the nearest unit sits from the shopper. In Seattle and Boston, one seller's Prime inventory was close enough to promise two-day delivery. Everywhere else it wasn't, and a non-Prime offer won instead.

Amazon says this out loud in its developer docs: "Different offers can be featured based on other factors, including fulfillment capabilities to a specific customer." The listing you see from your ZIP code is one version of your listing. Every city gets its own.

WHERE THE AD DOLLARS GO

Losing the Buy Box costs you sales, but it rarely costs ad dollars. Sponsored Products only serve when you hold the Featured Offer, so in the cities where you've lost it, your ad mostly stops showing.

The expensive case is the quieter one: you keep the Buy Box everywhere, but your inventory is thin.

My second listing had one unit in stock. I owned the Buy Box in all sixteen cities. But in Seattle, Salt Lake City, Chicago, Detroit, Atlanta and Boston, the fastest delivery was four to eight days out on every reading, with no Prime-speed option at all.

At the time of writing, Sponsored Products can't be targeted by state or city. They run across the whole country. So a shopper in Chicago searches, sees your ad, and clicks. You pay for the click. Then they land on a page promising delivery in seven or eight days.

Andy Jassy, Amazon's CEO, described what happens next on the company's earnings call on August 3, 2023: "We have a lot of data that shows when we make faster delivery promises on a detail page, customers purchase more often, not just a little higher, meaningfully higher."

Flip that around and you have the leak. Every click from a city your inventory can't reach quickly is a click that converts worse. Your bids didn't change, your keywords didn't change, your listing didn't change, but your ACOS climbs. And nothing in your ad console tells you why, because the cause isn't in your ads. It's in where your inventory sits.

It gets worse right after a restock. A shipment can show as received while it is still sitting in one or two buildings, waiting to spread across the network. That is exactly when sellers tend to turn the budget back up.

HOW TO MAP YOUR OWN LISTING

Here's the check I ran. You can run it on your own listings.

1. Pick your thin listings first. Listings with deep stock mostly came back fast everywhere I looked. The regional gaps showed up on listings with a handful of units, or a fresh shipment that hadn't spread yet.

2. Check delivery from a spread of ZIP codes. Cover the coasts, the middle, and the cities where your buyers are. For each city, record three things: who holds the Buy Box, whether the offer shows Prime, and the fastest delivery date. I used RankGenius' Buy Box lookup with a ZIP code for this (disclosure: I have a personal stake in RankGenius), but any method that shows you the page as a shopper in that city sees it will work.

3. Read each city three times. A single reading can be off. Take three and trust the majority. Only call a city slow if it comes back slow at least twice.

4. Mark the map. Fast is next-day or two-day with a Prime promise. Slow is four days or more, or no Prime option. Note which cities have a different seller in the Buy Box.

WHAT TO DO WITH THE MAP

Pace the ads on patchy listings. If a listing is slow in a big part of the country, you're paying national prices for clicks that convert like a regional listing. Hold the budget, or keep it modest, until the map fills in.

Go deeper on stock. A listing with a handful of units can't be close to everyone. Sending more gives Amazon something to spread across its network. After the shipment is received, map again. "Received" and "distributed" are not the same thing.

Or choose where the next shipment goes, and know what it costs. At the time of writing, with Amazon-optimized shipment splits there's no placement fee, but Amazon decides where your inventory lands. With a minimal shipment split, you send everything to one location in a region you choose, and you pay a per-unit placement fee that varies by size tier and by region. If the map shows a hole in the West, sending your next shipment there is a real option. It just isn't free, so price it in Send to Amazon before you decide.

Working that out by hand is hours of spreadsheet work: the fee for each size tier and region, the split options, units on hand, and a map of which cities are slow. An AI assistant connected to live Amazon data can lay the options side by side in seconds, so your time goes into the decision instead of the arithmetic.

Then check the map again once it lands.

THE LISTING NOBODY SHOWS YOU

For years I checked my listings the same way: from my own ZIP code, on my own screen. Everything always looked fine.

It was fine, from there. The money was leaking from all the places I never looked.

▫️🚗 Mercedes CEO Warns EU Protectionism Could Raise Car Prices and Disrupt Global Supply Chains▫️

🔴 Mercedes CEO Sounds Alarm: Ola Källenius, CEO of Mercedes-Benz and president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), has warned that European Union efforts to protect domestic automakers could backfire by increasing manufacturing costs and disrupting international supply chains.

🏭 Made in Europe Strategy Under Fire: Källenius criticized proposed local production requirements that would encourage manufacturers to source more components within Europe. He argues that restricting access to international suppliers could make European vehicles more expensive and weaken their competitiveness.

🌍 Global Supply Chains at Risk: Modern vehicles contain thousands of components sourced from countries around the world. Källenius warned that forcing manufacturers to restructure these established networks could create inefficiencies, increase production expenses and complicate international trade.

🇨🇳 Growing Competition From China: The EU is pursuing stronger industrial protections amid increasing competition from Chinese automakers, particularly in electric vehicles. European policymakers argue that domestic production incentives are necessary to protect manufacturing jobs, strengthen economic security and reduce dependence on foreign suppliers.

🇺🇸 Warning Against Economic Isolation: Källenius emphasized that Europe cannot afford to isolate itself from major trading partners, including the United States, China, Japan and South Korea. He believes international cooperation remains essential to the European automotive industry's long term competitiveness.

🤝 Calls for Expanded Free Trade: Rather than introducing additional trade barriers, the Mercedes chief urged European leaders to accelerate trade agreements with India and South American countries. He argues that expanding market access and strengthening international partnerships would offer a more sustainable path to industrial growth.

💰 Potential Impact on Consumers: More restrictive sourcing requirements could increase the cost of producing vehicles, potentially pushing prices higher for European consumers. Automakers could also face reduced profit margins if they cannot pass additional expenses on to buyers.

⚖️ Europe Faces a Difficult Economic Tradeoff: The dispute highlights a growing divide between policymakers seeking greater industrial independence and manufacturers dependent on international trade. While protectionist measures could support European production and employment, industry leaders warn that poorly designed restrictions could undermine the very companies they are intended to protect.
