text:
"No punishment, in my opinion, is too great for the Man, who can build his greatness upon his Country's ruin." George Washington, Letter to Joseph Reed, December 12, 1778

Source: https://t.co/zN0xflWzP7

What can we learn?

George Washington wrote to Joseph Reed, who had just been elected president of Pennsylvania’s Supreme Executive Council and offered his congratulations regarding Reed's election and leadership role in Pennsylvania.

By late 1778, the American economy was devastated by severe inflation, causing a surge in "monopolizers, forestallers, and engrossers" who hoarded scarce goods to sell them at exorbitant prices to the public and the army.

Washington's letter was written to encourage Reed to crack down on these economic manipulators. He lamented that individual states had failed to hunt down these profiteers, whom he viewed as the "pests of society" and great enemies of the American cause, just as dangerous as British troops. 

In the letter, Washington vented his frustration over the lack of public virtue, writing that he wished "one of the most atrocious in each State was hung in Gibbets, up on a gallows five times as high as the one prepared by Haman" alongside his famous condemnation of building personal greatness upon national ruin.

Washington reflected on the biblical principle that personal gain built through betrayal of the common good is fundamentally evil—a conviction rooted in Scripture’s consistent condemnation of those who profit from others’ suffering. The principle appears throughout the Bible: in the prohibition against taking advantage of the vulnerable, in Jesus’s teaching that “no one can serve two masters” when wealth and righteousness conflict, and in the apostolic warning that the love of money is the root of all evil.

We saw this principle in action through British diplomat George Johnstone’s attempt to bribe American leaders, including Joseph Reed, with money and political office in exchange for undermining the revolutionary cause[1]. Reed’s response—“I am not worth purchasing, but, such as I am, the King of England is not rich enough to do it”—echoes Washington’s conviction. Both men embodied the biblical principle that personal integrity cannot be compromised for material advancement, particularly when doing so would harm one’s nation.

Washington’s leadership throughout the Revolution demonstrates this principle operationally. When victory seemed impossible, Washington “firmly clung to a belief in the providence of God,” writing that “he must be worse than an infidel that lacks faith” if he didn’t acknowledge God’s hand in events[2]. This faith-grounded perspective meant Washington viewed his role not as an opportunity for personal enrichment but as stewardship—a sacred trust to preserve the nation’s future rather than exploit its crisis for personal greatness. His moral severity toward those who would “build greatness upon his Country’s ruin” reflects the biblical conviction that leaders answer to God for how they wield power.

1. Benson Lossing, ed., Harper’s Encyclopedia of United States History (Medford, MA: Perseus Digital Library, n.d.).
2. R. J. L. and H. S. L., The Leadership Dynamic: A Biblical Model for Raising Effective Leaders (Wheaton, IL: Crossway Books, 2008).

Pete eliminated DEI offices and initiatives throughout the Department of Defense and directed the military back toward merit-based policies—placing qualifications, performance and readiness ahead of race or sex. The Pentagon later reported that the DEI-elimination directive had been implemented department-wide.  

He ordered a military-wide review of physical fitness, body composition and grooming standards. For combat jobs, he directed the services to develop physical standards based on the actual demands of the job rather than having different requirements based on sex.  

He welcomed back service members who had been separated over the COVID-19 vaccine mandate. The Pentagon said nearly 8,000 active-duty and reserve personnel had been involuntarily separated, and eligible troops were offered a route back, including restoration of rank and back pay in qualifying cases.  

Military recruiting and retention improved dramatically. Early in his tenure all five services met their February 2025 recruiting goals, and the Army reported reaching its 12-month retention goal six months early.  

He started attacking Pentagon waste and bureaucracy. In his first 100 days, the department identified billions of dollars for potential redirection, terminated hundreds of millions in contracts it considered unnecessary, and ordered billions more in reductions involving consulting and IT services so resources could be shifted toward military priorities.  

He pushed major acquisition reform because America’s weapons-buying system can take years to deliver new technology. He ordered reviews of major defense acquisition programs and emphasized faster software and weapons procurement so troops can receive useful technology sooner.  

He ordered the Army to move away from obsolete and redundant equipment and put more resources into long-range precision weapons, missile defense, cyber warfare, electronic warfare and counter-space capabilities.  

He accelerated drones and counter-drone technology. His Army transformation directive called for unmanned systems in every division by the end of 2026 and improved counter-drone capabilities down to maneuver units.  

He pushed artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing into military operations, including AI-assisted command-and-control systems and expanded use of technologies such as 3-D printing closer to operational units.  

He worked on rebuilding America’s defense industrial base—expanding ammunition production, strengthening domestic critical-mineral supplies and addressing shipbuilding and supply-chain weaknesses.  

He pushed America’s NATO allies to carry more of the cost of their own defense instead of relying so heavily on American taxpayers. NATO members subsequently committed to a new 5% defense-and-security spending target, although that was an achievement involving President Trump and the entire administration, not Hegseth alone.  

And he made his overall priority very clear: combat readiness, military standards, merit, accountability and deterrence.

text:
How was an ancient Egyptian soldier equipped for battle? ⚔️

During Egypt’s New Kingdom (c. 1550–1070 BCE), the army used a combination of spears, shields, bows, and curved swords known as the khopesh.

The spear was a practical weapon for infantry, while shields made from wood and animal hide offered protection. The khopesh, with its distinctive curved blade, became one of the most recognisable weapons associated with ancient Egypt.

But there’s an important detail often missed in modern illustrations: not every Egyptian soldier wore elaborate armour. Many ordinary infantrymen had relatively simple equipment, while more protective scale armour was associated with specialised troops and charioteers.

Linen garments and kilts were common, but the exact appearance of a soldier depended on the period, role, and status.

I find this fascinating because ancient military strength wasn’t just about weapons. It also depended on organisation, materials, and the ability to equip an army.
